## 1:7/q12 How is the pronoun in 'upon them' pronounced?  [عَلَيْهِمْ · readings]
- 1:7/q12/p1 Kasra on hāʾ and still mīm — NAHHAS reporting أهل المدينة: The people of Medina read ʿalayhim with kasra on hāʾ and a still mīm, a Najdi dialect. FARISI-HUJJA reporting عاصم وأبو عمرو والكسائي وابن عامر: Their kasra-hāʾ, still-mim reading deletes wāw because the plural mim itself prevents confusion with the dual, and deletion lightens speech. FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Plural mim always follows a kasra or damma, both heavy, unlike singular pronoun hāʾ, which can follow fatha or sukūn; this licenses still mim. THALABI: The common reading has ʿalayhim with kasra on hāʾ and a still mīm. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting الجمهور: The majority read the hāʾ of ʿalayhim with kasra and leave the mīm quiescent. SAMIN-DURR: The pronoun hāʾ is normally damma, but non-Hijazis use kasra after a silent yāʾ or kasra; mīm is usually silent before a vowel and kasra before silence when hāʾ is kasra. IBNASHUR-FULL reporting الجمهور: Most readers kasra the pronoun hāʾ after a silent yāʾ to avoid heaviness; this is the dialect of Qays, Tamīm, and Saʿd b. Bakr. [7 notes: NAHHAS(أهل المدينة); FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي,عاصم وأبو عمرو والكسائي وابن عامر); THALABI; ABUHAYYAN-FULL(الجمهور); SAMIN-DURR; IBNASHUR-FULL(الجمهور)]
- 1:7/q12/p2 Ḍamma on hāʾ and still mīm — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting حمزة: Hamza reads ʿalayhim with ḍamma on hāʾ and a quiescent mīm; he does likewise for ladayhim and ilayhim. TABRISI reporting حمزة ويعقوب: Hamza pronounces the hā in ʿalayhim and its parallels with ḍamma and the mīm quiescent; Yaqub uses ḍamma on hā preceded by a silent yā in duals and masculine and feminine plurals. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting حمزة: Among ten reported forms of ʿalayhim, Ḥamza reads the hāʾ with ḍamma and the mīm quiescent. IBNASHUR reporting ورش: Warsh lengthens a damma on the plural mīm when a hamza follows, but not before ghayr here; all readers leave the mīm silent at pause. [4 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(حمزة); TABRISI(حمزة ويعقوب); ABUHAYYAN-FULL(حمزة); IBNASHUR(ورش)]
- 1:7/q12/p3 Ten transmitted forms vary both vowels and connecting glides — IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting ابن الأنباري: Ibn al-Anbārī says grammarians record ten forms of ʿalayhim: six attested among reciters, with varying hāʾ/mīm vowels and added yāʾ or wāw, and four transmitted from Arabs. QURTUBI: Ten alayhim forms include six transmitted reader forms (varying hāʾ/mīm vowels, added yāʾ or wāw) and four further forms transmitted from Arabs: عليهُمِ, عليهُم, عليهِمُ, عليهِمِ. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting الأعرج والخفاف عن أبي عمرو: Abū Ḥayyān lists forms that lengthen the mīm with wāw or omit it, and other combinations of hāʾ and mīm vowels, among the ten reported ʿalayhim readings. [3 notes: IBNJAWZI-ZAD(ابن الأنباري); QURTUBI; ABUHAYYAN-FULL(الأعرج والخفاف عن أبي عمرو)]
- 1:7/q12/p4 The hāʾ in ʿalayhim may carry ḍamma or kasra, the two forms used by most readers; a form with an added wāw is also possible. — ZAJJAJ: The hāʾ in ʿalayhim may carry ḍamma or kasra, the two forms used by most readers; a form with an added wāw is also possible. [1 notes: ZAJJAJ]
- 1:7/q12/p5 Al-ḍāllīn is coordinated with al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim; lā is allowed because ghayr already carries negation, as in ghayr ḍārib meaning “not striking.” — ZAJJAJ: Al-ḍāllīn is coordinated with al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim; lā is allowed because ghayr already carries negation, as in ghayr ḍārib meaning “not striking.” [1 notes: ZAJJAJ]
- 1:7/q12/p6 Ibn Kathīr connects plural mīm to wāw whether the preceding hāʾ is kasra or ḍamma. — IBNMUJAHID reporting ابن كثير: Ibn Kathīr connects plural mīm to wāw whether the preceding hāʾ is kasra or ḍamma. [1 notes: IBNMUJAHID(ابن كثير)]
- 1:7/q12/p7 Kasra on hāʾ, raised mīm, and connecting wāw — IBNMUJAHID reporting عاصم وأبو عمرو وابن عامر والكسائي: These readers keep hāʾ kasra and mīm sukūn; the dual alif already distinguishes two, while plural mīm distinguishes many, so wāw can be omitted for ease. [1 notes: IBNMUJAHID(عاصم وأبو عمرو وابن عامر والكسائي)]
- 1:7/q12/p8 Ibn Abī Isḥāq reads ʿalayhimu with a ḍamma and retained wāw, the original form. — NAHHAS reporting ابن أبي إسحاق: Ibn Abī Isḥāq reads ʿalayhimu with a ḍamma and retained wāw, the original form. [1 notes: NAHHAS(ابن أبي إسحاق)]
- 1:7/q12/p9 Al-Ḥasan reads ʿalayhimī with kasra and a retained yāʾ, avoiding yāʾ next to ḍamma and changing wāw after kasra. — NAHHAS reporting الحسن: Al-Ḥasan reads ʿalayhimī with kasra and a retained yāʾ, avoiding yāʾ next to ḍamma and changing wāw after kasra. [1 notes: NAHHAS(الحسن)]
- 1:7/q12/p10 Al-Aʿraj reads ʿalayhimu with kasra on hāʾ and a retained wāw. — NAHHAS reporting الأعرج: Al-Aʿraj reads ʿalayhimu with kasra on hāʾ and a retained wāw. [1 notes: NAHHAS(الأعرج)]
- 1:7/q12/p11 Ḥamza alone uses a damma on the hāʾ and a still mim in ʿalayhim, ladayhim, and ilayhim; the others use a kasra on hāʾ. — FARISI-HUJJA: Ḥamza alone uses a damma on the hāʾ and a still mim in ʿalayhim, ladayhim, and ilayhim; the others use a kasra on hāʾ. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA]
- 1:7/q12/p12 Ibn Kathīr joins the plural mim to a wāw after either a kasra or damma on hāʾ. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting ابن كثير: Ibn Kathīr joins the plural mim to a wāw after either a kasra or damma on hāʾ. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(ابن كثير)]
- 1:7/q12/p13 They preserve kasra on hāʾ because it is the same pronoun hāʾ as in ʿalayhi and its cause for kasra remains unchanged after mim is added. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting عاصم وأبو عمرو والكسائي وابن عامر: They preserve kasra on hāʾ because it is the same pronoun hāʾ as in ʿalayhi and its cause for kasra remains unchanged after mim is added. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(عاصم وأبو عمرو والكسائي وابن عامر)]
- 1:7/q12/p14 Ḥamza limits damma to these three forms because before a visible noun, ʿalā, ladā, and ilā end in alif and hāʾ is not kasra after alif. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting حمزة: Ḥamza limits damma to these three forms because before a visible noun, ʿalā, ladā, and ilā end in alif and hāʾ is not kasra after alif. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(حمزة)]
- 1:7/q12/p15 When the next word begins with sukūn, kasra mim is preferred as lighter; it restores an original vowel, and Ḥasan’s alayhimi preserves the connecting yāʾ. — FARISI-HUJJA: When the next word begins with sukūn, kasra mim is preferred as lighter; it restores an original vowel, and Ḥasan’s alayhimi preserves the connecting yāʾ. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA]
- 1:7/q12/p16 The attachment of weak vowels to kāf and hāʾ further supports kasra in ʿalayhim because hāʾ has many similar features. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The attachment of weak vowels to kāf and hāʾ further supports kasra in ʿalayhim because hāʾ has many similar features. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q12/p17 An objection says damma is the default for genitive pronoun hāʾ, as its accusative counterpart is damma and damma works in more environments than kasra. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: An objection says damma is the default for genitive pronoun hāʾ, as its accusative counterpart is damma and damma works in more environments than kasra. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q12/p18 Because diminutive and broken plural formation are analogous processes, adjacent kasra may replace damma in a plural; this supports kasra in ʿalayhim for harmony and ease. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Because diminutive and broken plural formation are analogous processes, adjacent kasra may replace damma in a plural; this supports kasra in ʿalayhim for harmony and ease. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q12/p19 These analogies lead to the reading that deletes the weak glide after the plural mim rather than counting moving hāʾ as a separator. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: These analogies lead to the reading that deletes the weak glide after the plural mim rather than counting moving hāʾ as a separator. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q12/p20 Deleting waw or yāʾ after ʿalayhim is light and unambiguous because these suffixes are often dropped, even when nothing remains to mark them. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Deleting waw or yāʾ after ʿalayhim is light and unambiguous because these suffixes are often dropped, even when nothing remains to mark them. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q12/p21 Since plural mim can take alif, wāw, or yāʾ and alif is not deleted, loss of wāw or yāʾ creates no ambiguity. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Since plural mim can take alif, wāw, or yāʾ and alif is not deleted, loss of wāw or yāʾ creates no ambiguity. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q12/p22 Ḥamza’s damma reading treats the derived yāʾ as nonessential, like alif, so hāʾ takes damma as it does after alif; forms ʿalāk and ilāk support this. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Ḥamza’s damma reading treats the derived yāʾ as nonessential, like alif, so hāʾ takes damma as it does after alif; forms ʿalāk and ilāk support this. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q12/p23 Ṭayyiʾ uses yāʾ where other dialects use final alif in both pause and liaison, as in afʿay for afʿā; this supports treating yāʾ in ʿalayhim like alif. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Ṭayyiʾ uses yāʾ where other dialects use final alif in both pause and liaison, as in afʿay for afʿā; this supports treating yāʾ in ʿalayhim like alif. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q12/p24 A derived letter can retain the behavior of its source: yāʾ originating from alif in ʿalayhim is treated as alif, so hāʾ is rounded as after alif. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: A derived letter can retain the behavior of its source: yāʾ originating from alif in ʿalayhim is treated as alif, so hāʾ is rounded as after alif. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q12/p25 Therefore the yāʾ in ʿalayhim may behave as the alif from which it derives, supporting Ḥamza’s damma on hāʾ. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Therefore the yāʾ in ʿalayhim may behave as the alif from which it derives, supporting Ḥamza’s damma on hāʾ. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q12/p26 Umar ibn al-Khattab and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr read min an‘amta alayhim instead of alladhina an‘amta alayhim. — MAWARDI reporting عمر بن الخطاب وعبد الله بن الزبير: Umar ibn al-Khattab and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr read min an‘amta alayhim instead of alladhina an‘amta alayhim. [1 notes: MAWARDI(عمر بن الخطاب وعبد الله بن الزبير)]
- 1:7/q12/p27 They read sirat man anʿamta ʿalayhim instead of sirat alladhina anʿamta ʿalayhim. — MAWARDI-FULL reporting عمر بن الخطاب وعبد الله بن الزبير: They read sirat man anʿamta ʿalayhim instead of sirat alladhina anʿamta ʿalayhim. [1 notes: MAWARDI-FULL(عمر بن الخطاب وعبد الله بن الزبير)]
- 1:7/q12/p28 The hāʾ in ʿalayhim may be pronounced with either kasra or ḍamma; kasra follows because yāʾ is related to kasra and the lighter transition is preferred. — WAHIDI-BASIT: The hāʾ in ʿalayhim may be pronounced with either kasra or ḍamma; kasra follows because yāʾ is related to kasra and the lighter transition is preferred. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT]
- 1:7/q12/p29 Because hāʾ is a weak barrier, the preceding kasra acts as if it directly preceded the added wāw; that explains kasra in ʿalayhi and its retention in ʿalayhim. — WAHIDI-BASIT: Because hāʾ is a weak barrier, the preceding kasra acts as if it directly preceded the added wāw; that explains kasra in ʿalayhi and its retention in ʿalayhim. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT]
- 1:7/q12/p30 Ibn al-Sarrāj explains the plural mīm's sukūn as lightening: the dual's alif already signals two, while the indispensable plural mīm lets speakers drop wāw without ambiguity. — WAHIDI-BASIT reporting ابن السراج: Ibn al-Sarrāj explains the plural mīm's sukūn as lightening: the dual's alif already signals two, while the indispensable plural mīm lets speakers drop wāw without ambiguity. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT(ابن السراج)]
- 1:7/q12/p31 Warsh from Nāfiʿ pronounces plural mīm with ḍamma and links a following initial hamza with wāw; dropping hamza and moving its vowel requires the mīm to recover its original ḍamma and lengthen. — WAHIDI-BASIT reporting ورش عن نافع: Warsh from Nāfiʿ pronounces plural mīm with ḍamma and links a following initial hamza with wāw; dropping hamza and moving its vowel requires the mīm to recover its original ḍamma and lengthen. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT(ورش عن نافع)]
- 1:7/q12/p32 Ḥamza reads the hāʾ in ʿalayhim, ilayhim, and ladayhim with ḍamma throughout the Qur’an. — JISHUMI reporting حمزة: Ḥamza reads the hāʾ in ʿalayhim, ilayhim, and ladayhim with ḍamma throughout the Qur’an. [1 notes: JISHUMI(حمزة)]
- 1:7/q12/p33 Yaʿqūb gives ḍamma to each hāʾ preceded by a vowelless yāʾ, including forms such as ʿalayhim and fīhim, and reportedly also where that yāʾ drops. — JISHUMI reporting يعقوب: Yaʿqūb gives ḍamma to each hāʾ preceded by a vowelless yāʾ, including forms such as ʿalayhim and fīhim, and reportedly also where that yāʾ drops. [1 notes: JISHUMI(يعقوب)]
- 1:7/q12/p34 Ibn Kathir and Abu Jaʿfar lengthen the plural mīm in connected reading unless a quiescent letter follows, in which case they do not lengthen it. — BAGHAWI reporting ابن كثير وأبو جعفر: Ibn Kathir and Abu Jaʿfar lengthen the plural mīm in connected reading unless a quiescent letter follows, in which case they do not lengthen it. [1 notes: BAGHAWI(ابن كثير وأبو جعفر)]
- 1:7/q12/p35 Nafiʿ allows a choice in the plural mīm's lengthening. — BAGHAWI reporting نافع: Nafiʿ allows a choice in the plural mīm's lengthening. [1 notes: BAGHAWI(نافع)]
- 1:7/q12/p36 Hamza pronounces the hāʾ in ʿalayhim, ladayhim, and ilayhim with ḍamma. — BAGHAWI reporting حمزة: Hamza pronounces the hāʾ in ʿalayhim, ladayhim, and ilayhim with ḍamma. [1 notes: BAGHAWI(حمزة)]
- 1:7/q12/p37 Hamza reads the hāʾ of ʿalayhim, ladayhim, and ilayhim with ḍamma; Yaʿqub does so for dual and plural forms preceded by a silent yāʾ, with a stated exception.; cited verses: 60:12 — BAGHAWI-FULL reporting حمزة ويعقوب: Hamza reads the hāʾ of ʿalayhim, ladayhim, and ilayhim with ḍamma; Yaʿqub does so for dual and plural forms preceded by a silent yāʾ, with a stated exception. | mentions 60:12 [1 notes: BAGHAWI-FULL(حمزة ويعقوب)]
- 1:7/q12/p38 Ibn Kathir and Abu Jaʿfar fully prolong the plural mīm in connected recitation unless a following consonant is silent; Nafiʿ may choose. — BAGHAWI-FULL reporting ابن كثير وأبو جعفر: Ibn Kathir and Abu Jaʿfar fully prolong the plural mīm in connected recitation unless a following consonant is silent; Nafiʿ may choose. [1 notes: BAGHAWI-FULL(ابن كثير وأبو جعفر)]
- 1:7/q12/p39 Ibn Masud reads sirat man anʿamta ʿalayhim. — KASHSHAF reporting ابن مسعود: Ibn Masud reads sirat man anʿamta ʿalayhim. [1 notes: KASHSHAF(ابن مسعود)]
- 1:7/q12/p40 Al-Hasan and ʿAmr ibn Faʾid read ʿalayhimi with a final kasra on the mīm. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting الحسن وعمرو بن فائد: Al-Hasan and ʿAmr ibn Faʾid read ʿalayhimi with a final kasra on the mīm. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(الحسن وعمرو بن فائد)]
- 1:7/q12/p41 Before a consonant, ʿAsim, Ibn Kathir, and Nafiʿ keep hāʾ kasra and give mīm ḍamma, as in “upon them is humiliation.”; cited verses: 2:61, 3:112 — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting عاصم وابن كثير ونافع: Before a consonant, ʿAsim, Ibn Kathir, and Nafiʿ keep hāʾ kasra and give mīm ḍamma, as in “upon them is humiliation.” | mentions 2:61, 3:112 [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(عاصم وابن كثير ونافع)]
- 1:7/q12/p42 The word maghdūb need not be pluralized because the plural pronoun in ʿalayhim already marks those who incur anger. — TABRISI: The word maghdūb need not be pluralized because the plural pronoun in ʿalayhim already marks those who incur anger. [1 notes: TABRISI]
- 1:7/q12/p43 The ḍamma on hā in ʿalayhim restores the original form hum; al-Sarraj calls it the old recitation and a Qurayshi and Hijazi dialect. — TABRISI reporting السراج: The ḍamma on hā in ʿalayhim restores the original form hum; al-Sarraj calls it the old recitation and a Qurayshi and Hijazi dialect. [1 notes: TABRISI(السراج)]
- 1:7/q12/p44 Most readers pronounce the pronoun in ʿalayhim with kasra, as in ladayhim and ilayhim. — IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting الأكثرون: Most readers pronounce the pronoun in ʿalayhim with kasra, as in ladayhim and ilayhim. [1 notes: IBNJAWZI-ZAD(الأكثرون)]
- 1:7/q12/p45 Ibn Kathīr reads ghayr in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in ʿalayhim, governed by anʿamta. — BAYDAWI reporting ابن كثير: Ibn Kathīr reads ghayr in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in ʿalayhim, governed by anʿamta. [1 notes: BAYDAWI(ابن كثير)]
- 1:7/q12/p46 Ibn al-Anbārī records ten pronunciations of ʿalayhim, including variations in hāʾ and mīm vowels and added wāw or yāʾ; some were read in Qur'anic recitation. — SAMIN-DURR reporting أبو بكر ابن الأنباري: Ibn al-Anbārī records ten pronunciations of ʿalayhim, including variations in hāʾ and mīm vowels and added wāw or yāʾ; some were read in Qur'anic recitation. [1 notes: SAMIN-DURR(أبو بكر ابن الأنباري)]
- 1:7/q12/p47 Ghayr is also read in the accusative as a circumstantial from alladhīna or ʿalayhim, or as a disjoint exception; al-Farrāʾ rejects the latter because lā lacks a preceding negation. — SAMIN-DURR: Ghayr is also read in the accusative as a circumstantial from alladhīna or ʿalayhim, or as a disjoint exception; al-Farrāʾ rejects the latter because lā lacks a preceding negation. [1 notes: SAMIN-DURR]
- 1:7/q12/p48 Al-Zamakhshari reports an accusative circumstantial reading of ghayr, attributed to the Prophet and ʿUmar and also transmitted from Ibn Kathir; its circumstantial referent is the pronoun in ʿalayhim. — IBNKATHIR reporting الزمخشري: Al-Zamakhshari reports an accusative circumstantial reading of ghayr, attributed to the Prophet and ʿUmar and also transmitted from Ibn Kathir; its circumstantial referent is the pronoun in ʿalayhim. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR(الزمخشري)]
- 1:7/q12/p49 Yaqub pronounces the hāʾ of dual and plural pronouns with ḍamma after silent yāʾ; Hamza agrees for ʿalayhim, ilayhim, and ladayhim. — NASHR reporting يعقوب: Yaqub pronounces the hāʾ of dual and plural pronouns with ḍamma after silent yāʾ; Hamza agrees for ʿalayhim, ilayhim, and ladayhim. [1 notes: NASHR(يعقوب)]
- 1:7/q12/p50 Before a following vowel, Ibn Kathir and Abu Jaʿfar join plural mīm with a wāw; Qalun varies by route, with many authorities selecting sukūn via Abu Nishit and others selecting ṣila via al-Hulwani. — NASHR reporting ابن كثير وأبو جعفر وقالون: Before a following vowel, Ibn Kathir and Abu Jaʿfar join plural mīm with a wāw; Qalun varies by route, with many authorities selecting sukūn via Abu Nishit and others selecting ṣila via al-Hulwani. [1 notes: NASHR(ابن كثير وأبو جعفر وقالون)]
- 1:7/q12/p51 Ḍamma on hāʾ and mīm with connecting wāw — NASHR reporting عبد الرحمن بن هرمز الأعرج ومسلم بن جندب وعيسى بن عمر الثقفي البصري وعبد الله بن يزيد القصير: These readers pronounce the hāʾ of ʿalayhim with ḍamma and connect the mīm with a wāw. [1 notes: NASHR(عبد الرحمن بن هرمز الأعرج ومسلم بن جندب وعيسى بن عمر الثقفي البصري وعبد الله بن يزيد القصير)]
- 1:7/q12/p52 Al-Akhfash describes three further theoretically permissible dialects for ʿalayhim; none of the readers differs about using sukūn when pausing. — NASHR reporting أبو الحسن الأخفش: Al-Akhfash describes three further theoretically permissible dialects for ʿalayhim; none of the readers differs about using sukūn when pausing. [1 notes: NASHR(أبو الحسن الأخفش)]
- 1:7/q12/p53 Umar read “ṣirāṭ man anʿamta ʿalayhim” and repeated “ghayr” before “al-ḍāllīn.” — DURR reporting عمر بن الخطاب: Umar read “ṣirāṭ man anʿamta ʿalayhim” and repeated “ghayr” before “al-ḍāllīn.” [1 notes: DURR(عمر بن الخطاب)]
- 1:7/q12/p54 ʿIkrima and al-Aswad read “ṣirāṭ man anʿamta ʿalayhim” and repeated “ghayr.” — DURR reporting عكرمة والأسود: ʿIkrima and al-Aswad read “ṣirāṭ man anʿamta ʿalayhim” and repeated “ghayr.” [1 notes: DURR(عكرمة والأسود)]
- 1:7/q12/p55 Kasra on both consonants with connecting yāʾ — DURR-FULL reporting الحسن: Al-Hasan read “alayhim” with kasra on the ha and mim and an added ya. [1 notes: DURR-FULL(الحسن)]
- 1:7/q12/p56 Ibn Masʿūd and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read ṣirāṭ man anʿamta ʿalayhim; this is also transmitted from ʿUmar and the Ahl al-Bayt. — ALUSI: Ibn Masʿūd and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read ṣirāṭ man anʿamta ʿalayhim; this is also transmitted from ʿUmar and the Ahl al-Bayt. [1 notes: ALUSI]
- 1:7/q12/p57 ʿUmar read ghayra in the accusative; it is also transmitted irregularly from Ibn Kathir, most plausibly as a circumstantial accusative referring to the pronoun in “upon them.” — ALUSI-FULL reporting عمر إبن الخطاب: ʿUmar read ghayra in the accusative; it is also transmitted irregularly from Ibn Kathir, most plausibly as a circumstantial accusative referring to the pronoun in “upon them.” [1 notes: ALUSI-FULL(عمر إبن الخطاب)]
- 1:7/q12/p58 Ḥamza dammas the hāʾ in ʿalayhim, ilayhim, and ladayhim only, while Yaʿqūb dammas it in every pronoun of this class; the former follows a Quraysh and Ḥijāzī dialect. — IBNASHUR reporting حمزة ويعقوب: Ḥamza dammas the hāʾ in ʿalayhim, ilayhim, and ladayhim only, while Yaʿqūb dammas it in every pronoun of this class; the former follows a Quraysh and Ḥijāzī dialect. [1 notes: IBNASHUR(حمزة ويعقوب)]
- 1:7/q12/p59 At pause-free connection before a vowel, most readers leave the plural mīm silent; Ibn Kathīr, Abū Jaʿfar, and Qālūn in one transmission lengthen its damma, a dialect also illustrated by Labīd. — IBNASHUR reporting الجمهور وابن كثير وأبو جعفر وقالون: At pause-free connection before a vowel, most readers leave the plural mīm silent; Ibn Kathīr, Abū Jaʿfar, and Qālūn in one transmission lengthen its damma, a dialect also illustrated by Labīd. [1 notes: IBNASHUR(الجمهور وابن كثير وأبو جعفر وقالون)]
- 1:7/q12/p60 Most readers leave the plural mīm silent before a following vowel; Ibn Kathīr, Abū Jaʿfar, and Qālūn in one transmission lengthen its ḍamma. — IBNASHUR-FULL reporting الجمهور: Most readers leave the plural mīm silent before a following vowel; Ibn Kathīr, Abū Jaʿfar, and Qālūn in one transmission lengthen its ḍamma. [1 notes: IBNASHUR-FULL(الجمهور)]
- 1:7/q12/p61 Labīd's verse وهمو فوارسها وهم حكامها witnesses the dialect with a lengthened plural mīm; Warsh lengthens it only before hamza, and all readers silence it at pause. — IBNASHUR-FULL reporting لبيد: Labīd's verse وهمو فوارسها وهم حكامها witnesses the dialect with a lengthened plural mīm; Warsh lengthens it only before hamza, and all readers silence it at pause. ## 1:7/q13 What does 'other than' mean and how definite is it?  [غَيْرِ · meaning]
- 1:7/q13/p1 The people under divine anger are the Jews, whom God turned into apes and pigs; the requested path is other than their religion. — MUQATIL: The people under divine anger are the Jews, whom God turned into apes and pigs; the requested path is other than their religion. [1 notes: MUQATIL]
- 1:7/q13/p2 Sībawayh analyzes ghayr in 1:7 as an adjective meaning other than, not as an exceptive construction. — SIBAWAYH: Sībawayh analyzes ghayr in 1:7 as an adjective meaning other than, not as an exceptive construction. [1 notes: SIBAWAYH]
- 1:7/q13/p3 Labīd's phrase غير الجمل supplies a poetic example of ghayr used descriptively to mean other than the camel. — SIBAWAYH: Labīd's phrase غير الجمل supplies a poetic example of ghayr used descriptively to mean other than the camel. [1 notes: SIBAWAYH]
- 1:7/q13/p4 Genitive ghayri is an adjective of alladhīna, not of the pronoun in ʿalayhim; its definite annexation permits this description because neither expression denotes a specified person. — FARRA: Genitive ghayri is an adjective of alladhīna, not of the pronoun in ʿalayhim; its definite annexation permits this description because neither expression denotes a specified person. [1 notes: FARRA]
- 1:7/q13/p5 Ghayri can be accusative as a detached description of ʿalayhim, or genitive after repeating ṣirāṭ as “the path of those other than …”. — FARRA: Ghayri can be accusative as a detached description of ʿalayhim, or genitive after repeating ṣirāṭ as “the path of those other than …”. [1 notes: FARRA]
- 1:7/q13/p6 In wa-lā al-ḍāllīn, ghayr means lā, so lā is repeated; if ghayr meant “other than,” repeating lā would be ungrammatical. — FARRA: In wa-lā al-ḍāllīn, ghayr means lā, so lā is repeated; if ghayr meant “other than,” repeating lā would be ungrammatical. [1 notes: FARRA]
- 1:7/q13/p7 Ghayr al-maghḍūbi can be an adjective for those blessed, though ghayr and mithl are ordinarily used with indefinites and can modify definite forms that carry an indefinite sense. — AKHFASH: Ghayr al-maghḍūbi can be an adjective for those blessed, though ghayr and mithl are ordinarily used with indefinites and can modify definite forms that carry an indefinite sense. [1 notes: AKHFASH]
- 1:7/q13/p8 Ghayr may alternatively be accusative as a circumstantial expression because it is indefinite while its antecedent is definite. — AKHFASH: Ghayr may alternatively be accusative as a circumstantial expression because it is indefinite while its antecedent is definite. [1 notes: AKHFASH]
- 1:7/q13/p9 On one parsing, ghayr is an adjective of alladhīna: the relative phrase is not a specific proper-name-like definite, so an indefinite adjective can describe it. — TAB: On one parsing, ghayr is an adjective of alladhīna: the relative phrase is not a specific proper-name-like definite, so an indefinite adjective can describe it. [1 notes: TAB]
- 1:7/q13/p10 The first genitive parse makes ghayr an adjective for alladhīna: the relative phrase is not a fully specified proper name but indefinite-like, so it can take this adjective. — TAB-FULL: The first genitive parse makes ghayr an adjective for alladhīna: the relative phrase is not a fully specified proper name but indefinite-like, so it can take this adjective. [1 notes: TAB-FULL]
- 1:7/q13/p11 The same Basran analysis takes ghayr as meaning other than, so the favored are those other than the objects of wrath and the astray. — TAB-FULL reporting بعض أهل البصرة: The same Basran analysis takes ghayr as meaning other than, so the favored are those other than the objects of wrath and the astray. [1 notes: TAB-FULL(بعض أهل البصرة)]
- 1:7/q13/p12 He prefers the Kufan analysis: lā cannot begin as an omitted negative or coordinate with other than or an exception; since ghayr can mean exception, negation, or other than, the only valid reading here is negation, making… — TAB-FULL: He prefers the Kufan analysis: lā cannot begin as an omitted negative or coordinate with other than or an exception; since ghayr can mean exception, negation, or other than, the only valid reading here is negation, making the verse ask to avoid both groups. [1 notes: TAB-FULL+]
- 1:7/q13/p13 In Arabic, anyone deviating from the intended road is astray; Christians are so called because they miss the truth and take a religious route other than the straight one. — TAB-FULL: In Arabic, anyone deviating from the intended road is astray; Christians are so called because they miss the truth and take a religious route other than the straight one. [1 notes: TAB-FULL]
- 1:7/q13/p14 With genitive ghayr, one analysis makes it a substitute for alladhīna, yielding “the path of those other than the angered.” — ZAJJAJ: With genitive ghayr, one analysis makes it a substitute for alladhīna, yielding “the path of those other than the angered.” [1 notes: ZAJJAJ]
- 1:7/q13/p15 Alternatively, genitive ghayr qualifies alladhīna; although ghayr usually describes an indefinite noun, alladhīna here denotes a category rather than particular people. — ZAJJAJ: Alternatively, genitive ghayr qualifies alladhīna; although ghayr usually describes an indefinite noun, alladhīna here denotes a category rather than particular people. [1 notes: ZAJJAJ]
- 1:7/q13/p16 Accusative ghayr can instead be a circumstantial, meaning the path of those blessed, not angered. — ZAJJAJ: Accusative ghayr can instead be a circumstantial, meaning the path of those blessed, not angered. [1 notes: ZAJJAJ]
- 1:7/q13/p17 Al-ḍāllīn is coordinated with al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim; lā is allowed because ghayr already carries negation, as in ghayr ḍārib meaning “not striking.” — ZAJJAJ: Al-ḍāllīn is coordinated with al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim; lā is allowed because ghayr already carries negation, as in ghayr ḍārib meaning “not striking.” [1 notes: ZAJJAJ]
- 1:7/q13/p18 Ghayr functions as an adjective for alladhīna despite the usual definiteness mismatch, because alladhīna here is not a fully specified definite but means whoever is truthful rather than lying. — THALABI: Ghayr functions as an adjective for alladhīna despite the usual definiteness mismatch, because alladhīna here is not a fully specified definite but means whoever is truthful rather than lying. [1 notes: THALABI]
- 1:7/q13/p19 The intended sense is ‘other than the path of those upon whom You were angry.’ — THALABI: The intended sense is ‘other than the path of those upon whom You were angry.’ [1 notes: THALABI]
- 1:7/q13/p20 Al-Zajjāj says lā may coordinate with ghayr because ghayr already carries negation, effectively meaning neither those angered nor those astray; this is not possible when ghayr means ‘other than.’ — THALABI reporting الزجاج: Al-Zajjāj says lā may coordinate with ghayr because ghayr already carries negation, effectively meaning neither those angered nor those astray; this is not possible when ghayr means ‘other than.’ [1 notes: THALABI(الزجاج)]
- 1:7/q13/p21 Ghayr may instead be accusative as a circumstantial expression or an exception meaning except those under wrath; as a circumstantial phrase it means not those under wrath. — WAHIDI-BASIT: Ghayr may instead be accusative as a circumstantial expression or an exception meaning except those under wrath; as a circumstantial phrase it means not those under wrath. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT]
- 1:7/q13/p22 The author chooses genitive: although ghayr and mithl are usually indefinite even when annexed to a definite word, a known thing with one known opposite makes ghayr definite. — WAHIDI-BASIT: The author chooses genitive: although ghayr and mithl are usually indefinite even when annexed to a definite word, a known thing with one known opposite makes ghayr definite. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT+]
- 1:7/q13/p23 If a known thing has one known opposite, ghayr annexed to that opposite is definite, as in movement versus stillness. — WAHIDI-BASIT: If a known thing has one known opposite, ghayr annexed to that opposite is definite, as in movement versus stillness. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT]
- 1:7/q13/p24 As apposition, ghayr has a clear meaning whether construed definite or indefinite, since both definite and indefinite apposition are accepted. — WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب الحجة: As apposition, ghayr has a clear meaning whether construed definite or indefinite, since both definite and indefinite apposition are accepted. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT(صاحب الحجة)]
- 1:7/q13/p25 As an adjective, ghayr can modify alladhīna here only because the relative phrase does not single out a particular group, making it like an indefinite description. — WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب الحجة: As an adjective, ghayr can modify alladhīna here only because the relative phrase does not single out a particular group, making it like an indefinite description. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT(صاحب الحجة)]
- 1:7/q13/p26 In the verse, ghayr al-maghḍūb describes the favored people and is definite because one favored with faith is not under wrath. — WAHIDI-BASIT: In the verse, ghayr al-maghḍūb describes the favored people and is definite because one favored with faith is not under wrath. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT]
- 1:7/q13/p27 “Not those angered” means a path other than that of those God wills to punish for disobedience. — BAGHAWI: “Not those angered” means a path other than that of those God wills to punish for disobedience. [1 notes: BAGHAWI]
- 1:7/q13/p28 Here ghayr means “not” and lā means “other than,” allowing coordination; when ghayr means “except,” it cannot be coordinated with lā, as in the rejected phrase “I have Abdullah except Zayd.” — BAGHAWI: Here ghayr means “not” and lā means “other than,” allowing coordination; when ghayr means “except,” it cannot be coordinated with lā, as in the rejected phrase “I have Abdullah except Zayd.” [1 notes: BAGHAWI]
- 1:7/q13/p29 Here ghayr functions as ‘not,’ which permits coordination with lā; if it meant ‘other than,’ such coordination would be ungrammatical. — BAGHAWI-FULL: Here ghayr functions as ‘not,’ which permits coordination with lā; if it meant ‘other than,’ such coordination would be ungrammatical. [1 notes: BAGHAWI-FULL]
- 1:7/q13/p30 Ghayr can modify the definite relative phrase because it is undelimited and the angry and astray are opposites of the blessed. — KASHSHAF: Ghayr can modify the definite relative phrase because it is undelimited and the angry and astray are opposites of the blessed. [1 notes: KASHSHAF]
- 1:7/q13/p31 Ghayr can be appositive to those blessed, meaning they are spared God's anger and error. — KASHSHAF: Ghayr can be appositive to those blessed, meaning they are spared God's anger and error. [1 notes: KASHSHAF]
- 1:7/q13/p32 Ghayr can qualify the definite phrase because alladhina is not temporally delimited and the contrary identities of the two groups remove its ambiguity; it can also be accusative as a circumstantial phrase. — KASHSHAF-FULL: Ghayr can qualify the definite phrase because alladhina is not temporally delimited and the contrary identities of the two groups remove its ambiguity; it can also be accusative as a circumstantial phrase. [1 notes: KASHSHAF-FULL]
- 1:7/q13/p33 On the genitive reading, ghayr can be an appositive to الذين or an adjective to an indefinite, since الذين here is not specifically singled out. — IBNATIYYA reporting أبو علي: On the genitive reading, ghayr can be an appositive to الذين or an adjective to an indefinite, since الذين here is not specifically singled out. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q13/p34 Ibn al-Sarrāj argues that ghayr plus its definite complement is definite here: an understood, unique opposite makes “other than the recipients of favor” identifiable. — IBNATIYYA reporting أبو بكر بن السراج: Ibn al-Sarrāj argues that ghayr plus its definite complement is definite here: an understood, unique opposite makes “other than the recipients of favor” identifiable. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA(أبو بكر بن السراج)]
- 1:7/q13/p35 Ordinarily ghayr and mithl remain indefinite despite annexation because “other than you” and likenesses have innumerable possible referents; a single known opposite makes ghayr definite. — IBNATIYYA reporting أبو بكر بن السراج: Ordinarily ghayr and mithl remain indefinite despite annexation because “other than you” and likenesses have innumerable possible referents; a single known opposite makes ghayr definite. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA(أبو بكر بن السراج)]
- 1:7/q13/p36 He explains that Ibn al-Sarrāj preserves الذين as definite and permits a definite adjective, while others treat ghayr as indefinite and approximate الذين to a general noun. — IBNATIYYA: He explains that Ibn al-Sarrāj preserves الذين as definite and permits a definite adjective, while others treat ghayr as indefinite and approximate الذين to a general noun. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA]
- 1:7/q13/p37 The pro-accusative argument is that ghayr is indefinite and cannot describe a definite noun; the author prefers the unambiguous genitive reading transmitted from Ibn Kathir and the canonical readers. — IBNATIYYA-FULL: The pro-accusative argument is that ghayr is indefinite and cannot describe a definite noun; the author prefers the unambiguous genitive reading transmitted from Ibn Kathir and the canonical readers. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL+]
- 1:7/q13/p38 Ibn al-Sarraj says ghayr and mithl usually remain indefinite with a definite complement because their meanings allow endlessly many alternatives or likenesses. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting أبو بكر بن السراج: Ibn al-Sarraj says ghayr and mithl usually remain indefinite with a definite complement because their meanings allow endlessly many alternatives or likenesses. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(أبو بكر بن السراج)]
- 1:7/q13/p39 In this context ghayr can become definite when it contrasts two known, exclusive alternatives: one favored person either has been angered or has not. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting أبو بكر بن السراج: In this context ghayr can become definite when it contrasts two known, exclusive alternatives: one favored person either has been angered or has not. - 1:7/q13/p40 Abu Bakr keeps alladhina definite and allows ghayr to describe it because context makes ghayr definite; other grammarians treat alladhina as a common, near-indefinite term and allow an indefinite adjective. — IBNATIYYA-FULL: Abu Bakr keeps alladhina definite and allows ghayr to describe it because context makes ghayr definite; other grammarians treat alladhina as a common, near-indefinite term and allow an indefinite adjective. - 1:7/q13/p41 Some say la is emphatic and means ghayr, “other than.” — IBNATIYYA-FULL: Some say la is emphatic and means ghayr, “other than.” [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL]
- 1:7/q13/p42 In the genitive, ghayr may be an apposition to the pronoun in ʿalayhim or to alladhīna, or an adjective of the relative phrase despite ghayr usually modifying an indefinite noun. — TABRISI: In the genitive, ghayr may be an apposition to the pronoun in ʿalayhim or to alladhīna, or an adjective of the relative phrase despite ghayr usually modifying an indefinite noun. [1 notes: TABRISI]
- 1:7/q13/p43 Al-Sarraj says ghayr becomes definite when its definite complement has one known opposite: the favored people are the ones other than those under anger. — TABRISI reporting أبو بكر السراج: Al-Sarraj says ghayr becomes definite when its definite complement has one known opposite: the favored people are the ones other than those under anger. [1 notes: TABRISI(أبو بكر السراج)]

[1 notes: TABRISI(أبو بكر السراج)]

- 1:7/q13/p46 The wording avoids saying that those favored are simply other than the angered, out of courtesy and preference for refined expression. — TABRISI: The wording avoids saying that those favored are simply other than the angered, out of courtesy and preference for refined expression. - 1:7/q13/p48 The genitive may make ghayr an appositive to alladhina or to the pronoun in alayhim, or an adjective; although definite nouns usually are not modified by indefinite ones, alladhina is general here or ghayr is definite between… — QURTUBI-FULL: The genitive may make ghayr an appositive to alladhina or to the pronoun in alayhim, or an adjective; although definite nouns usually are not modified by indefinite ones, alladhina is general here or ghayr is definite between exclusive opposites. - 1:7/q13/p49 The Kufans say lā means “other than,” as in ʿUmar’s and Ubayy’s variant reading. — QURTUBI-FULL reporting الكوفيون: The Kufans say lā means “other than,” as in ʿUmar’s and Ubayy’s variant reading. [1 notes: QURTUBI-FULL(الكوفيون)]

- 1:7/q13/p52 ‘Other than those under anger, nor those astray’ can be an apposition to ‘those favored’ or an adjective describing them; they unite the full blessing of faith with safety from anger and error. — NASAFI: ‘Other than those under anger, nor those astray’ can be an apposition to ‘those favored’ or an adjective describing them; they unite the full blessing of faith with safety from anger and error. ## 1:7/q14 How is 'other than those angered' construed and inflected?  [غَيْرِ ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ · grammar]
turns on: The case reading, whether ghayr is definite, and whether lā can follow an exception.
- 1:7/q14/p1 Ghayr is an adjective qualifying the favored — SIBAWAYH: Sībawayh analyzes ghayr in 1:7 as an adjective meaning other than, not as an exceptive construction. SIBAWAYH: Amr ibn Maʿdīkarib's verse is paraphrased as كل أخ غير الفرقدين, with the ghayr phrase qualifying كل. SIBAWAYH: Al-Shammākh's verse gives another poetic example of a ghayr phrase qualifying a noun, rather than forming an exception. SIBAWAYH: He cites 4:95, غير أولي الضرر, as another Quranic example of ghayr used as an adjective. | mentions 4:95 SIBAWAYH: In another Labīd line, the second ghayr is an adjective for the first; the intended point is that events cannot alter the sharp sword. FARRA: Genitive ghayri is an adjective of alladhīna, not of the pronoun in ʿalayhim; its definite annexation permits this description because neither expression denotes a specified person. AKHFASH: Ghayr al-maghḍūbi can be an adjective for those blessed, though ghayr and mithl are ordinarily used with indefinites and can modify definite forms that carry an indefinite sense. TAB: On one parsing, ghayr is an adjective of alladhīna: the relative phrase is not a specific proper-name-like definite, so an indefinite adjective can describe it. TAB: The possible accusative parse treats ghayr as a detached adjective of the pronoun in ʿalayhim, which is syntactically governed by anʿamta. TAB-FULL: The first genitive parse makes ghayr an adjective for alladhīna: the relative phrase is not a fully specified proper name but indefinite-like, so it can take this adjective. TAB-FULL: Even if ghayr repeats ṣirāṭ rather than qualifying those favored, their evident description as guided by God already implies they are neither objects of His anger nor astray. TAB-FULL: An accusative reading of ghayr is grammatically possible but al-Ṭabarī dislikes it because it departs from the established, widely transmitted reading; it would qualify the object pronoun in عليهم and mean not objects of anger or misguidance. TAB-FULL: He prefers the universally transmitted genitive reading, taking ghayr as an adjective of those favored or as repeated ṣirāṭ; either parse is sound, and he explains the grammatical alternatives because they produce different interpretations. ZAJJAJ: Alternatively, genitive ghayr qualifies alladhīna; although ghayr usually describes an indefinite noun, alladhīna here denotes a category rather than particular people. IBNMUJAHID reporting نافع وعاصم وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي: These readers take غير المغضوب عليهم in the genitive as an adjective of الذين; Ibn Kathīr is reported with a different form, though another transmission agrees with the majority. IBNMUJAHID reporting الخليل بن أحمد: Al-Khalīl permits Ibn Kathīr’s form as a detached adjective or as an accusative circumstantial phrase; he also allows repeating صراط before غير. IBNMUJAHID reporting الأخفش: Al-Akhfash analyzes the accusative as an exception, but Ibn Mujāhid explicitly calls this mistaken; genitive غير is the adjective of الذين. THALABI: Ghayr functions as an adjective for alladhīna despite the usual definiteness mismatch, because alladhīna here is not a fully specified definite but means whoever is truthful rather than lying. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب الحجة: As an adjective, ghayr can modify alladhīna here only because the relative phrase does not single out a particular group, making it like an indefinite description. WAHIDI-BASIT: In 4:95, ghayr can modify the believers sitting out: the intended contrast is healthy nonparticipants versus those who strive. | mentions 4:95 KASHSHAF: Ghayr can modify the definite relative phrase because it is undelimited and the angry and astray are opposites of the blessed. KASHSHAF: Alternatively, ghayr is an adjective: the blessed combine faith with safety from anger and error. KASHSHAF-FULL: Ghayr al-maghḍūb may substitute for those blessed, describing them as safe from anger and error, or qualify them as combining faith with safety from both. KASHSHAF-FULL: Ghayr can qualify the definite phrase because alladhina is not temporally delimited and the contrary identities of the two groups remove its ambiguity; it can also be accusative as a circumstantial phrase. IBNATIYYA: He explains that Ibn al-Sarrāj preserves الذين as definite and permits a definite adjective, while others treat ghayr as indefinite and approximate الذين to a general noun. IBNATIYYA-FULL: Abu Bakr keeps alladhina definite and allows ghayr to describe it because context makes ghayr definite; other grammarians treat alladhina as a common, near-indefinite term and allow an indefinite adjective. TABRISI reporting الزجاج: Al-Zajjaj allows ghayr as an adjective of alladhīna because the relative phrase does not target named individuals, much like a generic man like you. TABRISI reporting أبو بكر السراج: In the accusative, ghayr may be a circumstantial qualifier, a disconnected exception, or an explanatory specification meaning 'I mean'. BAYDAWI: The adjective reading works by treating the relative phrase as an indefinite, or by making ghayr definite through its contrastive genitive. BAYDAWI reporting ابن كثير: Ibn Kathīr reads ghayr in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in ʿalayhim, governed by anʿamta. BAYDAWI-FULL: The adjective-like reading is possible if the relative is treated as indefinite or if غير becomes definite by annexation to the unique opposite group. BAYDAWI-FULL reporting ابن كثير: Ibn Kathīr reads غير in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier or by an implied verb, and it can also be an exception if favors include both groups. NASAFI: Although ghayr normally does not become definite through annexation, it can modify the definite alladhina here: between opposites it takes definiteness, and both terms are generic yet partly specified, balancing their ambiguity and particularity. NASAFI-FULL: Alternatively, the phrase qualifies the favored, who combine the full blessing of faith with safety from divine anger and error; the source explains why “other than” can qualify a definite antecedent. ABUHAYYAN: Ghayr is always masculine singular; it expresses difference in some respect, originates as an adjective, can mark exception, and remains annexed. It cannot take al and does not ordinarily become definite by annexation. ABUHAYYAN reporting سيبويه: Sībawayh parses genitive ghayr as an adjective, treating it as definite through annexation to عليهم; Ibn al-Sarrāj offers a different account of its definiteness. ABUHAYYAN: The suggestion that الذين denotes a generic class, allowing ghayr to modify it despite definiteness, undermines the rule that a definite noun is modified only by a definite; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this account. ABUHAYYAN reporting المهدوي: Al-Mahdawī and others parse accusative ghayr as a circumstantial accusative from عليهم, or from الذين; Abū Ḥayyān rejects the latter because the genitive complement has no syntactic position for a circumstantial modifier. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: “Ghayr” is originally an adjective, can mark exception, must be annexed, and cannot take the definite article or become definite merely through annexation. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting سيبويه: Sībawayh permits the genitive as an adjective, taking “ghayr” as definite through annexation; Abū Ḥayyān also reports Ibn al-Sarrāj’s narrower rationale and rejects a generic-plural rationale. SAMIN-DURR: Ghayr can function like illā for exception, as an adjective by analogy with illā, or like lā for negation, permitting its governed object to precede it. IBNKATHIR: The Nabigha al-Dhubyani line illustrates omitting the described noun and retaining its adjective; here “path” is omitted before “other than the angered.” IBNKATHIR reporting الجمهور: The majority read ghayr in the genitive as an adjective modifying the path. NASHR reporting ابن كثير: Khalil transmits from Ibn Kathir accusative ghayra al-maghḍūb, judged sound as a circumstantial phrase or adjective. BIQAI: Ghayr is made definite by annexation to its opposite and serves as an adjective for those who were blessed, like motion being other than rest. ITQAN: غير is an annexed, indefinite noun; it becomes definite only between two opposites, which permits it to modify the definite phrase “those who incurred anger,” though it usually modifies an indefinite. ITQAN: In 4:95, غير is read nominative as an adjective to “those who sit,” or as an exception/substitute; accusative as an exception; and, outside the seven readings, genitive as an adjective to “believers.” | mentions 4:95 ALUSI: Treating ghayr as an adjective meaning different is weak: ghayr has become a noun and usually does not modify an expressed noun. ALUSI reporting سيبويه: Sībawayh analyzes ghayr as an explanatory or restrictive adjective of alladhīna; al-Ālūsī explains that the relative is definite generically but can function like an indefinite when only an unspecified subset is intended. ALUSI-FULL reporting سيبويه: Sibawayh treats ghayr as an explanatory or restrictive adjective of “those”; Alusi argues the partly specified group can function like an indefinite despite the relative phrase's definiteness. IBNASHUR-FULL: All ten readers put ghayr in the genitive; it can modify the favored people or stand as a substitute, with no difference in intended meaning. [47 notes: SIBAWAYH; FARRA; AKHFASH; TAB; TAB-FULL; ZAJJAJ; IBNMUJAHID(الخليل بن أحمد,نافع وعاصم وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي); THALABI; WAHIDI-BASIT(صاحب الحجة); KASHSHAF; KASHSHAF-FULL; IBNATIYYA; IBNATIYYA-FULL; TABRISI(أبو بكر السراج,الزجاج); BAYDAWI(ابن كثير); BAYDAWI-FULL(ابن كثير); NASAFI; NASAFI-FULL; ABUHAYYAN(المهدوي,سيبويه); ABUHAYYAN-FULL(سيبويه); SAMIN-DURR; IBNKATHIR(الجمهور); NASHR(ابن كثير); BIQAI; ITQAN; ALUSI(سيبويه); ALUSI-FULL(سيبويه); IBNASHUR-FULL; TAB-FULL+; TAB-FULL-; IBNMUJAHID(الأخفش)-; ABUHAYYAN-; ALUSI-]
- 1:7/q14/p2 Ghayr is an apposition to the favored or an understood path — NAHHAS reporting ابن كيسان: Ibn Kaysān permits ghayr al-maghḍūbi as an adjective or apposition to alladhīna, and also as apposition to their pronoun in ʿalayhim. WAHIDI-BASIT: Ghayr can be genitive as an appositive to alladhīna or as its adjective; the adjective is valid because the relative phrase here is not a particular, singled-out group. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب الحجة: The author of al-Ḥujja says genitive ghayr is either apposition or adjective; apposition implies repeating the governing factor, as the repeated prepositions in 7:75 show. | mentions 7:75 WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب الحجة: As apposition, ghayr has a clear meaning whether construed definite or indefinite, since both definite and indefinite apposition are accepted. WAHIDI-BASIT: Lā may also be added after ghayr as a circumstantial expression, adjective, or appositive; the Qur'an uses it in 57:29. | mentions 57:29 KASHSHAF: Ghayr can be appositive to those blessed, meaning they are spared God's anger and error. IBNATIYYA reporting أبو علي: On the genitive reading, ghayr can be an appositive to الذين or an adjective to an indefinite, since الذين here is not specifically singled out. TABRISI: In the genitive, ghayr may be an apposition to the pronoun in ʿalayhim or to alladhīna, or an adjective of the relative phrase despite ghayr usually modifying an indefinite noun. QURTUBI reporting عمر بن الخطاب وأبي بن كعب: Umar and Ubayy read ghayr with accusative or genitive r; genitive parses as apposition or adjective, with two explanations for its definiteness, attributed respectively to al-Farisi and al-Zamakhshari. QURTUBI-FULL: The genitive may make ghayr an appositive to alladhina or to the pronoun in alayhim, or an adjective; although definite nouns usually are not modified by indefinite ones, alladhina is general here or ghayr is definite between exclusive opposites. BAYDAWI: Ghayr can be an appositive to those blessed, or an adjective that clarifies or restricts them. BAYDAWI-FULL: “Not those angered nor astray” may be an apposition to “those You favored,” or a qualifying description showing that true favor joins faith with safety from anger and error. NASAFI: ‘Other than those under anger, nor those astray’ can be an apposition to ‘those favored’ or an adjective describing them; they unite the full blessing of faith with safety from anger and error. NASAFI-FULL: “Other than those under anger” is an appositive: those favored are the ones spared God's anger and misguidance. ABUHAYYAN reporting أبو علي: Abū ʿAlī parses genitive ghayr as an apposition either to الذين or to the pronoun in عليهم; Abū Ḥayyān calls both analyses weak because apposition by an adjective is weak. ABUHAYYAN: Some supply an omitted صراط before ghayr; Abū Ḥayyān finds the estimate weak because it creates awkward apposition or adjective order and other difficult attachment analyses. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting أبو علي: Abū ʿAlī analyzes the genitive as an apposition to “those” or to the pronoun in “upon them,” but Abū Ḥayyān says both are weak because “ghayr” is adjectival. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Supplying an omitted “path” before “ghayr” yields weak analyses, including an adjective before its apposition or repeated apposition. SAMIN-DURR: Ghayr is an indefinite apposition to alladhīna; calling it an adjective is difficult because ghayr is indefinite and the relative is definite. SAMIN-DURR: An omitted ṣirāṭ after ghayr is proposed, but this adjective analysis is weak because when an adjective and apposition coexist, the adjective ordinarily comes first; ghayr can instead modify ṣirāṭ alladhīna. SAMIN-DURR: Accusative ghayr may also replace either ṣirāṭ, despite a possible repeated-apposition problem, or serve as a circumstantial from either one. ALUSI: Ghayr is a matching apposition to alladhīna. Making it an apposition to the pronoun in ʿalayhim is semantically awkward; the relative clause still contains its pronoun because the antecedent is not truly discarded. ALUSI: The objection from 35:37 does not disprove this definiteness: ṣāliḥan may be a fronted circumstantial accusative, or ghayr alladhī may be an apposition to it. | mentions 35:37 ALUSI-FULL: “Other than those who incurred anger” is a complete appositive for “those whom You favored”; taking it as an appositive for their pronoun is semantically awkward, though the relative clause remains grammatically attached. IBNASHUR reporting القراء العشرة: All ten readers pronounce ghayr in the genitive; syntactically it may modify the favored or stand in apposition, with the author preferring the adjectival reading. IBNASHUR: He prefers treating ghayr as an adjective: its descriptive sense outweighs apposition, which conventionally names the same entity as its antecedent. [23 notes: NAHHAS(ابن كيسان); WAHIDI-BASIT(صاحب الحجة); KASHSHAF; IBNATIYYA(أبو علي); TABRISI; QURTUBI(عمر بن الخطاب وأبي بن كعب); QURTUBI-FULL; BAYDAWI; BAYDAWI-FULL; NASAFI; NASAFI-FULL; ABUHAYYAN(أبو علي); ABUHAYYAN-FULL(أبو علي); SAMIN-DURR; ALUSI; ALUSI-FULL; IBNASHUR(القراء العشرة); IBNASHUR+; ABUHAYYAN-; ABUHAYYAN-FULL-; SAMIN-DURR-]
- 1:7/q14/p3 Ghayr is an exception, possibly disconnected — SIBAWAYH: He adduces 21:22 as a parallel in which إلا الله is understood adjectivally, like non-exceptive ghayr. | mentions 21:22 SIBAWAYH: Dhu al-Rumma's line uses إلا بغامها descriptively in place of غير بغامها, demonstrating a non-exceptive use of إلا. AKHFASH reporting قوم: Some readers construe ghayr al-maghḍūbi as an exception outside the initial statement. TAB reporting نحويو الكوفة: Kufan grammarians reject an unmotivated added lā at the start of a phrase and reject coordinating it with ghayr if ghayr means “other than” or an exception. TAB-FULL reporting بعض نحويي البصريين: One Basran grammarian takes accusative ghayr as an exception from those favored: exclude those not favored or guided, and do not make us among them. TAB-FULL: He prefers the Kufan analysis: lā cannot begin as an omitted negative or coordinate with other than or an exception; since ghayr can mean exception, negation, or other than, the only valid reading here is negation, making the verse ask to avoid both groups. ZAJJAJ: Accusative ghayr can be an exception, equivalent to “except the angered”; exception ghayr is accusative when what follows illā is accusative. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting الفراء: Al-Farrāʾ rejects accusative ghayr as an exception, arguing that a positive exception cannot be followed by negative lā in coordination. WAHIDI-BASIT: The identification also fits a rare accusative reading of ghayr as exception, excluding Jews and Christians from those favored; the author notes that this reading is anomalous. BAYDAWI: Other parses take an implied aʿnī, or treat ghayr as an exception if blessings include both groups. ABUHAYYAN reporting الأخفش والزجاج: Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjāj allow accusative ghayr as a disconnected exception because the preceding wording does not include those who are astray; some readers reject this analysis because of lā. ABUHAYYAN: Some permit accusative ghayr as an exception by treating lā as extra, since they say lā is extra only after prior negation; they cite Qurʾanic and poetic examples, while other grammarians take lā as genuinely negative. IBNKATHIR reporting بعض النحاة: Some grammarians take ghayr as an exception, making it a disconnected exception because the angered are outside the favored group; Ibn Kathir says his own account is better. BIQAI: Ghayr conveys negation rather than an exception: the wording excludes those characterized by the trait from the outset and avoids suggesting a merely lesser class. BIQAI-FULL: Using غير rather than an exception marks exclusion from the outset, making clear that the requested universal blessing means the special honor granted to the faithful, not the general gift of existence. ITQAN reporting الراغب: Raghib says غير can mean “except,” allowing it to mark an exception or describe an indefinite noun. | mentions 2:163, 35:3 ALUSI reporting الفراء: Al-Farrāʾ rejects the exception analysis because ghayr then means siwā and the negative lā cannot be coordinated with it unless lā is treated as extra; al-Ālūsī notes the usage after wāw is unattested. | mentions 7:12 ALUSI-FULL reporting الأخفش: Al-Akhfash allows the accusative as a connected or disconnected exception if “favor” is broad; al-Farraʾ forbids joining negative lā to an exceptive phrase meaning “other than.” [16 notes: SIBAWAYH; AKHFASH(قوم); TAB-FULL(بعض نحويي البصريين); ZAJJAJ; WAHIDI-BASIT; BAYDAWI; ABUHAYYAN(الأخفش والزجاج); IBNKATHIR(بعض النحاة); BIQAI; BIQAI-FULL; ITQAN(الراغب); ALUSI(الفراء); ALUSI-FULL(الأخفش); TAB-FULL+; TAB(نحويو الكوفة)-; WAHIDI-BASIT(الفراء)-]
- 1:7/q14/p4 Ghayr is an accusative circumstantial phrase — AKHFASH: Ghayr may alternatively be accusative as a circumstantial expression because it is indefinite while its antecedent is definite. ZAJJAJ: Accusative ghayr can instead be a circumstantial, meaning the path of those blessed, not angered. WAHIDI-BASIT: Ghayr may instead be accusative as a circumstantial expression or an exception meaning except those under wrath; as a circumstantial phrase it means not those under wrath. KASHSHAF reporting النبي وعمر بن الخطاب وابن كثير: The accusative ghayra is a circumstantial reading attributed to the Prophet, Umar, and Ibn Kathir. KASHSHAF-FULL reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وعمر بن الخطاب: A circumstantial accusative reading of ghayr is attributed to the Prophet and Umar, and also reported from Ibn Kathir. IBNATIYYA reporting أبو علي: On the accusative reading, ghayr can be circumstantial, exceptive, or an implied direct object of “I mean.” QURTUBI: Accusative ghayr can be circumstantial or an exception; al-Khalil also permits an implied “I mean.” QURTUBI-FULL reporting الخليل: The accusative may be circumstantial, exceptive, or understood as “I mean,” a construction attributed to al-Khalil. SAMIN-DURR: Ghayr is also read in the accusative as a circumstantial from alladhīna or ʿalayhim, or as a disjoint exception; al-Farrāʾ rejects the latter because lā lacks a preceding negation. IBNKATHIR reporting الزمخشري: Al-Zamakhshari reports an accusative circumstantial reading of ghayr, attributed to the Prophet and ʿUmar and also transmitted from Ibn Kathir; its circumstantial referent is the pronoun in ʿalayhim. ITQAN: غير can function as a circumstantial accusative where “not” fits, or as an exception where “except” fits; as an exception it takes the case of the following noun in the corresponding construction. ALUSI reporting عمر بن الخطاب: ʿUmar read ghayra in the accusative; a noncanonical report attributes the same reading to Ibn Kathīr. It is best parsed as a circumstantial accusative governed by anʿamta, though other analyses are discussed. ALUSI reporting الخليل: Al-Khalīl parses the accusative as governed by an omitted verb, aʿnī, and al-Ālūsī endorses him: exception is problematic and the circumstantial analysis requires an unpersuasive indefinite ghayr. ALUSI-FULL reporting عمر إبن الخطاب: ʿUmar read ghayra in the accusative; it is also transmitted irregularly from Ibn Kathir, most plausibly as a circumstantial accusative referring to the pronoun in “upon them.” ALUSI-FULL reporting الخليل: Al-Khalil's analysis, which Alusi endorses, supplies an omitted verb meaning “I mean”; Alusi rejects the circumstantial analysis because it requires indefiniteness or a strained sense of ghayr. [15 notes: AKHFASH; ZAJJAJ; WAHIDI-BASIT; KASHSHAF(النبي وعمر بن الخطاب وابن كثير); KASHSHAF-FULL(رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وعمر بن الخطاب); IBNATIYYA(أبو علي); QURTUBI; QURTUBI-FULL(الخليل); SAMIN-DURR; IBNKATHIR(الزمخشري); ITQAN; ALUSI(عمر بن الخطاب); ALUSI-FULL(عمر إبن الخطاب); ALUSI-FULL(الخليل)+; ALUSI(الخليل)+]

## 1:7/q15 What readings replace or vary 'other than'?  [غَيْرِ · readings]
