## 1:7/q16 Who are those under anger?  [ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ · referent]
turns on: Whether the Prophetic identifications specify the only referents or exemplify wider classes of disobedience and error.
- 1:7/q16/p1 The Jews, as an identified example or restricted referent — MUQATIL: The people under divine anger are the Jews, whom God turned into apes and pigs; the requested path is other than their religion. ABDURRAZZAQ reporting النبي: The Prophet points to Jews as those under divine anger, in response to a question at Wādī al-Qurā. IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB: Those under wrath are the Jews. TAB reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: In reports from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, the Prophet identifies the wrathful as the Jews. TAB reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: At the siege of Wādī al-Qurā, the Prophet answers a man's question by identifying the besieged Jews as the wrathful. TAB reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbās, through al-Ḍaḥḥāk, identifies the wrathful as Jews whom God has angered. TAB reporting أبو مالك، أبو صالح، ابن عباس، مرة الهمداني، ابن مسعود، وناس من أصحاب النبي: A report collected by al-Suddī from several early authorities identifies the wrathful as the Jews. TAB reporting مجاهد: Mujāhid identifies the wrathful as the Jews. TAB reporting الربيع: Al-Rabīʿ identifies the wrathful as the Jews. TAB reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbās, in a report through Ibn Jurayj, identifies the wrathful as the Jews. TAB reporting عبد الرحمن بن زيد: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd identifies the wrathful as the Jews. TAB reporting زيد: Zayd, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd's father, identifies the wrathful as the Jews. TAB reporting ابن عباس: In Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation, the prayer asks God to inspire true monotheistic religion, spare the worshippers His anger like the Jews, and keep them from Christian error and punishment. TAB: Jews and Christians are both astray and under wrath; God labels each group by a real, recognizable trait, without implying that it lacks the other's blameworthy traits. TAB-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عدي بن حاتم: The Prophet identifies those under wrath as the Jews in reports transmitted from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim. TAB-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عبد الله بن شقيق: Reports from the Prophet at the siege of Wādī al-Qurā identify the besieged people under wrath as Jews. TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas glosses those under wrath as Jews whom God has been angry with. TAB-FULL reporting السدي عن أبي مالك وأبي صالح عن ابن عباس ومرة الهمداني عن ابن مسعود وناس من أصحاب النبي: The report attributed through al-Suddī to these early authorities identifies those under wrath as Jews. TAB-FULL reporting مجاهد: Mujāhid identifies those under wrath as Jews. TAB-FULL reporting ربيع: Rabīʿ says those under wrath are the Jews. TAB-FULL reporting ابن زيد: Ibn Zayd says those under wrath are the Jews; he also transmits the same identification from his father. TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas glosses the astray as Christians whom God led astray through their fabrication about Him; the prayer asks for the true monotheistic faith, protection from Jewish wrath and Christian error, and mercy to prevent their punishment. TAB-FULL: Both Jews and Christians are astray and under wrath, but God labels each by a true, recognizable characteristic, without listing every blameworthy trait of either group. TAB-FULL reporting بعض أهل الغباء من القدرية: Some Qadariyyah wrongly infer from calling Christians astray and Jews objects of wrath that human acts belong only to people and that God does not cause their misguidance; al-Ṭabarī says this betrays ignorance of Arabic attribution and the many verses naming God as guide and misguider. | mentions 10:22, 45:23 IBNABIHATIM reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; the author says exegetes do not disagree on this wording. IBNABIHATIM: The author says he knows no disagreement among exegetes over the identification of those astray as Christians and those under wrath as Jews. IBNABIHATIM reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: A second report from the Prophet likewise says the Jews incurred wrath and the Christians went astray. THALABI reporting رسول الله: In a report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, the Prophet identifies those angered with the Jews and those astray with the Christians. THALABI reporting رسول الله: At Wādī al-Qurā, the Prophet points to Jews fighting him as those angered and to Christians as the other party, those astray. THALABI: The author links divine anger against Jews to 5:60 and the description of Christians as astray to 5:77. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 MAWARDI: God singles out Jews as the objects of wrath because they are the most hostile. MAWARDI reporting عدي بن حاتم: Adi ibn Hatim reports that the Prophet identified those under wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians; al-Mawardi says all exegetes agree. MAWARDI: Al-Mawardi says all exegetes agree that those under wrath are Jews and those astray are Christians. MAWARDI-FULL reporting عدي بن حاتم: He asked the Prophet who the angered and astray groups were; the Prophet identified them as Jews and Christians, respectively, as all exegetes agree. MAWARDI-FULL: Misguidance is the opposite of guidance, and Jews are singled out for anger because they are more intensely hostile. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting عدي بن حاتم: A report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, attributed to the Prophet, identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; no grading is stated. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting النبي: A second report says the Prophet at Wādī al-Qurā was asked by a man from Bali about two groups; he pointed to Jews as those under wrath and Christians as astray; no grading is stated. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting ابن عباس وابن مسعود ومجاهد وغيرهم: Commentators support this interpretation by citing God's anger against Jews in 5:60 and the description of people who strayed in 5:77; Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and Mujāhid hold it. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 WAHIDI-QT: Those under wrath are Jews; God's wrath means His willing punishment. WAHIDI-QT: Those astray are Christians, and Muslims ask to avoid both their error and the Jews' incurred wrath. WAHIDI-WAJIZ: Those under divine anger are the Jews; God's anger means His willing punishment. WAHIDI-WAJIZ: The people who went astray are the Christians; Muslims ask to avoid their deviation from truth as well as the Jews' incurred anger. BAGHAWI reporting عمر بن الخطاب: ʿUmar read “the path of those whom You favored,” and Baghawi links this to verses describing the Jews as recipients of anger and a people who strayed. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 BAGHAWI: An unnamed view identifies those angered as the Jews and those astray as the Christians, citing verses on their anger and earlier deviation. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 BAGHAWI-FULL: A reported identification makes the objects of wrath Jews and the straying ones Christians, supported by Quranic descriptions of each group. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 KASHSHAF: Those who incurred anger are identified as Jews, with 5:60 cited. | mentions 5:60 KASHSHAF-FULL: An unnamed view identifies the angered as Jews, citing the verse that says God cursed them and was angry with them. IBNATIYYA reporting ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد وعدي بن حاتم عن النبي: They identify those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; the same interpretation is reported from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim from the Prophet. IBNATIYYA: The author says scripture repeatedly describes God’s wrath against Jews, citing their incurring wrath and the punishment of Sabbath-breakers. | mentions 2:61, 3:112, 5:60, 2:65 IBNATIYYA: In answer to al-Ṭabarī’s question about assigning one label to each group, the author says Jewish transgression, obstinacy, rejection despite signs, and killing prophets characteristically warrant wrath; Christians’ basic unbelief is astray shared by all unbelievers. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد: Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd identify those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians; ʿAdi ibn Hatim transmits this from the Prophet. IBNATIYYA-FULL: The Qur'an repeatedly associates divine wrath with Jews, including 2:61, 3:112, and 5:60; 2:65 identifies the people turned into apes as Sabbath violators. | mentions 2:61, 3:112, 5:60, 2:65 IBNATIYYA-FULL: The author finds this answer insufficient: Jewish aggression, defiance, disbelief despite signs, and killing prophets especially warrant wrath, while Christians strayed from the start without these specific acts. TABRISI reporting جميع المفسرين: Commentators broadly identify those under anger as Jews, supported by verses about divine anger and the Sabbath violators turned into apes. | mentions 5:60, 2:65 TABRISI reporting الحسن البصري: Hasan says both Jews and Christians are both astray and under anger, though God marks each group by a distinguishing epithet despite their shared traits. TABRISI: This explanation identifies the angered as Jews and the astray as Christians. IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting عدي بن حاتم عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, from the Prophet, identifies the objects of anger as Jews and the astray as Christians. RAZI-FULL reporting المشهور: The commonly reported identification makes those under wrath the Jews and those astray the Christians, citing the Qur'an's descriptions of each. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 QURTUBI reporting جمهور المفسرين: Most commentators identify those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; 2:61, 3:112, and 48:6 concern Jewish wrath, and 5:77 Christian error. | mentions 2:61, 3:112, 48:6, 5:77 QURTUBI-FULL reporting الجمهور: Most interpreters identify those under wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians; the Prophet’s explanation to ʿAdi ibn Hatim supports it, as do verses about their wrath and error. | mentions 3:112, 48:6, 5:77 BAYDAWI: One reported identification makes those under wrath the Jews, citing the description in 5:60. | mentions 5:60 BAYDAWI-FULL: A reported interpretation identifies those under anger as Jews and those astray as Christians, linking them to 5:60 and 5:77; the identification is also transmitted as a Prophetic report. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 NASAFI reporting قيل: One view identifies those under anger as Jews, citing God’s curse and anger in 5:60, and those astray as Christians, citing their earlier error in 5:77. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 NASAFI-FULL: A reported identification takes those under anger as Jews, citing the verse about those God cursed and angered. | mentions 5:60 QASHANI: Those under wrath are like Jews who stop at outward forms and bodily pleasures, veiling themselves from spiritual truths and intellectual delight; wrath entails expulsion, distance, and darkness of appearances. ABUHAYYAN reporting ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd identify those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians. ABUHAYYAN: Another reported identification makes those angered the Jews and those astray the polytheists; Abū Ḥayyān notes other views without specifying them here. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting ابن مسعود: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd identify those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting قيل: Other identifications say the angered are Jews and polytheists; Sufi restrictions also circulate but are not supported by the verse’s wording. IBNKATHIR: Jews are characterized by abandoning known truth and thus anger, while Christians seek a goal without knowledge of its way because they do not follow the true Messenger; each group is also both astray and under anger. IBNKATHIR: The Qurʾan calls the Jews recipients of anger and specifically describes Christians as astray, supporting the verse's characteristic labels. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 IBNKATHIR: Qurʾanic references to Jewish anger and wrongdoing support the identification: Israel's children incur anger for rejecting revelation and are condemned for sin and failure to stop wrongdoing. | mentions 2:90, 5:60, 5:78, 5:79 IBNKATHIR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: In the report from ʿAdi ibn Hatim, the Prophet identifies the angered as Jews and the astray as Christians; al-Tirmidhi grades this route hasan gharīb, and Ibn Kathir notes other routes and wordings. IBNKATHIR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: At Wadi al-Qura the Prophet points to Jews as the angered and Christians as the astray; other transmitters send the report without naming the eyewitness, while ʿUrwa's route names Ibn ʿUmar. IBNKATHIR reporting السدي: Al-Suddi, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud, and Companions of the Prophet, identifies the Jews as angered and Christians as astray. IBNKATHIR: A report about Zayd ibn ʿAmr says he refused Jewish or Christian conversion because each demanded a share in divine anger, remained on his natural disposition and avoided idols, while his companions became Christians; Waraqa later accepted the Prophet's revelation. BURHAN: Putting those under wrath before those astray may convey disparagement: Jews preceded Christians historically and were nearer to the Muslims. DURR reporting الله: Those under wrath are identified as Jews, with 5:60 cited. | mentions 5:60 DURR reporting قتادة: In Qatada's sequential gloss, the Day of Recompense is when creatures are repaid; the worship-prayer is what people should say and directs them to God; the straight path is named, the favored are prophets, the objects of anger are Jews, and the astray are Christians. DURR reporting الربيع بن أنس: Al-Rabīʿ b. Anas identifies the favored as prophets, those under wrath as Jews, and the astray as Christians. DURR reporting مجاهد: Mujāhid identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians. DURR reporting سعيد بن جبير: Saʿīd b. Jubayr identifies the objects of wrath and the astray as Jews and Christians. DURR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: At Wādī al-Qurā, the Prophet identified the objects of wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; ʿAbd Allāh b. Shaqīq reports the exchange. DURR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: During the siege of Wādī al-Qurā, the Prophet identified one group as Jews under wrath and the other as astray Christians. DURR reporting أبو ذر: Abū Dharr reports asking the Prophet, who answered that those under wrath are Jews and the astray are Christians. DURR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid transmits the Prophet’s identification of Jews under wrath and Christians astray. DURR reporting عدي بن حاتم: ʿAdī b. Ḥātim reports the Prophet’s identification of the objects of wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; al-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan. DURR reporting ابن مسعود: Ibn Masʿūd identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians. DURR reporting ابن أبي حاتم: Ibn Abī Ḥātim knows of no exegetical disagreement identifying those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians. DURR-FULL reporting ابن عباس: The people under anger are Jews and the misguided are Christians; the account links their fate to the cited description of apes, swine, and evil destination. | mentions 5:60 DURR-FULL reporting الربيع بن أنس: Al-Rabi ibn Anas identifies the favored as prophets, those under anger as Jews, and the astray as Christians. DURR-FULL reporting مجاهد: Mujahid identifies those under anger as Jews and the astray as Christians. DURR-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Asked at Wadi al-Qura who the people under anger and those astray were, the Prophet answered Jews and Christians respectively. DURR-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Several reports from questions at Wadi al-Qura say the Prophet identified those under anger as Jews and the other group as Christians who are astray. DURR-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Asked by Abu Dharr, the Prophet identifies the maghdub as Jews and the dalin as Christians. DURR-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A report through a man of Balayn likewise records the Prophet's answer: Jews are under anger and Christians astray. DURR-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Reports from Ismail ibn Abi Khalid, Adi ibn Hatim, Ibn Masud, and Mujahid repeat the identification of Jews with anger and Christians with misguidance. DURR-FULL reporting ابن أبي حاتم: Ibn Abi Hatim says he knows of no disagreement among exegetes that the maghdub are Jews and the dalin are Christians. ITQAN: Despite many later interpretations, the Prophet, Companions, Successors, and their followers identify those who incurred anger as Jews and those astray as Christians; Ibn Abi Hatim knew of no exegetical disagreement. BURSEVI: A common reading identifies those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians, but neither group's label is exclusive because Scripture attributes both traits to both. BURSEVI: Anger fits the Jews especially because of their rebellious unbelief, aggression, killing prophets, and saying God is poor while they are rich. ALUSI reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: Aḥmad transmits and Ibn Ḥibbān grades as ḥasan a Prophetic report identifying the objects of anger as Jews and the astray as Christians. ALUSI: Al-Ālūsī also reads the general terms broadly: those erring in outward works, such as sinners, are under anger; those erring in belief are astray. The Prophetic Jewish and Christian identifications remain sound specifications of the general wording. ALUSI: Al-Ālūsī prefers the hadith as evidence: anger and straying are also ascribed generally to unbelievers, and both terms apply specifically to Jews and Christians. | mentions 16:106, 4:167, 5:60, 5:77 ALUSI-FULL reporting رسول الله: The Prophet identifies those under anger as Jews and those astray as Christians; Ahmad transmits it and Ibn Hibban grades it sound, and Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud also transmit the interpretation. ALUSI-FULL: Qur'anic citations can support the Jewish and Christian identifications, but anger and straying also describe unbelievers generally; Alusi says the hadith is the better proof. | mentions 5:60, 5:77, 16:106, 4:167 ELMALILI: The Quran associates Jews with wrath and Christians with deviation, citing 2:61 for Jews; 5:77 separately identifies Christians with deviation. | mentions 2:61 ELMALILI: Ibn Abi Hatim, as quoted by al-Durr al-Manthur, says he knows of no exegetical disagreement identifying those under wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians. ELMALILI reporting Resûlullah: Elmalılı cites a hadith that Tirmidhi grades hasan, transmitted from Adi b. Hatim, in which the Prophet says Jews are under wrath and Christians are astray. ELMALILI: Saying that Jews are among those under wrath is not equivalent to saying that all those under wrath are Jews; the hadiths make them examples, not the exhaustive referent. IBNASHUR: He says their earlier error was not yet deliberate and had not incurred divine anger; Jews exemplify the first group and Christians the second, but neither label is exclusive. IBNASHUR reporting النبي: A report in al-Tirmidhī, which the author grades ḥasan, names Jews as an example of the angered and Christians as an example of the straying, not as exclusive referents. IBNASHUR-FULL: The groups had apparently not earned divine wrath before Islam because their error was not deliberate; Jews exemplify the first and Christians the second, without exhausting either category. IBNASHUR-FULL: Reports identifying the angered with Jews and the astray with Christians allude to famous examples, not exclusive meanings; asking to avoid both escalates protection from the more severe fate to the lesser. IBNASHUR-FULL reporting النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم: Jews exemplify the angered and Christians the astray; a ḥasan prophetic report in Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī supports the examples, not an exclusive interpretation. IBNASHUR-FULL: Reports from companions who witnessed revelation identify those who incurred wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians. CORPUSCORANICUM reporting Nöldeke: On the hypothesis that the Fātiḥa draws on Christian traditions, Nöldeke’s reading takes the second group as Jews, stereotyped in Christian polemic as subject to divine wrath. CORPUSCORANICUM: Identifying the wrath-stricken with Jews would be anachronistic for the Fātiḥa’s first proclamation: this image appears only in Medina and never becomes a Quranic stereotype. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: Some reports identify the strayed as Christians and those under wrath as Jews; the author says these are nearby examples in time and place, not an exhaustive identification. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: The angered precede the astray because they know truth and reject it, are more culpable than the ignorant, and Jews preceded Christians; an authentic hadith identifies the groups accordingly. STUDYQURAN: A prophetic saying, not considered highly authentic, identifies those under wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians. | mentions 2:61, 2:90, 3:112, 5:60, 5:77 [121 notes: MUQATIL; ABDURRAZZAQ(النبي); IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB; TAB(أبو مالك، أبو صالح، ابن عباس، مرة الهمداني، ابن مسعود، وناس من أصحاب النبي,ابن عباس,الربيع,رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم,زيد,عبد الرحمن بن زيد,مجاهد); TAB-FULL(ابن زيد,ابن عباس,السدي عن أبي مالك وأبي صالح عن ابن عباس ومرة الهمداني عن ابن مسعود وناس من أصحاب النبي,النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عبد الله بن شقيق,النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عدي بن حاتم,بعض أهل الغباء من القدرية,ربيع,مجاهد); IBNABIHATIM(رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم); THALABI(رسول الله); MAWARDI(عدي بن حاتم); MAWARDI-FULL(عدي بن حاتم); WAHIDI-BASIT(ابن عباس وابن مسعود ومجاهد وغيرهم,النبي,عدي بن حاتم); WAHIDI-QT; WAHIDI-WAJIZ; BAGHAWI(عمر بن الخطاب); BAGHAWI-FULL; KASHSHAF; KASHSHAF-FULL; IBNATIYYA(ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد وعدي بن حاتم عن النبي); IBNATIYYA-FULL(ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد); TABRISI(الحسن البصري,جميع المفسرين); IBNJAWZI-ZAD(عدي بن حاتم عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم); RAZI-FULL(المشهور); QURTUBI(جمهور المفسرين); BAYDAWI; BAYDAWI-FULL; NASAFI(قيل); NASAFI-FULL; QASHANI; ABUHAYYAN(ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد); ABUHAYYAN-FULL(ابن مسعود,قيل); IBNKATHIR(السدي,النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم); BURHAN; DURR(أبو ذر,ابن أبي حاتم,ابن مسعود,الربيع بن أنس,الله,النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم,سعيد بن جبير,عدي بن حاتم,قتادة,مجاهد); DURR-FULL(ابن أبي حاتم,ابن عباس,الربيع بن أنس,النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم,مجاهد); ITQAN; BURSEVI; ALUSI(رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم); ALUSI-FULL; ELMALILI(Resûlullah); IBNASHUR(النبي); IBNASHUR-FULL(النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم); CORPUSCORANICUM(Nöldeke); KURANYOLU-TEFSIR; SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT; STUDYQURAN; ALUSI-FULL(رسول الله)+; ALUSI+; QURTUBI-FULL(الجمهور)+]
- 1:7/q16/p2 People who know the truth yet disobey in outward conduct — TAB: Recounting punishments for disobedience warns people away from sin and from incurring God's anger, whose consequences lead to destruction. THALABI reporting قوم: One group explains God's anger as His will to take vengeance on sinners. THALABI reporting قيل: A third explanation defines anger as condemnation of sinners for the ugliness of their acts. BAGHAWI: “Not those angered” means a path other than that of those God wills to punish for disobedience. BAGHAWI-FULL: Those under wrath are people whose path incurred God’s anger; divine anger is the will to punish sinners, but does not befall sinful believers, only disbelievers. KASHSHAF: God's anger is His will to avenge sinners and punish them, acting as a king does when angry with a subordinate. KASHSHAF-FULL: God's anger means His will to take vengeance on sinners, punish them, and treat them as a king does those under his authority. RAZI-FULL: Connection with purified spirits increases strength, while connection with evil spirits brings failure and deprivation; Razi identifies those under wrath as immoral people and the astray as unbelievers. RAZI-FULL: A broader reading takes those under wrath as people who err in outward deeds, including sinners, and those astray as people who err in belief; the wording is general and should not be restricted without cause. RAZI-FULL: The verse divides people into the obedient who are favored, sinners under wrath, and those ignorant of religion or unbelievers who are astray. RAZI-FULL: Those with complete favor unite knowledge of truth for its own sake with doing good for its own sake; lacking practice makes sinners under wrath, while lacking knowledge makes people astray. | mentions 4:93, 10:32 BAYDAWI: Bayḍāwī also finds apt a general reading: sinners fail in action and incur wrath, while those ignorant of God fail in understanding and go astray. BAYDAWI-FULL: A further interpretation calls deliberate sinners angered and those ignorant of God astray: failure of action is impiety, while failure of understanding is error. | mentions 4:93 ALUSI reporting الزمخشري: Al-Zamakhsharī explains God’s anger as His will to punish sinners, bringing punishment upon them as an angry king does to subjects under his authority. ALUSI-FULL reporting الكشاف: Al-Zamakhshari explains God's anger as His will to exact vengeance and punish sinners, acting as an angry ruler acts toward a subordinate. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: The closing description covers all accountable people: the favored know and follow truth, the angered know but oppose it (some exegetes call them sinners), and the astray do not know it. | mentions 18:103, 18:104 [16 notes: TAB; THALABI(قوم,قيل); BAGHAWI; BAGHAWI-FULL; KASHSHAF; KASHSHAF-FULL; RAZI-FULL; BAYDAWI-FULL; ALUSI(الزمخشري); ALUSI-FULL(الكشاف); SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT; BAYDAWI+; RAZI-FULL+]
- 1:7/q16/p3 Unbelievers — THALABI: God's anger does not reach sinful believers; it reaches unbelievers. BAGHAWI: God's anger does not befall sinful believers; it befalls only disbelievers. RAZI-FULL: Razi also offers a possible reading in which those under wrath are unbelievers and those astray are hypocrites, following the order of groups in the opening of al-Baqara. | mentions 2:6, 2:8 BURHAN: In الذين أنعمت عليهم غير المغضوب عليهم, غضب is the single opposite of blessing: the first group is believers and the second disbelievers. ALUSI reporting الرازي: Al-Rāzī suggests that those under anger are unbelievers and the astray are hypocrites, analogizing to al-Baqara’s order of believers, unbelievers, and hypocrites; al-Ālūsī rejects the analogy against the Prophetic report. | mentions 2:1, 2:6, 2:8 ELMALILI: Qur'an also attributes divine wrath to disbelievers generally and describes those who reject God's way as far astray, supporting the comprehensive reading. | mentions 16:106 STUDYQURAN: The verse prays to follow those whom God elevates in belief, knowledge, and uncorrupted faith, and to avoid disbelievers, some astray and some under wrath. | mentions 6:83, 58:11, 6:82 [6 notes: THALABI; BAGHAWI; RAZI-FULL; BURHAN; ELMALILI; STUDYQURAN; ALUSI(الرازي)-]
- 1:7/q16/p4 People of innovation — SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Anger follows innovations, while error is abandoning guidance and Sunnah, including the Sunnah of saying Amin aloud after the chapter in prayer. THALABI reporting التستري: Al-Tustarī identifies innovation with those angered and departure from Sunna with those astray. BAGHAWI reporting سهل بن عبد الله: Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah says those angered are people of innovation. BAGHAWI-FULL reporting سهل بن عبد الله: Sahl b. Abd Allah interprets those under wrath as innovators and the straying ones as people departing from the Sunnah. QURTUBI-FULL: Another view calls innovators recipients of wrath and those who leave the sunnas astray; the author says this is good, though the Prophet’s interpretation is best. [5 notes: SULAMI(بعضهم); THALABI(التستري); BAGHAWI(سهل بن عبد الله); BAGHAWI-FULL(سهل بن عبد الله); QURTUBI-FULL+]
- 1:7/q16/p5 Those abandoned and deprived of divine nearness — SULAMI reporting ابن عطاء: Those under anger are abandoned, expelled, and humiliated; the astray have left God's guidance, knowledge, and guardianship. SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Those under anger are consumed in Satan's wastelands; the astray are expelled from obedience to the Merciful. SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Anger is linked with ostentation, and error with abandoning Sunnah in the pillars of worship. QUSHAYRI: Those under wrath are struck by abandonment, deprivation, rejection, separation, and expulsion. [4 notes: SULAMI(ابن عطاء,بعضهم); QUSHAYRI]

## 1:7/q17 What does divine anger mean here?  [ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ · theology]
turns on: Whether the divine expression names an attribute, will to punish, condemnation, or the punishment itself.
- 1:7/q17/p1 Divine anger is the will to punish or avenge — THALABI reporting قوم: One group explains God's anger as His will to take vengeance on sinners. MAWARDI reporting unattributed: Another interpretation takes wrath as the will to exact vengeance, since the linguistic root implies harshness, which cannot be ascribed to God. MAWARDI-FULL: A second account interprets God's anger as a will to punish; anger linguistically means severity, a quality unsuitable for God. WAHIDI-QT: Those under wrath are Jews; God's wrath means His willing punishment. WAHIDI-WAJIZ: Those under divine anger are the Jews; God's anger means His willing punishment. BAGHAWI-FULL: Those under wrath are people whose path incurred God’s anger; divine anger is the will to punish sinners, but does not befall sinful believers, only disbelievers. KASHSHAF: God's anger is His will to avenge sinners and punish them, acting as a king does when angry with a subordinate. KASHSHAF-FULL: God's anger means His will to take vengeance on sinners, punish them, and treat them as a king does those under his authority. TABRISI: Divine anger is God's will to impose deserved punishment, curse the people, and disavow them; its root denotes severity. QURTUBI: Divine anger can mean God's will to punish, an essential attribute, or the punishment itself, an attribute of action; a hadith says charity extinguishes the Lord's anger. QURTUBI-FULL: Alayhim is grammatically understood as “wrath fell upon them”; wrath linguistically means severity, while in God’s attribute it is either His will to punish or punishment itself. NASAFI: God’s anger means His will to take vengeance on liars and punish them, treating them as a king does those under his authority when angry. NASAFI-FULL: The first “upon them” is an object and the second is a subject; God's anger means His will to exact revenge and impose punishment on deniers. ABUHAYYAN: God's anger may mean His intent to requite a sinner, making it an attribute of essence because His knowledge precedes creation and sin; alternatively it is imposing punishment, an attribute of action. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Divine anger can mean the will to punish, an attribute of essence given God’s prior knowledge, or the act of inflicting punishment, an attribute of action. SAMIN-DURR: Anger is described as the heart's blood surging in intent to take revenge; a prophetic report warns against anger and describes its bodily signs. SAMIN-DURR: Alternative definitions make anger a heart's change toward something disliked, or distinguish divine action-attribute when it means punishment from essential attribute when it means the will to punish. ALUSI reporting السعد: In his commentary on al-Miftāḥ, al-Saʿd defines anger as a movement of the soul whose origin is the will to take revenge. ALUSI reporting السعد: In his commentary on al-Kashshāf, al-Saʿd defines divine anger as the will to take revenge. ALUSI reporting الزمخشري: Al-Zamakhsharī explains God’s anger as His will to punish sinners, bringing punishment upon them as an angry king does to subjects under his authority. ALUSI-FULL: The source gives several technical definitions of anger: a movement arising from desire for vengeance, the will to exact vengeance, or an inward condition producing outward movement; a report likens anger to a glowing ember in the heart. ALUSI-FULL reporting الكشاف: Al-Zamakhshari explains God's anger as His will to exact vengeance and punish sinners, acting as an angry ruler acts toward a subordinate. ELMALILI: When attributed to God, anger means its ultimate end, the will to retaliate or impose punishment, and is compatible with merciful lordship: punishing an oppressor serves mercy to the oppressed. - 1:7/q17/p2 Divine anger is punitive action or its effects — TAB: The wrathful are identified with those described in the Qur'an as cursed and punished for disobedience; God also shows the community the way to avoid their fate. | mentions 5:60 TAB reporting بعضهم: One view explains God's anger as His imposing punishment on those He is angry with, in this world or the next. | mentions 43:55, 5:60 TAB reporting ابن عباس: In Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation, the prayer asks God to inspire true monotheistic religion, spare the worshippers His anger like the Jews, and keep them from Christian error and punishment. TAB: Recounting punishments for disobedience warns people away from sin and from incurring God's anger, whose consequences lead to destruction. TAB-FULL: Those under anger are the people God describes as cursed and punished in Qur'an 5:60; He informs believers of their fate and shows them the route to salvation out of mercy. | mentions 5:60 TAB-FULL reporting بعضهم: One theological account says God's anger is the imposition of punishment in this life or the next, citing the drowning of Pharaoh's people and the punishment described in Qur'an 5:60. | mentions 43:55, 5:60 TAB-FULL reporting بعضهم: A third account treats anger as a real divine attribute, intelligible by affirmation but unlike human anger, which involves agitation, pain, or harm; it is an attribute like knowledge and power without creaturely limitations. TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas glosses the astray as Christians whom God led astray through their fabrication about Him; the prayer asks for the true monotheistic faith, protection from Jewish wrath and Christian error, and mercy to prevent their punishment. THALABI reporting قيل: Another explanation calls anger a kind of punishment opposite to divine pleasure. MAWARDI reporting unattributed: A fourth interprets wrath as a kind of punishment named anger, just as God’s blessings are named mercy. MAWARDI-FULL: A fourth account calls a kind of punishment anger, just as God's bounty is called mercy. BAGHAWI: “Not those angered” means a path other than that of those God wills to punish for disobedience. IBNATIYYA: The author says scripture repeatedly describes God’s wrath against Jews, citing their incurring wrath and the punishment of Sabbath-breakers. | mentions 2:61, 3:112, 5:60, 2:65 IBNATIYYA: Here divine wrath means God’s manifesting ordeals, punishments, humiliation, and similar signs that He has emphatically distanced them from His mercy. IBNATIYYA-FULL: God's anger means that he exposes them to trials, punishments, and humiliation, showing their decisive removal from his mercy. RAZI-FULL: Razi poses the problem that divine anger follows knowledge of human sin: if God's knowledge is eternal, why create people destined for endless punishment and why create what He is angry with? RAZI-FULL: Human anger is a bodily change, impossible for God; psychological terms applied to God signify their final effect, so divine anger means willing harm, while divine modesty means leaving an act. QURTUBI: Arabic anger connotes severity: a harsh person is ghadub, a fierce serpent al-ghadub, and a folded camel-hide shield ghadba for its toughness. QURTUBI-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A hadith says charity extinguishes the Lord’s wrath, treating wrath as an attribute of action when it means the punishment. BAYDAWI-FULL: Divine anger denotes its ultimate effect, punishment; عليهم is a passive-subject phrase, unlike the earlier construction, and لا reinforces the negation in غير. ABUHAYYAN: The passive wording for those angered is tactful in a humble plea: the worshipper attributes favor to the One asked for guidance but avoids confronting Him with the description of vengeance. SAMIN-DURR: When attributed to God, anger means retribution; غضبت لفلان is said of a living person and غضبت به of a dead one. BURSEVI: Divine anger cannot mean its human beginning, so it denotes its end or effect, such as punishment, retribution, or painful seizure. BURSEVI: Divine anger perfects the function of the left hand: mercy and severity have distinct effects, and severity completes what cannot be repaired by mercy. | mentions 39:67 ELMALILI: A temporary punishment or pain that prepares future blessings does not make someone one of those under wrath; outcomes determine the judgment, as 2:155 illustrates. | mentions 2:155 IBNASHUR: Because literal anger entails change, which cannot apply to God, the attribution means its consequence—punishment, humiliation, or worldly exclusion—or a representational metaphor. IBNASHUR: Divine anger is God’s treatment of those who oppose guidance, ranging up to the lasting punishment of polytheists and hypocrites; dislike is lesser, and both differ from creative will. | mentions 39:7, 6:112, 10:99 IBNASHUR reporting بعض ملوك الفرس: An unnamed Persian king said his reign endured because he punished according to the offense rather than according to anger. IBNASHUR-FULL: Divine anger means God's treatment of those who leave guidance and disobey, culminating in punishment; anger, dislike, pleasure, and love differ from creative will. | mentions 39:7, 6:112, 10:99 IBNASHUR-FULL: God cannot literally undergo anger or change; the attribution must mean its effects, such as punishment, humiliation, curse, or exclusion, or function as a representational metaphor. - 1:7/q17/p3 Divine anger is condemnation or blame — TAB reporting بعضهم: Another view takes divine anger as God's blame of people and their deeds, and verbal condemnation of them. TAB: Jews and Christians are both astray and under wrath; God labels each group by a real, recognizable trait, without implying that it lacks the other's blameworthy traits. TAB-FULL reporting بعضهم: A second account understands divine anger as blame for their conduct and verbal reproach or insult. TAB-FULL: Both Jews and Christians are astray and under wrath, but God labels each by a true, recognizable characteristic, without listing every blameworthy trait of either group. THALABI reporting قيل: A third explanation defines anger as condemnation of sinners for the ugliness of their acts. MAWARDI reporting unattributed: A third interpretation is that God’s wrath means His condemnation of them. MAWARDI-FULL: A third account interprets God's anger as His condemnation of them. IBNKATHIR: Qurʾanic references to Jewish anger and wrongdoing support the identification: Israel's children incur anger for rejecting revelation and are condemned for sin and failure to stop wrongdoing. | mentions 2:90, 5:60, 5:78, 5:79 BIQAI-FULL reporting الحرالي: Al-Harali defines the condemned as those who intentionally oppose guidance and thereby incur divine wrath, or those who turn toward guidance then stray without intending to. | mentions 93:6 ITQAN: The verse explicitly attributes favor to God, but avoids saying “those with whom You were angry,” shifting expression so anger is not verbally attributed to God in direct address. IBNASHUR-FULL: Angered people represent deliberate religious disregard or far-fetched interpretation, while astray people err through poor understanding or inattention; both are blameworthy. IBNASHUR-FULL: Anger for oneself is blameworthy, but anger defending public and religious interests is praiseworthy; the Prophet did not get angry for himself but did for God's limits. SAMARRAI-ASRAR: The Fātiḥa explicitly attributes favor to God (‘You bestowed favor’) while describing the blameworthy as those under anger and those astray. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: The passive المغضوب عليهم leaves the agent open so the condemned face anger from God, angels, people, and even their own skins. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: Repeating لا ensures exclusion of either condemned group on its own; without it the wording might exclude only those who combine anger and error, as the two-part prohibition analogy shows. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: The angered oppose the favored just as anger opposes grace; the chapter's ending gathers its opening praise, judgment, exclusive worship, reliance, and guidance into the fates of the condemned. [16 notes: TAB(بعضهم); TAB-FULL(بعضهم); THALABI(قيل); MAWARDI(unattributed); MAWARDI-FULL; IBNKATHIR; BIQAI-FULL(الحرالي); ITQAN; IBNASHUR-FULL; SAMARRAI-ASRAR; SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT]
- 1:7/q17/p4 Anger is a real divine attribute unlike human agitation — TAB reporting بعضهم: A third view affirms an intelligible divine attribute called anger, while distinguishing it from human agitation and affirming that God's essence is free of affliction. TAB-FULL reporting السدي عن أبي مالك وأبي صالح عن ابن عباس ومرة الهمداني عن ابن مسعود وناس من أصحاب النبي: The report attributed through al-Suddī to these early authorities identifies those under wrath as Jews. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting عدي بن حاتم: A report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, attributed to the Prophet, identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; no grading is stated. WAHIDI-BASIT: For the standard reading, the sense is the path of those favored who are neither under wrath nor astray; denying these traits implicitly attributes them to others, supporting implication in discourse. RAZI-FULL reporting أصحابنا: Razi's Ash'arite school reads the sequence as God's anger causing their misguidance; the reverse would make a human attribute affect God, which is impossible. BAYDAWI: When anger is attributed to God, it denotes the final outcome or endpoint, not an emotion in God. IBNKATHIR: The verse attributes favor directly to God, leaves the agent of anger unexpressed although God is its true agent, and assigns misguidance to those who embody it although He misleads by His decree; cited verses affirm His exclusive control of guidance and misguidance. | mentions 58:14, 18:17, 7:186 BURHAN reporting قيل: One explanation says praise uses third person because it ranks below worship, while direct address elevates the worshipper's encounter; similarly, blessing is explicitly attributed to God but anger is phrased obliquely as a matter of etiquette. | mentions 6:101 BURSEVI: A common reading identifies those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians, but neither group's label is exclusive because Scripture attributes both traits to both. ALUSI: Following the early generations, al-Ālūsī affirms anger as an eternal divine attribute fitting God’s majesty without specifying how or claiming to know its reality, like mercy. ALUSI: The blessing is directly attributed to God as a deferential appeal for guidance to those whose favor is established; anger is put in the passive and left unassigned out of courtesy in a humble request for kindness. ALUSI-FULL: Alusi follows the early community: anger is a divine attribute befitting God, whose reality and manner are unknown, like mercy; “My mercy precedes My anger” concerns the greater or earlier manifestation of mercy. ELMALILI: Qur'an also attributes divine wrath to disbelievers generally and describes those who reject God's way as far astray, supporting the comprehensive reading. | mentions 16:106 [13 notes: TAB(بعضهم); TAB-FULL(السدي عن أبي مالك وأبي صالح عن ابن عباس ومرة الهمداني عن ابن مسعود وناس من أصحاب النبي); WAHIDI-BASIT(عدي بن حاتم); BAYDAWI; IBNKATHIR; BURHAN(قيل); BURSEVI; ALUSI; ALUSI-FULL; ELMALILI; RAZI-FULL(أصحابنا)+; WAHIDI-BASIT+]

## 1:7/q20 What does the repeated negation before 'the astray' do?  [وَلَا · grammar]
turns on: Whether lā is a true negative, verbal addition, or disambiguating marker.
- 1:7/q20/p1 Lā is a genuine negation coordinated with ghayr — MAJAZ: Abū Khirāsh’s verse supplies a further example of lā continuing a negative coordination in ولا البكر. MAJAZ: In wa-lā al-ḍāllīn, lā reinforces the preceding negation; Arabic likewise says ‘without good or blessing’ and ‘no benefit nor defense.’ TAB reporting نحويو الكوفة: The Kufans reject the exception analysis: “nor” is a negative conjunction, and Arabic coordinates a negative with a negative, not a negation with an exception. TAB reporting بعض أهل البصرة: Some Basrans call lā before “the astray” an added particle that completes the expression but contributes no negation, citing poetry and “what prevented you from not prostrating?” | mentions 7:12 TAB: Al-Ṭabarī agrees with the Kufans: lā is a true negation coordinated with the negative sense of ghayr, so the request is for the path of the favored, not the wrathful or astray. TAB-FULL reporting نحويو الكوفيين: Kufan grammarians reject exception: coordinating the negative wa-lā al-ḍāllīn with an exception is unattested, since Arabic coordinates exception with exception and negation with negation. TAB-FULL reporting بعض نحويي الكوفة: A Kufan grammarian rejects ghayr meaning other than because lā cannot coordinate with سوى absent a prior negative; he also rejects starting lā with an omitted-negation sense without previous negation. TAB-FULL reporting نحوي من الكوفة: The Kufan answer reads al-ʿAjjāj's lā as genuine negation and explains the other poems' apparent filler lā by the negative earlier in each sentence, as in the line about Abū Bakr and ʿUmar. TAB-FULL: He prefers the Kufan analysis: lā cannot begin as an omitted negative or coordinate with other than or an exception; since ghayr can mean exception, negation, or other than, the only valid reading here is negation, making the verse ask to avoid both groups. ZAJJAJ: Al-ḍāllīn is coordinated with al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim; lā is allowed because ghayr already carries negation, as in ghayr ḍārib meaning “not striking.” NAHHAS: The Kufan objection is not binding because lā here carries a negative sense. THALABI reporting الزجاج: Al-Zajjāj says lā may coordinate with ghayr because ghayr already carries negation, effectively meaning neither those angered nor those astray; this is not possible when ghayr means ‘other than.’ WAHIDI-BASIT reporting الفراء: Al-Farrāʾ rejects accusative ghayr as an exception, arguing that a positive exception cannot be followed by negative lā in coordination. WAHIDI-BASIT: Those allowing exception say an exception resembles negation, so all came except Zayd can mean all came, not Zayd; lā can coordinate by meaning or be an addition. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب النظم: The author of al-Naẓm says lā in wa-lā al-ḍāllīn prevents misreading al-ḍāllīn as coordinated with those favored; it marks coordination with ghayr, which implies negation. KASHSHAF: La appears because ghayr already carries negation: neither the angered nor the astray. KASHSHAF-FULL: The negative lā before astray is included because ghayr already carries a negative sense. ABUHAYYAN reporting الأخفش والزجاج: Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjāj allow accusative ghayr as a disconnected exception because the preceding wording does not include those who are astray; some readers reject this analysis because of lā. ABUHAYYAN: Lā reinforces the negation already contained in ghayr and is attached to المغضوب عليهم to avoid suggesting that الضالين is coordinated with الذين. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The lā before “those astray” reinforces negation; placing it in the coordination prevents “those astray” from being mistaken as part of “those You favored.” SAMIN-DURR: Ghayr can function like illā for exception, as an adjective by analogy with illā, or like lā for negation, permitting its governed object to precede it. SAMIN-DURR: Ghayr is also read in the accusative as a circumstantial from alladhīna or ʿalayhim, or as a disjoint exception; al-Farrāʾ rejects the latter because lā lacks a preceding negation. SAMIN-DURR: Lā reinforces the negation already carried by ghayr and blocks reading al-ḍāllīn as coordinated with those blessed; Kufans instead equate it with ghayr, and ʿUmar reportedly read that way. IBNKATHIR reporting عمر بن الخطاب: ʿUmar read “and other than the astray”; Ibn Kathir says this report has a sound chain and treats it as explanatory, supporting emphatic negation and separation of the two paths. BIQAI: Ghayr conveys negation rather than an exception: the wording excludes those characterized by the trait from the outset and avoids suggesting a merely lesser class. BIQAI-FULL: Removing the object of bestowed favor broadens the wording; the negation excludes the angry and astray as separate failures, one in action and the other in knowledge. ALUSI reporting الأخفش: A report ascribed to al-Akhfash treats the exception as semantically negative, allowing lā to coordinate by meaning and removing al-Farrāʾ’s objection. ALUSI reporting عمر بن الخطاب: A reading with wa-ghayr in place of wa-lā is reported from ʿUmar and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr; the muṣḥaf’s mutawātir reading is wa-lā, which reinforces the negation implicit in ghayr. ALUSI-FULL reporting عمر بن الخطاب وعبدالله بن الزبير: A reading attributed to ʿUmar and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr adds ghayr before “those astray”; the canonical reading is otherwise, and al-Kufis treat ghayr as negation reinforcing the phrase. ALUSI-FULL reporting الأخفش: Al-Akhfash allows the accusative as a connected or disconnected exception if “favor” is broad; al-Farraʾ forbids joining negative lā to an exceptive phrase meaning “other than.” IBNASHUR-FULL: Ibn ʿĀshūr calls that explanation far-fetched: لا simply reinforces the negation already conveyed by ghayr in a normal negative coordination. | mentions 5:19 SAMARRAI-LAMASAT reporting حاشية الجرجاني على الكشاف: In negation, the added lā after the coordinating conjunction explicitly attaches negation to each item and prevents reading only the combined pair as negated. [27 notes: MAJAZ; TAB(بعض أهل البصرة); TAB-FULL(نحوي من الكوفة); ZAJJAJ; THALABI(الزجاج); WAHIDI-BASIT(صاحب النظم); KASHSHAF; KASHSHAF-FULL; ABUHAYYAN(الأخفش والزجاج); ABUHAYYAN-FULL; SAMIN-DURR; IBNKATHIR(عمر بن الخطاب); BIQAI; BIQAI-FULL; ALUSI(الأخفش,عمر بن الخطاب); ALUSI-FULL(الأخفش,عمر بن الخطاب وعبدالله بن الزبير); IBNASHUR-FULL; SAMARRAI-LAMASAT(حاشية الجرجاني على الكشاف); SAMIN-DURR+; TAB-FULL+; TAB+; TAB(نحويو الكوفة)-; TAB-FULL(بعض نحويي الكوفة,نحويو الكوفيين)-; NAHHAS-; WAHIDI-BASIT(الفراء)-]
- 1:7/q20/p2 Lā is added or redundant, reinforcing the expression — FARRA: Farra rejects the claim that ghayr in al-ḥamd means “other than” and lā is extra; extra lā requires a preceding negation. FARRA: The verse “in a well without ḥawr” does not prove an extra lā: here lā is a true negation, while poetry allows an extra lā after an earlier negation. MAJAZ: In ghayr al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim wa-lā al-ḍāllīn, the first lā is an extra particle completing the phrase, effectively ‘and the straying.’ MAJAZ: Al-ʿAjjāj’s phrase fī biʾr lā ḥawr has an extra lā; the intended sense is a well of ruin or destruction. MAJAZ: Abū al-Najm’s ألا تسخرا means أن يسخرن, showing an extra lā; al-qafandar means ugly and repulsive. MAJAZ: In the cited line, ‘they reproach me in amusement ألا أحبه’ means ‘that I love it,’ with lā treated as extra. NAHHAS reporting البصريون: Basrans treat lā as extra; the Kufans understand it as ghayr. WAHIDI-BASIT: Before an indefinite, lā may be extra; if not extra, it either joins the noun as one genitive compound or contributes negation without affecting the noun's case. IBNATIYYA reporting الطبري: Al-Ṭabarī calls lā extra, citing a rajaz line where ألا تسخرا is understood as أن تسخر. IBNATIYYA: The author rejects al-Ṭabarī’s reading of al-Aḥwaṣ’s line as proof that lā is extra: it means they reproach him for wanting not to love amusement, so lā is operative. TABRISI reporting البصريون: The Basran grammarians take lā as an emphatic extra particle of negation, eliminating an ambiguity that could otherwise allow separate readings of the coordinated words. TABRISI reporting علي بن عيسى الرماني: Al-Rummani explains lā in the exception reading as an extra particle, like in the line about a pit of destruction and the Qur'anic phrase 'that you should not prostrate'. | mentions 7:12 QURTUBI-FULL reporting الطبري: Al-Tabari treats lā in “and not those astray” as redundant, as in the verse “what prevented you from not prostrating.” | mentions 7:12 BAYDAWI: The lā is an extra particle reinforcing the negation already expressed by ghayr, as in the cited grammatical examples. ABUHAYYAN: Some permit accusative ghayr as an exception by treating lā as extra, since they say lā is extra only after prior negation; they cite Qurʾanic and poetic examples, while other grammarians take lā as genuinely negative. ABUHAYYAN: Abū Ḥayyān says the alleged proof that lā is extra in the verse of the generous man is not decisive: lā itself is the object of أبى, and البخل is its apposition or a causal object. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: ʿAlā can also mean about, with, in, alongside, because of, from, or serve as an extra particle. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting القراء: Al-Qurrāʾ allow lā to be extra only after a prior negation, citing poetic usage and 17:61; Abū Ḥayyān discusses competing analyses of the cited poems. | mentions 17:61 IBNKATHIR reporting بعض النحاة: Some grammarians call la before the astray redundant and cite an al-ʿAjjaj line; Ibn Kathir rejects this and treats it as reinforcing the negation. BURHAN: After a conjunction preceded by negation or prohibition, extra لا reinforces the negation; he classifies لا in this verse that way. ALUSI reporting الفراء: Al-Farrāʾ rejects the exception analysis because ghayr then means siwā and the negative lā cannot be coordinated with it unless lā is treated as extra; al-Ālūsī notes the usage after wāw is unattested. | mentions 7:12 IBNASHUR: He takes the extra lā as verbal reinforcement of negation after ghayr, following Arabic coordination under negation, as in 5:19. | mentions 5:19 IBNASHUR reporting السيد: Al-Sayyid says lā prevents the mistaken inference that only the combined group is excluded, allowing one group to remain affirmed; the author distinguishes this from the semantic extra lā in 7:12. | mentions 7:12 IBNASHUR-FULL: This extra لا is only verbal reinforcement and keeps the meaning negative, unlike the particle in the command to Adam not to prostrate. | mentions 7:12 [20 notes: MAJAZ; NAHHAS(البصريون); WAHIDI-BASIT; IBNATIYYA(الطبري); TABRISI(البصريون,علي بن عيسى الرماني); QURTUBI-FULL(الطبري); BAYDAWI; ABUHAYYAN; ABUHAYYAN-FULL(القراء); IBNKATHIR(بعض النحاة); BURHAN; ALUSI(الفراء); IBNASHUR(السيد); IBNASHUR-FULL; FARRA-; IBNATIYYA-; ABUHAYYAN-]
- 1:7/q20/p3 Lā prevents attaching the astray to those favored — IBNATIYYA reporting مكي: Makkī says lā prevents readers from mistaking the astray for a coordinate of الذين. BURHAN reporting أبو عبيدة: Abu Ubayda explains the added لا as preventing the mistaken reading that those astray are the same people as those under wrath. BURHAN reporting قيل: Another explanation is that لا prevents readers from treating الضالين as coordinated directly with الذين. IBNASHUR: Lā coordinates the straying with the objects of ghayr; contrary to the reported view of Makki ibn Abī Ṭālib, it is not needed to prevent attachment to the favored. IBNASHUR-FULL reporting مكي ابن أبي طالب: Makkī b. Abī Ṭālib says the repeated لا prevents readers from connecting those astray to the favored people. [5 notes: IBNATIYYA(مكي); BURHAN(أبو عبيدة,قيل); IBNASHUR-FULL(مكي ابن أبي طالب); IBNASHUR+]
