## 1:7/q21 What does 'the astray' mean in Arabic?  [ٱلضَّآلِّينَ · meaning]
- 1:7/q21/p1 In wa-lā al-ḍāllīn, ghayr means lā, so lā is repeated; if ghayr meant “other than,” repeating lā would be ungrammatical. — FARRA: In wa-lā al-ḍāllīn, ghayr means lā, so lā is repeated; if ghayr meant “other than,” repeating lā would be ungrammatical. [1 notes: FARRA]
- 1:7/q21/p2 In Arabic, anyone deviating from the intended road is astray; Christians are so called because they miss the truth and take a religious route other than the straight one. — TAB-FULL: In Arabic, anyone deviating from the intended road is astray; Christians are so called because they miss the truth and take a religious route other than the straight one. [1 notes: TAB-FULL]
- 1:7/q21/p3 The misguided are those who have strayed from guidance; the root suggests loss or disappearance, and a poetic line uses it of a people who lost their way. — THALABI: The misguided are those who have strayed from guidance; the root suggests loss or disappearance, and a poetic line uses it of a people who lost their way. [1 notes: THALABI]
- 1:7/q21/p4 Al-Zajjāj says lā may coordinate with ghayr because ghayr already carries negation, effectively meaning neither those angered nor those astray; this is not possible when ghayr means ‘other than.’ — THALABI reporting الزجاج: Al-Zajjāj says lā may coordinate with ghayr because ghayr already carries negation, effectively meaning neither those angered nor those astray; this is not possible when ghayr means ‘other than.’ [1 notes: THALABI(الزجاج)]
- 1:7/q21/p5 The root of ḍalāl is disappearance: water disappears into milk, and a disbeliever disappears from the path of truth; 32:10 uses the word for bodies lost in earth after death.; cited verses: 32:10 — WAHIDI-BASIT: The root of ḍalāl is disappearance: water disappears into milk, and a disbeliever disappears from the path of truth; 32:10 uses the word for bodies lost in earth after death. | mentions 32:10 [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT]
- 1:7/q21/p6 Thus the astray person is absent from truth and has deviated from right guidance; the verb has reported variant forms. — WAHIDI-BASIT: Thus the astray person is absent from truth and has deviated from right guidance; the verb has reported variant forms. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT]
- 1:7/q21/p7 The people who went astray are the Christians; Muslims ask to avoid their deviation from truth as well as the Jews' incurred anger. — WAHIDI-WAJIZ: The people who went astray are the Christians; Muslims ask to avoid their deviation from truth as well as the Jews' incurred anger. [1 notes: WAHIDI-WAJIZ]
- 1:7/q21/p8 The phrase means those who are not astray from guidance; the root of misguidance conveys destruction and disappearance, like water disappearing in milk. — BAGHAWI: The phrase means those who are not astray from guidance; the root of misguidance conveys destruction and disappearance, like water disappearing in milk. [1 notes: BAGHAWI]
- 1:7/q21/p9 An unnamed view identifies those angered as the Jews and those astray as the Christians, citing verses on their anger and earlier deviation.; cited verses: 5:60, 5:77 — BAGHAWI: An unnamed view identifies those angered as the Jews and those astray as the Christians, citing verses on their anger and earlier deviation. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 [1 notes: BAGHAWI]
- 1:7/q21/p10 The straying ones are those who departed from guidance; the root sense of straying is perishing or disappearing, like water disappearing into milk. — BAGHAWI-FULL: The straying ones are those who departed from guidance; the root sense of straying is perishing or disappearing, like water disappearing into milk. [1 notes: BAGHAWI-FULL]
- 1:7/q21/p11 Ḍalāl fundamentally means destruction and, in religion, departure from truth; the author cites 'we were lost in the earth' and 'He destroyed their works'.; cited verses: 47:8 — TABRISI: Ḍalāl fundamentally means destruction and, in religion, departure from truth; the author cites 'we were lost in the earth' and 'He destroyed their works'. | mentions 47:8 [1 notes: TABRISI]
- 1:7/q21/p12 Following the second, misguided party brings loss and destruction; Razi introduces the Quranic rebuke against worshipping what cannot hear, see, or help. — RAZI-FULL: Following the second, misguided party brings loss and destruction; Razi introduces the Quranic rebuke against worshipping what cannot hear, see, or help. [1 notes: RAZI-FULL]
- 1:7/q21/p13 Ḍalāl means leaving the proper course and the path of truth; milk disappearing in water illustrates the root’s sense of vanishing.; cited verses: 32:10 — QURTUBI-FULL: Ḍalāl means leaving the proper course and the path of truth; milk disappearing in water illustrates the root’s sense of vanishing. | mentions 32:10 [1 notes: QURTUBI-FULL]
- 1:7/q21/p14 The original form was al-ḍāllilīn; the first lām lost its vowel and assimilated into the next, and Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani uses a hamza reading to avoid adjacent still consonants. — QURTUBI-FULL: The original form was al-ḍāllilīn; the first lām lost its vowel and assimilated into the next, and Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani uses a hamza reading to avoid adjacent still consonants. [1 notes: QURTUBI-FULL]
- 1:7/q21/p15 The root of ḍalāl carries senses including perishing, disappearing, being lost or ignorant, straying, bewilderment, and wavering; Qurʾanic uses can mean lack of detailed knowledge or love. — ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The root of ḍalāl carries senses including perishing, disappearing, being lost or ignorant, straying, bewilderment, and wavering; Qurʾanic uses can mean lack of detailed knowledge or love. [1 notes: ABUHAYYAN-FULL]
- 1:7/q21/p16 Ḍalāl may mean concealment or disappearance, destruction, deviation from the straight path, or forgetfulness; the forgetfulness sense in 2:282 is supported by its following remembrance clause.; cited verses: 32:10, 2:282 — SAMIN-DURR: Ḍalāl may mean concealment or disappearance, destruction, deviation from the straight path, or forgetfulness; the forgetfulness sense in 2:282 is supported by its following remembrance clause. | mentions 32:10, 2:282 [1 notes: SAMIN-DURR]
- 1:7/q21/p17 Those subject to anger know the truth but turn away; the astray lack knowledge and wander without reaching the truth. — IBNKATHIR: Those subject to anger know the truth but turn away; the astray lack knowledge and wander without reaching the truth. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR]
- 1:7/q21/p18 Al-Harali says the condemned intentionally show defiance, while the astray turn toward guidance and deviate without intending it; Amin expresses a decisive plea for a response. — BIQAI-FULL reporting الحرالي: Al-Harali says the condemned intentionally show defiance, while the astray turn toward guidance and deviate without intending it; Amin expresses a decisive plea for a response. [1 notes: BIQAI-FULL(الحرالي)]
- 1:7/q21/p19 Misguidance means deliberately or accidentally leaving the sound path; sinners fail in action, while the ignorant fail in knowledge.; cited verses: 4:93, 10:32 — BURSEVI: Misguidance means deliberately or accidentally leaving the sound path; sinners fail in action, while the ignorant fail in knowledge. | mentions 4:93, 10:32 [1 notes: BURSEVI]
- 1:7/q21/p20 Ḍalāl originally means destruction, as in the verses about being lost in the earth and God destroying deeds; in religion it means departing from truth.; cited verses: 32:10, 47:8 — ALUSI: Ḍalāl originally means destruction, as in the verses about being lost in the earth and God destroying deeds; in religion it means departing from truth. | mentions 32:10, 47:8 [1 notes: ALUSI]
- 1:7/q21/p21 Ḍalāl originally means destruction, as in 32:10, and in religion means departure from truth; the text also cites a usage where God “destroys” deeds.; cited verses: 32:10, 47:1 — ALUSI-FULL: Ḍalāl originally means destruction, as in 32:10, and in religion means departure from truth; the text also cites a usage where God “destroys” deeds. | mentions 32:10, 47:1 [1 notes: ALUSI-FULL]
- 1:7/q21/p22 Dalaal means straying from the right path, intentionally or accidentally, opposite guidance; it can progress from heedlessness or bewilderment to loss and ruin. — ELMALILI: Dalaal means straying from the right path, intentionally or accidentally, opposite guidance; it can progress from heedlessness or bewilderment to loss and ruin. [1 notes: ELMALILI]
- 1:7/q21/p23 Ḍalāl is missing the intended road through error, knowingly or unknowingly, like a lost camel; its use for religious or intellectual error is metaphorical. — IBNASHUR: Ḍalāl is missing the intended road through error, knowingly or unknowingly, like a lost camel; its use for religious or intellectual error is metaphorical. [1 notes: IBNASHUR]
- 1:7/q21/p24 Religious misguidance opposes complete faith and can culminate in sealing and veiling; the angered deliberately deviate under worldly desire, while astray groups distort true religions through error. — IBNASHUR-FULL: Religious misguidance opposes complete faith and can culminate in sealing and veiling; the angered deliberately deviate under worldly desire, while astray groups distort true religions through error. [1 notes: IBNASHUR-FULL]
- 1:7/q21/p25 The Qur'an depicts an upward route and a downward route; those struck by wrath fall, while misguidance is associated with shirk, producing three groups: believers, the wrathful, and the wandering astray.; cited verses: 7:40, 20:81, 2:108 — TABATABAI: The Qur'an depicts an upward route and a downward route; those struck by wrath fall, while misguidance is associated with shirk, producing three groups: believers, the wrathful, and the wandering astray. | mentions 7:40, 20:81, 2:108 [1 notes: TABATABAI]
- 1:7/q21/p26 The blessed are those who have followed the straight path, while those astray are lost from it; the Quran often pairs guidance and misguidance as opposites.; cited verses: 16:93, 2:26 — SAMARRAI-LAMASAT: The blessed are those who have followed the straight path, while those astray are lost from it; the Quran often pairs guidance and misguidance as opposites. | mentions 16:93, 2:26 [1 notes: SAMARRAI-LAMASAT]
- 1:7/q21/p27 Corrupt knowledge produces misguidance and corrupt intention produces anger; these are the two root diseases of the heart. — SAMARRAI-LAMASAT reporting التفسير القيم: Corrupt knowledge produces misguidance and corrupt intention produces anger; these are the two root diseases of the heart. [1 notes: SAMARRAI-LAMASAT(التفسير القيم)]
- 1:7/q21/p28 On a vertical ascent reading, wrath represents descent from God and straying represents horizontal wandering; together they symbolize three spatial dimensions and human possibilities. — STUDYQURAN: On a vertical ascent reading, wrath represents descent from God and straying represents horizontal wandering; together they symbolize three spatial dimensions and human possibilities. [1 notes: STUDYQURAN]

## 1:7/q22 Who are the astray?  [ٱلضَّآلِّينَ · referent]
turns on: Whether the Prophetic identifications specify the only referents or exemplify wider classes of disobedience and error.
- 1:7/q22/p1 The Christians, as an identified example or restricted referent — MUQATIL: The straying people are the polytheists, identified here as the Christians. ABDURRAZZAQ reporting النبي: The Prophet identifies Christians as the astray when asked who they are at Wādī al-Qurā. IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB: Those who are astray are the Christians. TAB reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: In reports from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, the Prophet identifies the astray as the Christians. TAB reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: In the Wādī al-Qurā report, the Prophet answers that the people asked about are the astray, meaning the Christians. TAB reporting مجاهد: Mujāhid identifies the astray as the Christians. TAB reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbās, through al-Ḍaḥḥāk, glosses the phrase as the Christians' way, whom God led astray through their false claim about Him. TAB reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbās, in a report through Ibn Jurayj, identifies the astray as the Christians. TAB reporting ابن عباس، ابن مسعود، وناس من أصحاب النبي: The report transmitted by al-Suddī from early authorities identifies the astray as the Christians. TAB reporting الربيع: Al-Rabīʿ identifies the astray as the Christians. TAB reporting عبد الرحمن بن زيد: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd identifies the astray as the Christians. TAB reporting زيد: Zayd, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd's father, identifies the astray as the Christians. TAB: In Arabic, anyone who departs from the intended route and follows an unsound way is astray; Christians receive this label for missing the truth and taking a wrong religious path. TAB: Jews and Christians are both astray and under wrath; God labels each group by a real, recognizable trait, without implying that it lacks the other's blameworthy traits. TAB reporting بعض أهل الغباء من القدرية: Some ignorant Qadarites infer from calling Christians astray, without calling them those who mislead, that God has no causal role in their acts of misguidance. TAB-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عدي بن حاتم: The Prophet identifies those astray as Christians when asked about the verse. TAB-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عدي بن حاتم: The Prophet tells ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim that those astray are Christians; further routes repeat this identification. TAB-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عبد الله بن شقيق: Reports from a questioner during the siege at Wādī al-Qurā have the Prophet identify the people asked about as Christians, the astray. TAB-FULL reporting مجاهد: Mujāhid identifies those astray as Christians. TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas glosses the astray as Christians whom God led astray through their fabrication about Him; the prayer asks for the true monotheistic faith, protection from Jewish wrath and Christian error, and mercy to prevent their punishment. TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس والسدي عن ابن عباس وابن مسعود وناس من أصحاب النبي وربيع وعبد الرحمن بن زيد وأبوه: The cited authorities—through Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī's report, Rabīʿ, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd and his father—identify those astray as Christians. TAB-FULL: In Arabic, anyone deviating from the intended road is astray; Christians are so called because they miss the truth and take a religious route other than the straight one. TAB-FULL: Both Jews and Christians are astray and under wrath, but God labels each by a true, recognizable characteristic, without listing every blameworthy trait of either group. TAB-FULL reporting بعض أهل الغباء من القدرية: Some Qadariyyah wrongly infer from calling Christians astray and Jews objects of wrath that human acts belong only to people and that God does not cause their misguidance; al-Ṭabarī says this betrays ignorance of Arabic attribution and the many verses naming God as guide and misguider. | mentions 10:22, 45:23 IBNABIHATIM reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; the author says exegetes do not disagree on this wording. IBNABIHATIM: The author says he knows no disagreement among exegetes over the identification of those astray as Christians and those under wrath as Jews. IBNABIHATIM reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: A second report from the Prophet likewise says the Jews incurred wrath and the Christians went astray. THALABI reporting رسول الله: In a report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, the Prophet identifies those angered with the Jews and those astray with the Christians. THALABI reporting رسول الله: At Wādī al-Qurā, the Prophet points to Jews fighting him as those angered and to Christians as the other party, those astray. THALABI: The author links divine anger against Jews to 5:60 and the description of Christians as astray to 5:77. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 MAWARDI reporting عدي بن حاتم: Adi ibn Hatim reports that the Prophet identified those under wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians; al-Mawardi says all exegetes agree. MAWARDI: Al-Mawardi says all exegetes agree that those under wrath are Jews and those astray are Christians. MAWARDI-FULL reporting عدي بن حاتم: He asked the Prophet who the angered and astray groups were; the Prophet identified them as Jews and Christians, respectively, as all exegetes agree. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting عدي بن حاتم: A report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, attributed to the Prophet, identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; no grading is stated. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting النبي: A second report says the Prophet at Wādī al-Qurā was asked by a man from Bali about two groups; he pointed to Jews as those under wrath and Christians as astray; no grading is stated. WAHIDI-QT: Those astray are Christians, and Muslims ask to avoid both their error and the Jews' incurred wrath. WAHIDI-WAJIZ: The people who went astray are the Christians; Muslims ask to avoid their deviation from truth as well as the Jews' incurred anger. BAGHAWI: An unnamed view identifies those angered as the Jews and those astray as the Christians, citing verses on their anger and earlier deviation. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 BAGHAWI-FULL: A reported identification makes the objects of wrath Jews and the straying ones Christians, supported by Quranic descriptions of each group. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 KASHSHAF: Those astray are identified as Christians, with 5:77 cited. | mentions 5:77 IBNATIYYA reporting ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد وعدي بن حاتم عن النبي: They identify those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; the same interpretation is reported from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim from the Prophet. IBNATIYYA: The committed Christians had followed a true religious law before Muḥammad’s law arrived; once it came, they went astray. IBNATIYYA: Other Christians were already astray because their accounts of Jesus diverged from the beginning. IBNATIYYA: He links the Christians’ error to the verse describing a people who strayed earlier, misled many, and left the right way. | mentions 5:77 IBNATIYYA: In answer to al-Ṭabarī’s question about assigning one label to each group, the author says Jewish transgression, obstinacy, rejection despite signs, and killing prophets characteristically warrant wrath; Christians’ basic unbelief is astray shared by all unbelievers. IBNATIYYA: Calling Christians astray does not support the Qadari argument that they created their own misguidance: as with a wall collapsing or a tree moving, God created their misguidance while they acquired the act of straying. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد: Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd identify those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians; ʿAdi ibn Hatim transmits this from the Prophet. IBNATIYYA-FULL: Christians who followed their prior law went astray once Muhammad's law arrived; others had already gone astray through their divided claims about Jesus. IBNATIYYA-FULL: The Qur'an says Christians followed desires of people who had previously strayed and misled many in 5:77. | mentions 5:77 IBNATIYYA-FULL: The author finds this answer insufficient: Jewish aggression, defiance, disbelief despite signs, and killing prophets especially warrant wrath, while Christians strayed from the start without these specific acts. IBNATIYYA-FULL: Calling Christians “astray” does not support Qadarite claims that they made themselves astray: the intransitive phrasing works like “the wall collapsed” or “the tree moved”; God created their error and they acquired it. TABRISI: The astray are identified as Christians, supported by the warning against those who went astray and led many astray. | mentions 5:77 TABRISI reporting الحسن البصري: Hasan says both Jews and Christians are both astray and under anger, though God marks each group by a distinguishing epithet despite their shared traits. TABRISI: This explanation identifies the angered as Jews and the astray as Christians. IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting عدي بن حاتم عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A report from ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, from the Prophet, identifies the objects of anger as Jews and the astray as Christians. RAZI-FULL reporting المشهور: The commonly reported identification makes those under wrath the Jews and those astray the Christians, citing the Qur'an's descriptions of each. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 QURTUBI reporting جمهور المفسرين: Most commentators identify those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; 2:61, 3:112, and 48:6 concern Jewish wrath, and 5:77 Christian error. | mentions 2:61, 3:112, 48:6, 5:77 QURTUBI-FULL reporting الجمهور: Most interpreters identify those under wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians; the Prophet’s explanation to ʿAdi ibn Hatim supports it, as do verses about their wrath and error. | mentions 3:112, 48:6, 5:77 BAYDAWI: One reported identification makes those astray the Christians, citing 5:77. | mentions 5:77 BAYDAWI-FULL: A reported interpretation identifies those under anger as Jews and those astray as Christians, linking them to 5:60 and 5:77; the identification is also transmitted as a Prophetic report. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 NASAFI reporting قيل: One view identifies those under anger as Jews, citing God’s curse and anger in 5:60, and those astray as Christians, citing their earlier error in 5:77. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 NASAFI-FULL: The reported identification takes the astray as Christians, citing the verse that says they went astray before. | mentions 5:77 QASHANI: The astray are like Christians who stop at inner lights and special mercy, overlooking God’s outward manifestation and losing vision of the beloved’s beauty throughout creation. ABUHAYYAN reporting ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd identify those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting ابن مسعود: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd identify those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians. IBNKATHIR: Jews are characterized by abandoning known truth and thus anger, while Christians seek a goal without knowledge of its way because they do not follow the true Messenger; each group is also both astray and under anger. IBNKATHIR: The Qurʾan calls the Jews recipients of anger and specifically describes Christians as astray, supporting the verse's characteristic labels. | mentions 5:60, 5:77 IBNKATHIR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: In the report from ʿAdi ibn Hatim, the Prophet identifies the angered as Jews and the astray as Christians; al-Tirmidhi grades this route hasan gharīb, and Ibn Kathir notes other routes and wordings. IBNKATHIR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: At Wadi al-Qura the Prophet points to Jews as the angered and Christians as the astray; other transmitters send the report without naming the eyewitness, while ʿUrwa's route names Ibn ʿUmar. IBNKATHIR reporting السدي: Al-Suddi, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud, and Companions of the Prophet, identifies the Jews as angered and Christians as astray. BURHAN: Putting those under wrath before those astray may convey disparagement: Jews preceded Christians historically and were nearer to the Muslims. DURR reporting الله: The astray are identified as Christians, led astray after guidance; the report cites 5:60. | mentions 5:60 DURR reporting قتادة: In Qatada's sequential gloss, the Day of Recompense is when creatures are repaid; the worship-prayer is what people should say and directs them to God; the straight path is named, the favored are prophets, the objects of anger are Jews, and the astray are Christians. DURR reporting الربيع بن أنس: Al-Rabīʿ b. Anas identifies the favored as prophets, those under wrath as Jews, and the astray as Christians. DURR reporting مجاهد: Mujāhid identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians. DURR reporting سعيد بن جبير: Saʿīd b. Jubayr identifies the objects of wrath and the astray as Jews and Christians. DURR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: At Wādī al-Qurā, the Prophet identified the objects of wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; ʿAbd Allāh b. Shaqīq reports the exchange. DURR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: During the siege of Wādī al-Qurā, the Prophet identified one group as Jews under wrath and the other as astray Christians. DURR reporting أبو ذر: Abū Dharr reports asking the Prophet, who answered that those under wrath are Jews and the astray are Christians. DURR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid transmits the Prophet’s identification of Jews under wrath and Christians astray. DURR reporting عدي بن حاتم: ʿAdī b. Ḥātim reports the Prophet’s identification of the objects of wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians; al-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan. DURR reporting ابن مسعود: Ibn Masʿūd identifies those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians. DURR reporting ابن أبي حاتم: Ibn Abī Ḥātim knows of no exegetical disagreement identifying those under wrath as Jews and the astray as Christians. DURR-FULL reporting ابن عباس: The people under anger are Jews and the misguided are Christians; the account links their fate to the cited description of apes, swine, and evil destination. | mentions 5:60 DURR-FULL reporting الربيع بن أنس: Al-Rabi ibn Anas identifies the favored as prophets, those under anger as Jews, and the astray as Christians. DURR-FULL reporting مجاهد: Mujahid identifies those under anger as Jews and the astray as Christians. DURR-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Asked at Wadi al-Qura who the people under anger and those astray were, the Prophet answered Jews and Christians respectively. DURR-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Several reports from questions at Wadi al-Qura say the Prophet identified those under anger as Jews and the other group as Christians who are astray. DURR-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A report through a man of Balayn likewise records the Prophet's answer: Jews are under anger and Christians astray. DURR-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Reports from Ismail ibn Abi Khalid, Adi ibn Hatim, Ibn Masud, and Mujahid repeat the identification of Jews with anger and Christians with misguidance. ITQAN: Despite many later interpretations, the Prophet, Companions, Successors, and their followers identify those who incurred anger as Jews and those astray as Christians; Ibn Abi Hatim knew of no exegetical disagreement. BURSEVI: A common reading identifies those angered as Jews and those astray as Christians, but neither group's label is exclusive because Scripture attributes both traits to both. ALUSI reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: Aḥmad transmits and Ibn Ḥibbān grades as ḥasan a Prophetic report identifying the objects of anger as Jews and the astray as Christians. ALUSI: Al-Ālūsī also reads the general terms broadly: those erring in outward works, such as sinners, are under anger; those erring in belief are astray. The Prophetic Jewish and Christian identifications remain sound specifications of the general wording. ALUSI reporting بعضهم: Some support the Christian identification from the verse warning against following the desires of a people who went astray. | mentions 5:77 ALUSI: Al-Ālūsī prefers the hadith as evidence: anger and straying are also ascribed generally to unbelievers, and both terms apply specifically to Jews and Christians. | mentions 16:106, 4:167, 5:60, 5:77 ALUSI: He offers several reasons for the order: Jews precede Christians historically; bestowal contrasts with retribution rather than misguidance; and Jews are more obstinate, corrupt, hostile to believers, and abased. ALUSI: Al-Ālūsī says Christians are less culpable and closer to Islam, and a person who is merely astray may still find guidance. ALUSI-FULL reporting رسول الله: The Prophet identifies those under anger as Jews and those astray as Christians; Ahmad transmits it and Ibn Hibban grades it sound, and Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud also transmit the interpretation. ALUSI-FULL reporting إبن أبي حاتم: Ibn Abi Hatim says he knows no disagreement among exegetes that the angry are Jews and the astray are Christians; Alusi rejects replacing this with generic categories of sinners and doctrinally mistaken people. ALUSI-FULL: Qur'anic citations can support the Jewish and Christian identifications, but anger and straying also describe unbelievers generally; Alusi says the hadith is the better proof. | mentions 5:60, 5:77, 16:106, 4:167 ALUSI-FULL: The angry are named before those astray because Jews preceded Christians historically; alternatively, favor contrasts semantically with retribution, or Jews are more hostile and corrupt. | mentions 5:82 ELMALILI: The Quran describes Christians as having strayed from the right way, citing 5:77. | mentions 5:77 ELMALILI: Ibn Abi Hatim, as quoted by al-Durr al-Manthur, says he knows of no exegetical disagreement identifying those under wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians. ELMALILI reporting Resûlullah: Elmalılı cites a hadith that Tirmidhi grades hasan, transmitted from Adi b. Hatim, in which the Prophet says Jews are under wrath and Christians are astray. ELMALILI: The defining Christian traits he lists amount to departure from the prophetic truth, whose consequence is punishment and misguidance despite outward worldly prosperity. IBNASHUR reporting النبي: A report in al-Tirmidhī, which the author grades ḥasan, names Jews as an example of the angered and Christians as an example of the straying, not as exclusive referents. IBNASHUR-FULL: Reports identifying the angered with Jews and the astray with Christians allude to famous examples, not exclusive meanings; asking to avoid both escalates protection from the more severe fate to the lesser. IBNASHUR-FULL reporting النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم: Jews exemplify the angered and Christians the astray; a ḥasan prophetic report in Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī supports the examples, not an exclusive interpretation. IBNASHUR-FULL: Reports from companions who witnessed revelation identify those who incurred wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: Some reports identify the strayed as Christians and those under wrath as Jews; the author says these are nearby examples in time and place, not an exhaustive identification. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT: A sound hadith identifies the angry as Jews and the astray as Christians; the Jews came earlier, fitting their precedence in the verse. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: The angered precede the astray because they know truth and reject it, are more culpable than the ignorant, and Jews preceded Christians; an authentic hadith identifies the groups accordingly. STUDYQURAN: A prophetic saying, not considered highly authentic, identifies those under wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians. | mentions 2:61, 2:90, 3:112, 5:60, 5:77 [114 notes: MUQATIL; ABDURRAZZAQ(النبي); IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB; TAB(ابن عباس,ابن عباس، ابن مسعود، وناس من أصحاب النبي,الربيع,بعض أهل الغباء من القدرية,رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم,زيد,عبد الرحمن بن زيد,مجاهد); TAB-FULL(ابن عباس,ابن عباس والسدي عن ابن عباس وابن مسعود وناس من أصحاب النبي وربيع وعبد الرحمن بن زيد وأبوه,النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عبد الله بن شقيق,النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عن عدي بن حاتم,بعض أهل الغباء من القدرية,مجاهد); IBNABIHATIM(رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم); THALABI(رسول الله); MAWARDI(عدي بن حاتم); MAWARDI-FULL(عدي بن حاتم); WAHIDI-BASIT(النبي,عدي بن حاتم); WAHIDI-QT; WAHIDI-WAJIZ; BAGHAWI; BAGHAWI-FULL; KASHSHAF; IBNATIYYA(ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد وعدي بن حاتم عن النبي); IBNATIYYA-FULL(ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد); TABRISI(الحسن البصري); IBNJAWZI-ZAD(عدي بن حاتم عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم); RAZI-FULL(المشهور); QURTUBI(جمهور المفسرين); BAYDAWI; BAYDAWI-FULL; NASAFI(قيل); NASAFI-FULL; QASHANI; ABUHAYYAN(ابن مسعود وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وابن زيد); ABUHAYYAN-FULL(ابن مسعود); IBNKATHIR(السدي,النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم); BURHAN; DURR(أبو ذر,ابن أبي حاتم,ابن مسعود,الربيع بن أنس,الله,النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم,سعيد بن جبير,عدي بن حاتم,قتادة,مجاهد); DURR-FULL(ابن عباس,الربيع بن أنس,النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم,مجاهد); ITQAN; BURSEVI; ALUSI(بعضهم,رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم); ALUSI-FULL(إبن أبي حاتم); ELMALILI(Resûlullah); IBNASHUR(النبي); IBNASHUR-FULL(النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم); KURANYOLU-TEFSIR; SAMARRAI-LAMASAT; SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT; STUDYQURAN; ALUSI-FULL(رسول الله)+; ALUSI+; QURTUBI-FULL(الجمهور)+]
- 1:7/q22/p2 Those lacking true knowledge or belief — SULAMI reporting ابن عطاء: Those under anger are abandoned, expelled, and humiliated; the astray have left God's guidance, knowledge, and guardianship. RAZI-FULL: A broader reading takes those under wrath as people who err in outward deeds, including sinners, and those astray as people who err in belief; the wording is general and should not be restricted without cause. RAZI-FULL: The verse divides people into the obedient who are favored, sinners under wrath, and those ignorant of religion or unbelievers who are astray. RAZI-FULL: Those with complete favor unite knowledge of truth for its own sake with doing good for its own sake; lacking practice makes sinners under wrath, while lacking knowledge makes people astray. | mentions 4:93, 10:32 RAZI-FULL: The verse establishes the immunity of prophets and angels from actions or beliefs contrary to the favored path: otherwise they would stray and could not be models or belong among those favored. | mentions 10:32 RAZI-FULL: The favored are complete in knowledge and practice, the condemned neglect righteous deeds, and the astray lack sound belief; asking for the favored path seeks the example of the sound group. BAYDAWI: Bayḍāwī also finds apt a general reading: sinners fail in action and incur wrath, while those ignorant of God fail in understanding and go astray. BAYDAWI-FULL: A further interpretation calls deliberate sinners angered and those ignorant of God astray: failure of action is impiety, while failure of understanding is error. | mentions 4:93 ABUHAYYAN: Ḍalāl can mean ruin, concealment, loss, ignorance of an object's location, waste, neglect, forgetting, departure from the proper route, bewilderment, or hesitation; Qurʾanic usage also includes lack of detailed knowledge and love. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The root of ḍalāl carries senses including perishing, disappearing, being lost or ignorant, straying, bewilderment, and wavering; Qurʾanic uses can mean lack of detailed knowledge or love. IBNKATHIR: Those subject to anger know the truth but turn away; the astray lack knowledge and wander without reaching the truth. BURSEVI: Misguidance means deliberately or accidentally leaving the sound path; sinners fail in action, while the ignorant fail in knowledge. | mentions 4:93, 10:32 IBNASHUR reporting قالوا: In religious usage, misguidance opposes full faith and ranges from neglecting recommended practice to unbelief; the author defines it as absence of guidance and notes sealing as its extreme form. IBNASHUR-FULL: It also rejects the fate of people who received guidance but failed to preserve their course and became astray through poor understanding of the blessing of knowledge. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT: People are either blessed, or wretched in two ways: knowing truth but violating it, or lacking knowledge of truth and being astray. | mentions 18:103-104 SAMARRAI-LAMASAT reporting البيضاوي: One proposed reading identifies the angry as sinners and the astray as those ignorant of God. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT reporting التفسير القيم: People divide by knowledge and practice: the knowledgeable doer is blessed, the knowledgeable follower of desire is angry upon, and the ignorant is astray; the first is more deserving of anger. STUDYQURAN: The verse prays to follow those whom God elevates in belief, knowledge, and uncorrupted faith, and to avoid disbelievers, some astray and some under wrath. | mentions 6:83, 58:11, 6:82 STUDYQURAN: Another interpretation associates disbelief with wrath and lesser sins with straying. STUDYQURAN: The Quran frequently describes disbelievers, those who exchange belief for disbelief, and caprice-followers without guidance as astray. | mentions 3:90, 2:108, 4:136, 4:167, 28:50 [20 notes: SULAMI(ابن عطاء); RAZI-FULL; BAYDAWI-FULL; ABUHAYYAN; ABUHAYYAN-FULL; IBNKATHIR; BURSEVI; IBNASHUR(قالوا); IBNASHUR-FULL; SAMARRAI-LAMASAT(البيضاوي,التفسير القيم); STUDYQURAN; BAYDAWI+; RAZI-FULL+]
- 1:7/q22/p3 Those who leave the Sunnah — THALABI reporting التستري: Al-Tustarī identifies innovation with those angered and departure from Sunna with those astray. BAGHAWI reporting سهل بن عبد الله: Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah says those astray are people who have left the Sunna. BAGHAWI-FULL reporting سهل بن عبد الله: Sahl b. Abd Allah interprets those under wrath as innovators and the straying ones as people departing from the Sunnah. QURTUBI-FULL: Another view calls innovators recipients of wrath and those who leave the sunnas astray; the author says this is good, though the Prophet’s interpretation is best. IBNASHUR-FULL: Misguidance is mistakenly taking a path other than the intended one, whether consciously or unknowingly; its religious use is metaphorical and ranges from neglecting sunnahs to disbelief. [5 notes: THALABI(التستري); BAGHAWI(سهل بن عبد الله); BAGHAWI-FULL(سهل بن عبد الله); IBNASHUR-FULL; QURTUBI-FULL+]
- 1:7/q22/p4 Polytheists — QURTUBI reporting قيل: An alternative says those under wrath are polytheists and the astray are hypocrites. QURTUBI-FULL reporting بعضهم: Other interpreters identify those under wrath as polytheists and those astray as hypocrites. ABUHAYYAN: Another reported identification makes those angered the Jews and those astray the polytheists; Abū Ḥayyān notes other views without specifying them here. [3 notes: QURTUBI(قيل); QURTUBI-FULL(بعضهم); ABUHAYYAN]
- 1:7/q22/p5 Hypocrites — RAZI-FULL: Razi also offers a possible reading in which those under wrath are unbelievers and those astray are hypocrites, following the order of groups in the opening of al-Baqara. | mentions 2:6, 2:8 ALUSI reporting الرازي: Al-Rāzī suggests that those under anger are unbelievers and the astray are hypocrites, analogizing to al-Baqara’s order of believers, unbelievers, and hypocrites; al-Ālūsī rejects the analogy against the Prophetic report. | mentions 2:1, 2:6, 2:8 ALUSI-FULL reporting الرازي: Al-Razi proposes that the angry are unbelievers and the astray are hypocrites, paralleling the opening of al-Baqara; Alusi rejects the analogy against the Prophet's explicit report. | mentions 2:1 STUDYQURAN: Some commentators identify those incurring wrath with idolaters and those astray with hypocrites. [2 notes: RAZI-FULL; STUDYQURAN; ALUSI(الرازي)-; ALUSI-FULL(الرازي)-]

## 1:7/q23 How is 'the astray' read and formed?  [ٱلضَّآلِّينَ · readings]

## 1:7/q24 How do the favored, angered, and astray differ?  [غَيْرِ ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ · interpretation]

## 1:7/q25 Why are the angered named before the astray?  [ٱلْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ · rhetoric]
- 1:7/q25/p1 The order follows historical sequence — ABUHAYYAN: Anger precedes misguidance in the wording although it results from it because it contrasts with favor: favor brings good and requital brings harm; the order also suits the sūra's cadence. ABUHAYYAN: The conjunctive wāw does not itself establish temporal priority; if Jews and Christians are intended, the order may reflect chronology or the Jews' greater hostility, as they came earlier. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Anger precedes misguidance despite resulting from it because it is paired antithetically with favor; the order also suits the verse-ending cadence and the conjunction itself implies no sequence. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: If the groups mean Jews and Christians, Jews come first because they appeared earlier or are more hostile. BURHAN: Putting those under wrath before those astray may convey disparagement: Jews preceded Christians historically and were nearer to the Muslims. ALUSI: He offers several reasons for the order: Jews precede Christians historically; bestowal contrasts with retribution rather than misguidance; and Jews are more obstinate, corrupt, hostile to believers, and abased. ALUSI-FULL: The angry are named before those astray because Jews preceded Christians historically; alternatively, favor contrasts semantically with retribution, or Jews are more hostile and corrupt. | mentions 5:82 SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT: The angered precede the astray because they know truth and reject it, are more culpable than the ignorant, and Jews preceded Christians; an authentic hadith identifies the groups accordingly. [8 notes: ABUHAYYAN; ABUHAYYAN-FULL; BURHAN; ALUSI; ALUSI-FULL; SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT]
- 1:7/q25/p2 Anger is graver or more hostile — MAWARDI: God singles out Jews as the objects of wrath because they are the most hostile. MAWARDI-FULL: Misguidance is the opposite of guidance, and Jews are singled out for anger because they are more intensely hostile. ALUSI-FULL reporting السلفي والديلمي وإبن عدي: A report says whoever lacks charity should curse the Jews; Alusi cites it in support of judging Jewish hostility more severe than that of Christians. [3 notes: MAWARDI; MAWARDI-FULL; ALUSI-FULL(السلفي والديلمي وإبن عدي)]
- 1:7/q25/p3 ʿUmar and Ubay read ghayr before both “those angered” and “those astray,” with reports varying between accusative and genitive on each. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting عمر بن الخطاب وأبي بن كعب: ʿUmar and Ubay read ghayr before both “those angered” and “those astray,” with reports varying between accusative and genitive on each. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(عمر بن الخطاب وأبي بن كعب)]
- 1:7/q25/p4 Razi also offers a possible reading in which those under wrath are unbelievers and those astray are hypocrites, following the order of groups in the opening of al-Baqara.; cited verses: 2:6, 2:8 — RAZI-FULL: Razi also offers a possible reading in which those under wrath are unbelievers and those astray are hypocrites, following the order of groups in the opening of al-Baqara. | mentions 2:6, 2:8 [1 notes: RAZI-FULL]
- 1:7/q25/p5 The names Lord and King are close to Merciful and All-Merciful; the three names in the closing surah answer desire, anger, and caprice in that order.; cited verses: 36:58, 25:26, 114:1, 114:2, 114:3 — RAZI-FULL: The names Lord and King are close to Merciful and All-Merciful; the three names in the closing surah answer desire, anger, and caprice in that order. | mentions 36:58, 25:26, 114:1, 114:2, 114:3 [1 notes: RAZI-FULL]
- 1:7/q25/p6 ʿUmar and Ubayy read ghayr before both “those under wrath” and “those astray”; the two forms are read in genitive or accusative. — QURTUBI-FULL reporting عمر بن الخطاب وأبي بن كعب: ʿUmar and Ubayy read ghayr before both “those under wrath” and “those astray”; the two forms are read in genitive or accusative. [1 notes: QURTUBI-FULL(عمر بن الخطاب وأبي بن كعب)]
- 1:7/q25/p7 Adding the second negation advances from refuge against the graver fate to the lesser: escaping anger-inducing error does not cover lesser misguidance; the order also suits the verse endings. — IBNASHUR: Adding the second negation advances from refuge against the graver fate to the lesser: escaping anger-inducing error does not cover lesser misguidance; the order also suits the verse endings. [1 notes: IBNASHUR]
- 1:7/q25/p8 The order fits the verse's cadence — SAMARRAI-LAMASAT reporting قيل: The passive avoids attributing anger directly to the God being addressed in a humble request for favor and also prepares the ending’s parallelism and rhyme. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT reporting البحر المحيط: Although anger results from misguidance, anger is placed beside blessing because blessing and retribution correspond semantically; the final wording also suits the rhyme. [2 notes: SAMARRAI-LAMASAT(البحر المحيط,قيل)]
- 1:7/q25/p9 Adding lā before the astray makes the exclusion apply to either group separately, rather than only excluding people who combine anger and misguidance. — SAMARRAI-LAMASAT: Adding lā before the astray makes the exclusion apply to either group separately, rather than only excluding people who combine anger and misguidance. [1 notes: SAMARRAI-LAMASAT]
- 1:7/q25/p10 Al-Rāzī suggests that those under anger are unbelievers and the astray are hypocrites, analogizing to al-Baqara’s order of believers, unbelievers, and hypocrites; al-Ālūsī rejects the analogy against the Prophetic report.; cited verses: 2:1, 2:6, 2:8 — ALUSI reporting الرازي: Al-Rāzī suggests that those under anger are unbelievers and the astray are hypocrites, analogizing to al-Baqara’s order of believers, unbelievers, and hypocrites; al-Ālūsī rejects the analogy against the Prophetic report. | mentions 2:1, 2:6, 2:8 [0 notes: ALUSI(الرازي)-]

## 1:7/q27 What does Āmīn mean after this verse?  [* · meaning]
turns on: The cited reports, transmitted wording, and differing grammatical or legal inferences.
- 1:7/q27/p1 Āmīn asks God to answer — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting أبو موسى الأشعري عن النبي: The Prophet says to follow the imam: say Amin at al-Fatiha's end so God answers, follow his bowing and prostration, and say ‘Our Lord, praise belongs to You’ after he says God hears praise; his movements are offset so followers do not precede him. MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting النبي عن أبي هريرة: The Prophet teaches followers not to anticipate the imam, to say Amin at the end of al-Fatiha, and to answer ‘Our Lord, praise belongs to You’ after the imam says God hears praise; agreement with the angels brings forgiveness for those in the mosque. ZAJJAJ: Amīn and Āmīn mean “O God, answer”; they stand in place of a verbal noun for response, like ṣah standing for silence. SULAMI reporting بعض العراقيين: Amin expresses hope that God will answer the supplications just made. QUSHAYRI: Saying amin after the Fatiha is Sunnah and means “Lord, do and answer”; it seeks enabling for deeds and fulfillment of hopes through humble petition. BAGHAWI: Amin means “O God, hear and answer.” BAGHAWI-FULL: The reciter should say Amin after a separate pause; the word is normally light, though grammarians allow a long or short vowel, and means ‘God, hear and answer.’ KASHSHAF: Amin is a sound-form used as the name of the verb respond, like words meaning wait, hurry, and come. KASHSHAF reporting ابن عباس والنبي: Ibn Abbas asked the Prophet what Amin means, and the Prophet answered, do it. KASHSHAF-FULL: Amin is an indeclinable sound used for the verb respond; it has long and short forms, and a poetic line illustrates it. KASHSHAF-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas says the Prophet explained Amin as meaning do it or answer. IBNATIYYA reporting النبي: A report says the Prophet heard a man supplicate and said his request was assured if he concluded; when asked how, he answered: with Āmīn. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting الحسن بن أبي الحسن وثعلب: Most scholars, including al-Hasan and Thaʿlab, interpret amin as “O God, respond” or “Respond, Lord.” IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting الحسن والزجاج: A second explanation understands āmīn as “O God, answer,” held by al-Ḥasan and al-Zajjāj. BAYDAWI: Āmīn is an imperative-like expression meaning “answer” or “grant the prayer”; it is not part of the Qur'an, by consensus. BAYDAWI-FULL: Āmīn is an imperative noun meaning “answer/accept”; a report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet explained it as “do so.” It is built on fatḥa to avoid two adjacent still consonants. NASAFI: Amin is a spoken formula meaning ‘answer/respond,’ treated as a noun for the imperative just as ruwayd means ‘wait.’ It has long and short forms; the short vowel length is original, while the long form lengthens the hamza. NASAFI reporting ابن عباس عن رسول الله: Ibn Abbas asked the Messenger about amin’s meaning, and he answered, ‘Do it.’ SAMIN-DURR: Amin is not part of the Quran by consensus; it means respond and is an indeclinable imperative noun. IBNKATHIR: It is recommended to say amin after al-Fatiha, pronounced either with a long or short first vowel; it means “O God, answer.” A report from Waʾil says the Prophet lengthened it, and al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan. IBNKATHIR reporting أبو موسى: A Prophetic report in Muslim says that when the imam recites “nor the astray,” worshippers should say amin and God will answer them. IBNKATHIR reporting ابن عباس: A report through Juwaybir and al-Dahhak explains amin as “Lord, do”; al-Jawhari says “so let it be,” al-Tirmidhi says it means do not disappoint our hope, and most interpreters say “O God, answer us.” IBNKATHIR: The account of Moses' prayer and the dual reply that “your two prayers” were answered implies that Harun said amin; this makes the person who says amin to a prayer like one who prayed it. | mentions 10:88, 10:89 BIQAI: Amīn is a vocal form named for the imperative meaning respond. BIQAI-FULL reporting الحرالي: Amin means the petitioner trusts God not to reject the plea, since nothing can overcome or restrain Him; the word asks Him to respond. DURR reporting الحسن: Al-Ḥasan glosses Āmīn as “O God, answer.” DURR-FULL reporting الحسن: Ibn Shahin transmits Ubayy ibn Kab's variant with a repeated “ghayr” and amin; al-Hasan explains amin as “O God, respond.” ALUSI: Āmīn is an Arabic particle functioning as a verb, built on fatḥa to avoid meeting two quiescent letters; its correct meaning is respond, while another view gives it a broader sense including a synonym. ALUSI reporting قيل: Another view says Āmīn is used for a broader meaning that includes respond and its synonym. ALUSI-FULL: Amin is an Arabic indeclinable imperative-noun meaning “respond”; other views call it broader in meaning, foreign, a divine name, or a form with a doubled mīm, which the source discusses and disputes. ELMALILI: Amin is an imperative-like noun of action meaning 'answer' or 'accept'; it is not part of Qur'anic wording and therefore is not written in the codex. MUSLIM reporting أبو موسى الأشعري: Abu Musa says the Prophet taught worshippers to answer the recitation’s ending with Amin, so that God answers them; the teaching arose after a man spoke during prayer. NASAI reporting أبو موسى: Abū Mūsā reports that the Prophet taught worshippers to say amin after the imam recites 1:7, so God answers them. NASAI reporting أبو موسى: Ḥiṭṭān reports that a congregant declared prayer established through piety and almsgiving; Abū Mūsā recalled the Prophet’s rule to follow the imam, say amin after 1:7 for God’s answer, and mirror the imam’s movements. [34 notes: MUSNAD-AHMAD(أبو موسى الأشعري عن النبي,النبي عن أبي هريرة); ZAJJAJ; SULAMI(بعض العراقيين); QUSHAYRI; BAGHAWI; BAGHAWI-FULL; KASHSHAF(ابن عباس والنبي); KASHSHAF-FULL(ابن عباس); IBNATIYYA(النبي); IBNATIYYA-FULL(الحسن بن أبي الحسن وثعلب); IBNJAWZI-ZAD(الحسن والزجاج); BAYDAWI; BAYDAWI-FULL; NASAFI(ابن عباس عن رسول الله); SAMIN-DURR; IBNKATHIR(أبو موسى,ابن عباس); BIQAI; BIQAI-FULL(الحرالي); DURR(الحسن); DURR-FULL(الحسن); ALUSI(قيل); ALUSI-FULL; ELMALILI; MUSLIM(أبو موسى الأشعري); NASAI(أبو موسى)]
- 1:7/q27/p2 Āmīn seals the supplication — BAGHAWI: Another view calls Amin the seal of supplication. BAGHAWI: Another view says Amin is God's seal upon His servants, protecting them from afflictions like a letter's seal protects its contents. BAGHAWI-FULL: Other explanations call Amin the seal of a supplication or God’s seal protecting servants from harm, like a seal protecting a letter. KASHSHAF reporting النبي وجبريل: Gabriel taught the Prophet Amin at the end of al-Fatiha and called it a seal on a book. KASHSHAF-FULL reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet said Gabriel taught him Amin upon finishing al-Fatiha and called it like a seal on a book; it is not Quran because absent from the codices. IBNATIYYA reporting علي بن أبي طالب: ʿAlī calls Āmīn the seal of the Lord of the worlds, with which the believing servant seals his supplication. IBNATIYYA: A further report calls Āmīn the name of a seal used to stamp the books of the people of Paradise, which they receive by faith. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting علي بن أبي طالب: ʿAli ibn Abi Talib calls amin the seal of the Lord of the worlds that closes a believing servant's supplication. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting رسول الله: The Prophet says a supplication is assured when sealed, and identifies amin as the seal. IBNATIYYA-FULL: Another report calls Amin the seal stamped on the books of the people of Paradise who receive them in faith. BAYDAWI: It is recommended to end the sūra with āmīn, following the Prophet's report that Gabriel taught it at the end of al-Fātiḥa as a letter's seal. BAYDAWI reporting علي: ʿAlī calls āmīn the seal of the Lord of the worlds, sealing a servant's supplication. BAYDAWI-FULL: Āmīn is not Qur'an, but ending the sura with it is recommended because Gabriel taught it to the Prophet as a seal on the book; ʿAlī similarly calls it the seal of the Lord of the worlds. NASAFI reporting النبي عليه السلام: The Prophet said Gabriel taught him amin after he finished reciting the Fatiha and compared it to a seal on a letter; amin is not Qur’an because it does not appear in the codices. NASAFI-FULL: The poet's evidence shows both long and short forms of Amin, and a Prophetic report says Gabriel taught Amin at the end of al-Fatiha, like a seal on a letter; it is not Qur'an because codices omit it. IBNKATHIR reporting أبو هريرة: Ibn Mardawayh transmits from Abu Hurayra a Prophetic report calling amin the Lord of the worlds' seal upon His believing servants. DURR reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Abū Zuhayr al-Numayrī, a Companion, likens Āmīn sealing supplication to a stamp; Abū Dāwūd grades the report ḥasan. DURR reporting أبو هريرة: A weak report calls Āmīn the seal of the Lord of the worlds upon believers’ tongues. DURR-FULL reporting أبو زهير النميري: Abu Zuhayr recommends ending supplication with amin, like a seal on a page; the Prophet said a persistent supplicant had secured an answer when he sealed his prayer. [19 notes: BAGHAWI; BAGHAWI-FULL; KASHSHAF(النبي وجبريل); KASHSHAF-FULL(رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم); IBNATIYYA(علي بن أبي طالب); IBNATIYYA-FULL(رسول الله,علي بن أبي طالب); BAYDAWI(علي); BAYDAWI-FULL; NASAFI(النبي عليه السلام); NASAFI-FULL; IBNKATHIR(أبو هريرة); DURR(أبو هريرة,النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم); DURR-FULL(أبو زهير النميري)]
- 1:7/q27/p3 Āmīn means 'so be it' — BAGHAWI reporting ابن عباس وقتادة: Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada explain Amin as “so it is” or “so be it.” BAGHAWI-FULL reporting ابن عباس وقتادة: Ibn Abbas and Qatada gloss Amin as ‘so be it.’ IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting ابن الأنباري عن ابن عباس والحسن: One explanation makes āmīn mean “so be it,” as Ibn al-Anbārī relates from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan. NASAFI-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Asked about Amin, Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet explained it as “respond” or “so be it”; the word is a built verbal noun with long and short vowel forms. - 1:7/q27/p4 Āmīn is one of God's names — IBNATIYYA reporting الحسن بن أبي الحسن وأحمد بن يحيى ثعلب: Most scholars understand Āmīn as “O God, answer” or “Answer, Lord,” and al-Ḥasan and Thaʿlab are named for this explanation. ALUSI reporting قيل: Another unusual view treats Āmīn as a name of God because it contains a hidden pronoun referring to Him; al-Ālūsī finds this rationale even stranger. STUDYQURAN: Āmīn is commonly a supplication meaning O God, answer us; others call it a divine Name or say Thus shall it be, akin to Hebrew Amen as an affirmation and seal of prayer. DURR reporting ابن عباس: Through al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn ʿAbbās says Āmīn means “Lord, do it.” [2 notes: BAYDAWI(رسول الله); DURR(ابن عباس)]

- 1:7/q27/p7 Amin means heading toward God, who is too generous to refuse one who heads to Him. — SULAMI reporting جعفر: Amin means heading toward God, who is too generous to refuse one who heads to Him. [1 notes: SULAMI(جعفر)]
- 1:7/q27/p8 Amin means being content with God's decree for and against the servants. — SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Amin means being content with God's decree for and against the servants. [1 notes: SULAMI(بعضهم)]
- 1:7/q27/p9 Amin means asking that the prayer be accepted; it is not part of Fatiha or a verse, and hadiths say the Prophet said it after Fatiha and instructed others to do so. — KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: Amin means asking that the prayer be accepted; it is not part of Fatiha or a verse, and hadiths say the Prophet said it after Fatiha and instructed others to do so. ## 1:7/q29 How is Āmīn pronounced?  [* · readings]
turns on: The cited reports, transmitted wording, and differing grammatical or legal inferences.
- 1:7/q29/p1 Short Āmīn — BAGHAWI: The reader should say Amin after finishing al-Fatiha, separated from it by a brief pause; it may be pronounced short or long. BAGHAWI-FULL: The reciter should say Amin after a separate pause; the word is normally light, though grammarians allow a long or short vowel, and means ‘God, hear and answer.’ KASHSHAF: Amin has long and short alif, both attested by poetry. KASHSHAF-FULL: Amin is an indeclinable sound used for the verb respond; it has long and short forms, and a poetic line illustrates it. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting جبير بن الأضبط: Some Arabs shorten amin, as illustrated by Jubayr ibn al-Adbat's verse. IBNJAWZI-ZAD: The nūn is open in both pronunciations; āmīn has a short-vowel form amīn and a long-vowel form āmīn. BAYDAWI: The alif in āmīn may be lengthened or shortened; two poetic lines attest the forms, though their poets are unnamed. NASAFI: Amin is a spoken formula meaning ‘answer/respond,’ treated as a noun for the imperative just as ruwayd means ‘wait.’ It has long and short forms; the short vowel length is original, while the long form lengthens the hamza. NASAFI-FULL: The poet's evidence shows both long and short forms of Amin, and a Prophetic report says Gabriel taught Amin at the end of al-Fatiha, like a seal on a letter; it is not Qur'an because codices omit it. NASAFI-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Asked about Amin, Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet explained it as “respond” or “so be it”; the word is a built verbal noun with long and short vowel forms. SAMIN-DURR: Amin has long and short forms, each attested in poetry. IBNKATHIR: It is recommended to say amin after al-Fatiha, pronounced either with a long or short first vowel; it means “O God, answer.” A report from Waʾil says the Prophet lengthened it, and al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan. ALUSI reporting قيل: A strange view derives the Arabicized word from the foreign hamīn because fāʿīl is not an Arabic pattern; a response says it may be a unique pattern with analogues, or originally short and lengthened. ALUSI: Readers disagree whether the alif in Āmīn is inherently long or short; groups support each origin. [14 notes: BAGHAWI; BAGHAWI-FULL; KASHSHAF; KASHSHAF-FULL; IBNATIYYA-FULL(جبير بن الأضبط); IBNJAWZI-ZAD; BAYDAWI; NASAFI; NASAFI-FULL(ابن عباس); SAMIN-DURR; IBNKATHIR; ALUSI(قيل)]
- 1:7/q29/p2 Long Āmīn — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting أبو موسى الأشعري عن النبي: The Prophet says to follow the imam: say Amin at al-Fatiha's end so God answers, follow his bowing and prostration, and say ‘Our Lord, praise belongs to You’ after he says God hears praise; his movements are offset so followers do not precede him. MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting النبي عن أبي هريرة: The Prophet teaches followers not to anticipate the imam, to say Amin at the end of al-Fatiha, and to answer ‘Our Lord, praise belongs to You’ after the imam says God hears praise; agreement with the angels brings forgiveness for those in the mosque. IBNATIYYA: Some Arabs lengthen Āmīn; a poetic line repeats the long form and imagines needing two thousand Āmīns. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting الشاعر: Some Arabs lengthen amin; the cited verse uses the long form and repeats it. NASAFI: A cited poem witnesses the long form amina; another line uses amin and asks God to increase the distance between the lovers. ABUHAYYAN: The word Āmīn is not Qurʾān; Abū Ḥayyān omits discussion of its forms, meaning, and prayer ruling, along with introductory istiʿādha, as material outside his intended tafsīr scope. DURR reporting وائل بن حجر: Wāʾil b. Ḥujr heard the Prophet say Āmīn after al-Fātiḥa’s ending, prolonging his voice. DURR-FULL reporting وائل بن حجر: Wail ibn Hujr heard the Prophet say amin after the final words of al-Fatiha, prolonging his voice. ITQAN reporting وائل بن حجر: Wail ibn Hujr reports that the Prophet recited “Amen” after “those astray,” prolonging his voice. ALUSI-FULL: Amin is not part of the Qur'an by consensus, so a brief pause separates it from the next sura; the view attributed to Mujahid that it belongs to al-Fatiha is false. [10 notes: MUSNAD-AHMAD(أبو موسى الأشعري عن النبي,النبي عن أبي هريرة); IBNATIYYA; IBNATIYYA-FULL(الشاعر); NASAFI; ABUHAYYAN; DURR(وائل بن حجر); DURR-FULL(وائل بن حجر); ITQAN(وائل بن حجر); ALUSI-FULL]
- 1:7/q29/p3 Āmīn with doubled mīm — IBNKATHIR reporting الحسن: Al-Hasan and Jaʿfar al-Sadiq are reported to pronounce amin with a doubled mīm, like the Qurʾanic word in 5:2. | mentions 5:2 ALUSI reporting الواحدي: Al-Wāḥidī calls a doubled mīm a dialect form; another view calls it an error. Since Āmīn is a non-Qurʾānic supplication with a sound meaning, some say that pronunciation does not invalidate prayer. ALUSI-FULL: Amin is an Arabic indeclinable imperative-noun meaning “respond”; other views call it broader in meaning, foreign, a divine name, or a form with a doubled mīm, which the source discusses and disputes. - 1:7/q30/p3 Wa'il reports that the Prophet said Amin quietly after al-Fatiha, placed his right hand over his left in prayer, and gave salutation to both sides. — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting وائل بن حجر عن النبي: Wa'il reports that the Prophet said Amin quietly after al-Fatiha, placed his right hand over his left in prayer, and gave salutation to both sides.
