- 1:7/q30/p4 Wa'il saw the Prophet place his right hand over his left and raise his hands to his ears at the prayer's opening; the Prophet said Amin aloud after al-Fatiha. — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting وائل بن حجر: Wa'il saw the Prophet place his right hand over his left and raise his hands to his ears at the prayer's opening; the Prophet said Amin aloud after al-Fatiha. [1 notes: MUSNAD-AHMAD(وائل بن حجر)]
- 1:7/q30/p5 The Prophet says to follow the imam: say Amin at al-Fatiha's end so God answers, follow his bowing and prostration, and say ‘Our Lord, praise belongs to You’ after he says God hears praise; his movements are… — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting أبو موسى الأشعري عن النبي: The Prophet says to follow the imam: say Amin at al-Fatiha's end so God answers, follow his bowing and prostration, and say ‘Our Lord, praise belongs to You’ after he says God hears praise; his movements are offset so followers do not precede him. [1 notes: MUSNAD-AHMAD(أبو موسى الأشعري عن النبي)]
- 1:7/q30/p6 The Prophet teaches that the congregation says Amin after al-Fatiha and follows the imam's prayer movements; he moves first, with the imam's delay balanced by the followers' own delay. — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting أبو موسى الأشعري عن النبي: The Prophet teaches that the congregation says Amin after al-Fatiha and follows the imam's prayer movements; he moves first, with the imam's delay balanced by the followers' own delay. [1 notes: MUSNAD-AHMAD(أبو موسى الأشعري عن النبي)]
- 1:7/q30/p7 When the imam finishes al-Fatiha, worshippers should say Amin; if their response coincides with the angels' and imam's, their past sins are forgiven. — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting النبي عن أبي هريرة: When the imam finishes al-Fatiha, worshippers should say Amin; if their response coincides with the angels' and imam's, their past sins are forgiven. [1 notes: MUSNAD-AHMAD(النبي عن أبي هريرة)]
- 1:7/q30/p8 The Prophet instructs the congregation to say Amin after the imam's recitation; agreement with the angels' Amin brings forgiveness for past sins. — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting النبي عن أبي هريرة: The Prophet instructs the congregation to say Amin after the imam's recitation; agreement with the angels' Amin brings forgiveness for past sins. [1 notes: MUSNAD-AHMAD(النبي عن أبي هريرة)]
- 1:7/q30/p9 The Prophet teaches followers not to anticipate the imam, to say Amin at the end of al-Fatiha, and to answer ‘Our Lord, praise belongs to You’ after the imam says God hears praise; agreement with the angels… — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting النبي عن أبي هريرة: The Prophet teaches followers not to anticipate the imam, to say Amin at the end of al-Fatiha, and to answer ‘Our Lord, praise belongs to You’ after the imam says God hears praise; agreement with the angels brings forgiveness for those in the mosque. [1 notes: MUSNAD-AHMAD(النبي عن أبي هريرة)]
- 1:7/q30/p10 When the reciter finishes al-Fatiha, those behind him say Amin; agreement with the heavenly congregation's Amin brings forgiveness for past sins. — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting النبي عن أبي هريرة: When the reciter finishes al-Fatiha, those behind him say Amin; agreement with the heavenly congregation's Amin brings forgiveness for past sins. [1 notes: MUSNAD-AHMAD(النبي عن أبي هريرة)]
- 1:7/q30/p11 The Prophet orders worshippers to say Amin after the imam; whoever's response matches the angels' is forgiven past sins. — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting النبي عن أبي هريرة: The Prophet orders worshippers to say Amin after the imam; whoever's response matches the angels' is forgiven past sins. [1 notes: MUSNAD-AHMAD(النبي عن أبي هريرة)]
- 1:7/q30/p12 After praise and supplication, Arabs use both Amīn and Āmīn; two poems attest the forms. — ZAJJAJ: After praise and supplication, Arabs use both Amīn and Āmīn; two poems attest the forms. [1 notes: ZAJJAJ]
- 1:7/q30/p13 An unnamed poet uses Amīn in a prayer that God increase the distance between the speaker and Fataḥl. — ZAJJAJ: An unnamed poet uses Amīn in a prayer that God increase the distance between the speaker and Fataḥl. [1 notes: ZAJJAJ]
- 1:7/q30/p14 Another unnamed poet uses Āmīnā in a prayer for God's mercy on one who says it. — ZAJJAJ: Another unnamed poet uses Āmīnā in a prayer for God's mercy on one who says it. [1 notes: ZAJJAJ]
- 1:7/q30/p15 Nuaim reports that Abu Hurayra began with the basmala, recited the Fatiha, said amin at its end with the congregation, and performed the prayer actions before saying his prayer most resembled the Prophet's. — IBNHIBBAN reporting أبو هريرة: Nuaim reports that Abu Hurayra began with the basmala, recited the Fatiha, said amin at its end with the congregation, and performed the prayer actions before saying his prayer most resembled the Prophet's. [1 notes: IBNHIBBAN(أبو هريرة)]
- 1:7/q30/p16 The Prophet instructs worshippers to say amin when the imam reaches the verse's ending; the imam and angels say it too, and agreement with the angels brings forgiveness of past sins. — IBNHIBBAN reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: The Prophet instructs worshippers to say amin when the imam reaches the verse's ending; the imam and angels say it too, and agreement with the angels brings forgiveness of past sins. [1 notes: IBNHIBBAN(النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم)]
- 1:7/q30/p17 Abu Hatim explains that matching the angels means saying amin sincerely for God, free of vanity, showing off, or desire for reputation, as the angels do. — IBNHIBBAN reporting أبو حاتم: Abu Hatim explains that matching the angels means saying amin sincerely for God, free of vanity, showing off, or desire for reputation, as the angels do. [1 notes: IBNHIBBAN(أبو حاتم)]
- 1:7/q30/p18 Wail ibn Hujr reports that while praying with the Prophet, he heard him say amin after reciting ‘nor those astray.’ — IBNHIBBAN reporting وائل بن حجر: Wail ibn Hujr reports that while praying with the Prophet, he heard him say amin after reciting ‘nor those astray.’ [1 notes: IBNHIBBAN(وائل بن حجر)]
- 1:7/q30/p19 Amin admits incapacity to praise God through one's own attributes except by following Muhammad al-Amin. — SULAMI reporting الجنيد: Amin admits incapacity to praise God through one's own attributes except by following Muhammad al-Amin. [1 notes: SULAMI(الجنيد)]
- 1:7/q30/p20 Amin can ask to be spared from one's requests because God's choice is better than one's own. — SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Amin can ask to be spared from one's requests because God's choice is better than one's own. [1 notes: SULAMI(بعضهم)]
- 1:7/q30/p21 Anger follows innovations, while error is abandoning guidance and Sunnah, including the Sunnah of saying Amin aloud after the chapter in prayer. — SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Anger follows innovations, while error is abandoning guidance and Sunnah, including the Sunnah of saying Amin aloud after the chapter in prayer. [1 notes: SULAMI(بعضهم)]
- 1:7/q30/p22 Saying amin after the Fatiha is Sunnah and means “Lord, do and answer”; it seeks enabling for deeds and fulfillment of hopes through humble petition. — QUSHAYRI: Saying amin after the Fatiha is Sunnah and means “Lord, do and answer”; it seeks enabling for deeds and fulfillment of hopes through humble petition. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q30/p23 The reader should say Amin after finishing al-Fatiha, separated from it by a brief pause; it may be pronounced short or long. — BAGHAWI: The reader should say Amin after finishing al-Fatiha, separated from it by a brief pause; it may be pronounced short or long. [1 notes: BAGHAWI]
- 1:7/q30/p24 Mujahid says Amin is one of God's names. — BAGHAWI reporting مجاهد: Mujahid says Amin is one of God's names. [1 notes: BAGHAWI(مجاهد)]
- 1:7/q30/p25 Another view says Amin is God's seal upon His servants, protecting them from afflictions like a letter's seal protects its contents. — BAGHAWI: Another view says Amin is God's seal upon His servants, protecting them from afflictions like a letter's seal protects its contents. [1 notes: BAGHAWI]
- 1:7/q30/p26 Abu Hurayra reports that when the imam says the final phrase, the congregation should say Amin; imam and angels also say it, and agreement with the angels brings forgiveness of past sins. Baghawi grades it sahih. — BAGHAWI reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Abu Hurayra reports that when the imam says the final phrase, the congregation should say Amin; imam and angels also say it, and agreement with the angels brings forgiveness of past sins. Baghawi grades it sahih. [1 notes: BAGHAWI(النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم)]
- 1:7/q30/p27 Abu Hurayra reports that when the imam says Amin, worshippers should do so too; angels also say it, and agreement with them brings forgiveness of past sins. Al-Baghawi grades it sound. — BAGHAWI-FULL reporting أبو هريرة: Abu Hurayra reports that when the imam says Amin, worshippers should do so too; angels also say it, and agreement with them brings forgiveness of past sins. Al-Baghawi grades it sound. [1 notes: BAGHAWI-FULL(أبو هريرة)]
- 1:7/q30/p28 The reciter should say Amin after a separate pause; the word is normally light, though grammarians allow a long or short vowel, and means ‘God, hear and answer.’ — BAGHAWI-FULL: The reciter should say Amin after a separate pause; the word is normally light, though grammarians allow a long or short vowel, and means ‘God, hear and answer.’ [1 notes: BAGHAWI-FULL]
- 1:7/q30/p29 Mujahid says Amin is one of God’s names. — BAGHAWI-FULL reporting مجاهد: Mujahid says Amin is one of God’s names. [1 notes: BAGHAWI-FULL(مجاهد)]
- 1:7/q30/p30 Al-Hasan says the imam should not say Amin because the imam is the supplicant. — KASHSHAF reporting الحسن: Al-Hasan says the imam should not say Amin because the imam is the supplicant. [1 notes: KASHSHAF(الحسن)]
- 1:7/q30/p31 Abu Hanifa is reported to say the imam should not say Amin. — KASHSHAF reporting أبو حنيفة: Abu Hanifa is reported to say the imam should not say Amin. [1 notes: KASHSHAF(أبو حنيفة)]
- 1:7/q30/p32 The well-known position of Abu Hanifa and his followers is to say Amin silently. — KASHSHAF reporting أبو حنيفة وأصحابه: The well-known position of Abu Hanifa and his followers is to say Amin silently. [1 notes: KASHSHAF(أبو حنيفة وأصحابه)]
- 1:7/q30/p33 Ibn Abbas says the Prophet explained Amin as meaning do it or answer. — KASHSHAF-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas says the Prophet explained Amin as meaning do it or answer. [1 notes: KASHSHAF-FULL(ابن عباس)]
- 1:7/q30/p34 Hasan says the imam should not say Amin because he is the one supplicating; Abu Hanifa shares this view and is known to recite it quietly. — KASHSHAF-FULL reporting الحسن وأبو حنيفة: Hasan says the imam should not say Amin because he is the one supplicating; Abu Hanifa shares this view and is known to recite it quietly. [1 notes: KASHSHAF-FULL(الحسن وأبو حنيفة)]
- 1:7/q30/p35 The Prophet tells worshippers to say Āmīn when the imam says “nor those who are astray”; the angels in heaven say it, and agreement with them brings forgiveness of past sins. — IBNATIYYA reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي: The Prophet tells worshippers to say Āmīn when the imam says “nor those who are astray”; the angels in heaven say it, and agreement with them brings forgiveness of past sins. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA(أبو هريرة عن النبي)]
- 1:7/q30/p36 A report says Gabriel taught the Prophet al-Fātiḥa at its revelation; after the Prophet recited it, Gabriel told him to say Āmīn. — IBNATIYYA reporting جبريل: A report says Gabriel taught the Prophet al-Fātiḥa at its revelation; after the Prophet recited it, Gabriel told him to say Āmīn. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA(جبريل)]
- 1:7/q30/p37 A report says the Prophet heard a man supplicate and said his request was assured if he concluded; when asked how, he answered: with Āmīn. — IBNATIYYA reporting النبي: A report says the Prophet heard a man supplicate and said his request was assured if he concluded; when asked how, he answered: with Āmīn. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA(النبي)]
- 1:7/q30/p38 Another view makes Āmīn one of God’s names; it is reported from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, Mujāhid, and Hilāl ibn Yasāf. — IBNATIYYA reporting جعفر بن محمد ومجاهد وهلال بن يساف: Another view makes Āmīn one of God’s names; it is reported from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, Mujāhid, and Hilāl ibn Yasāf. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA(جعفر بن محمد ومجاهد وهلال بن يساف)]
- 1:7/q30/p39 The author infers from these reports that supplicants should say Āmīn at the end of every supplication and after al-Fātiḥa outside prayer, without loud recitation. — IBNATIYYA: The author infers from these reports that supplicants should say Āmīn at the end of every supplication and after al-Fātiḥa outside prayer, without loud recitation. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA]
- 1:7/q30/p40 One legal view has every worshipper—imam, praying alone, or follower—say Āmīn if they recite or hear al-Fātiḥa. — IBNATIYYA reporting بعض العلماء: One legal view has every worshipper—imam, praying alone, or follower—say Āmīn if they recite or hear al-Fātiḥa. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA(بعض العلماء)]
- 1:7/q30/p41 In the Mudawwana, Mālik says the imam does not say Āmīn, while followers say it quietly and a person praying alone says it. — IBNATIYYA reporting مالك: In the Mudawwana, Mālik says the imam does not say Āmīn, while followers say it quietly and a person praying alone says it. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA(مالك)]
- 1:7/q30/p42 Other reports from Mālik say that the imam says Āmīn either quietly or aloud, or does not say it during audible prayer. — IBNATIYYA reporting مالك: Other reports from Mālik say that the imam says Āmīn either quietly or aloud, or does not say it during audible prayer. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA(مالك)]
- 1:7/q30/p43 Ibn Ḥabīb holds that the imam should say Āmīn. — IBNATIYYA reporting ابن حبيب: Ibn Ḥabīb holds that the imam should say Āmīn. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA(ابن حبيب)]
- 1:7/q30/p44 Ibn Nāfiʿ says a follower says Āmīn only if he hears the imam reach “nor those who are astray”; if too far away to hear, he omits it. — IBNATIYYA reporting ابن نافع: Ibn Nāfiʿ says a follower says Āmīn only if he hears the imam reach “nor those who are astray”; if too far away to hear, he omits it. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA(ابن نافع)]
- 1:7/q30/p45 Ibn ʿAbdūs tells a distant follower to estimate the length of the recitation and then say Āmīn. — IBNATIYYA reporting ابن عبدوس: Ibn ʿAbdūs tells a distant follower to estimate the length of the recitation and then say Āmīn. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA(ابن عبدوس)]
- 1:7/q30/p46 Āmīn is built on fatḥa because two sukūns meet; fatḥa is lighter with yāʾ than the other vowel options. — IBNATIYYA: Āmīn is built on fatḥa because two sukūns meet; fatḥa is lighter with yāʾ than the other vowel options. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA]
- 1:7/q30/p47 Every worshipper—leader, solitary, or follower—says amin after reciting or hearing the closing phrase. — IBNATIYYA-FULL: Every worshipper—leader, solitary, or follower—says amin after reciting or hearing the closing phrase. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL]
- 1:7/q30/p48 Amin is indeclinable with fatḥa because two vowelless letters meet; fatḥa with yā is the lightest pronunciation. — IBNATIYYA-FULL: Amin is indeclinable with fatḥa because two vowelless letters meet; fatḥa with yā is the lightest pronunciation. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL]
- 1:7/q30/p49 In the Mudawwana, the imam does not say amin; followers say it quietly, while a solitary worshipper does say it. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting مالك: In the Mudawwana, the imam does not say amin; followers say it quietly, while a solitary worshipper does say it. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(مالك)]
- 1:7/q30/p50 A report from Malik allows the imam to say amin either silently or aloud. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting مالك: A report from Malik allows the imam to say amin either silently or aloud. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(مالك)]
- 1:7/q30/p51 Another report from Malik says the imam does not say amin during audible recitation. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting مالك: Another report from Malik says the imam does not say amin during audible recitation. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(مالك)]
- 1:7/q30/p52 Ibn Habib says the imam says amin. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting ابن حبيب: Ibn Habib says the imam says amin. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(ابن حبيب)]
- 1:7/q30/p53 A follower says amin only if he hears the imam reach walā al-ḍāllīn; if too far away to hear, he omits it. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting ابن نافع: A follower says amin only if he hears the imam reach walā al-ḍāllīn; if too far away to hear, he omits it. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(ابن نافع)]
- 1:7/q30/p54 Ibn Abdus advises estimating the length of the recitation and then saying amin. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting ابن عبدوس: Ibn Abdus advises estimating the length of the recitation and then saying amin. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(ابن عبدوس)]
- 1:7/q30/p55 Abu Hurayra and others report the Prophet instructing worshippers to say amin after the imam recites “those astray”; one who coincides with the angels is forgiven earlier sins. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting أبو هريرة وغيره: Abu Hurayra and others report the Prophet instructing worshippers to say amin after the imam recites “those astray”; one who coincides with the angels is forgiven earlier sins. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(أبو هريرة وغيره)]
- 1:7/q30/p56 A report says Gabriel told the Prophet to say amin after teaching him the opening sura at its revelation. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting جبريل: A report says Gabriel told the Prophet to say amin after teaching him the opening sura at its revelation. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(جبريل)]
- 1:7/q30/p57 The Prophet says a supplication is assured when sealed, and identifies amin as the seal. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting رسول الله: The Prophet says a supplication is assured when sealed, and identifies amin as the seal. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(رسول الله)]
- 1:7/q30/p58 Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, Mujahid, and Hilal ibn Yasaf reportedly say Amin is one of God's names. — IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting جعفر بن محمد ومجاهد وهلال بن يساف: Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, Mujahid, and Hilal ibn Yasaf reportedly say Amin is one of God's names. [1 notes: IBNATIYYA-FULL(جعفر بن محمد ومجاهد وهلال بن يساف)]
- 1:7/q30/p59 A third view treats āmīn as one of God's names, held by Mujāhid, Hilāl ibn Yasāf, and Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad. — IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting مجاهد وهلال بن يساف وجعفر بن محمد: A third view treats āmīn as one of God's names, held by Mujāhid, Hilāl ibn Yasāf, and Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad. [1 notes: IBNJAWZI-ZAD(مجاهد وهلال بن يساف وجعفر بن محمد)]
- 1:7/q30/p60 Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn ʿUbayd Allāh says it is Sunnah for a Fātiḥa reader to follow it with āmīn, whether inside or outside prayer. — IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting أبو الحسن علي بن عبيد الله: Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn ʿUbayd Allāh says it is Sunnah for a Fātiḥa reader to follow it with āmīn, whether inside or outside prayer. [1 notes: IBNJAWZI-ZAD(أبو الحسن علي بن عبيد الله)]
- 1:7/q30/p61 A report from Abū Hurayra, from the Prophet, says that when the congregation says āmīn after the imām, matching the angels, prior sins are forgiven. — IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A report from Abū Hurayra, from the Prophet, says that when the congregation says āmīn after the imām, matching the angels, prior sins are forgiven. [1 notes: IBNJAWZI-ZAD(أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم)]
- 1:7/q30/p62 A verse transmitted by Abū al-ʿAbbās from Ibn al-Aʿrābī uses āmīn in a prayer asking rain for a people and protection for a caravan. — IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting أبو العباس عن ابن الأعرابي: A verse transmitted by Abū al-ʿAbbās from Ibn al-Aʿrābī uses āmīn in a prayer asking rain for a people and protection for a caravan. [1 notes: IBNJAWZI-ZAD(أبو العباس عن ابن الأعرابي)]
- 1:7/q30/p63 Another verse transmitted through Abū al-ʿAbbās has a speaker say āmīn after praying for distance from Faṭḥal and his mother’s son. — IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting أبو العباس عن ابن الأعرابي: Another verse transmitted through Abū al-ʿAbbās has a speaker say āmīn after praying for distance from Faṭḥal and his mother’s son. [1 notes: IBNJAWZI-ZAD(أبو العباس عن ابن الأعرابي)]
- 1:7/q30/p64 A third poetic citation uses āmīn in a supplication that God never deprive the speaker of his beloved and have mercy on one who says āmīnā. — IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting أبو العباس: A third poetic citation uses āmīn in a supplication that God never deprive the speaker of his beloved and have mercy on one who says āmīnā. [1 notes: IBNJAWZI-ZAD(أبو العباس)]
- 1:7/q30/p65 The imam says āmīn aloud in audible prayers, based on the report that the Prophet raised his voice after al-ḍāllīn. — BAYDAWI: The imam says āmīn aloud in audible prayers, based on the report that the Prophet raised his voice after al-ḍāllīn. [1 notes: BAYDAWI]
- 1:7/q30/p66 A report from Abū Ḥanīfa says not to say āmīn; his better-known position is to say it quietly, as narrated from ʿAbd Allāh b. Mughaffal and Anas. — BAYDAWI reporting أبو حنيفة: A report from Abū Ḥanīfa says not to say āmīn; his better-known position is to say it quietly, as narrated from ʿAbd Allāh b. Mughaffal and Anas. [1 notes: BAYDAWI(أبو حنيفة)]
- 1:7/q30/p67 The follower says āmīn with the imam; agreement with the angels' āmīn brings forgiveness of prior sins, according to the Prophetic report. — BAYDAWI reporting رسول الله: The follower says āmīn with the imam; agreement with the angels' āmīn brings forgiveness of prior sins, according to the Prophetic report. [1 notes: BAYDAWI(رسول الله)]
- 1:7/q30/p68 Ḥudhayfa b. al-Yamān reports that a child's recitation of al-ḥamdu li-llāh rabbi l-ʿālamīn caused God to lift an otherwise decreed punishment from a people for forty years. — BAYDAWI reporting رسول الله: Ḥudhayfa b. al-Yamān reports that a child's recitation of al-ḥamdu li-llāh rabbi l-ʿālamīn caused God to lift an otherwise decreed punishment from a people for forty years. [1 notes: BAYDAWI(رسول الله)]
- 1:7/q30/p69 Āmīn is an imperative noun meaning “answer/accept”; a report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet explained it as “do so.” It is built on fatḥa to avoid two adjacent still consonants. — BAYDAWI-FULL: Āmīn is an imperative noun meaning “answer/accept”; a report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet explained it as “do so.” It is built on fatḥa to avoid two adjacent still consonants. [1 notes: BAYDAWI-FULL]
- 1:7/q30/p70 Āmīn is not Qur'an, but ending the sura with it is recommended because Gabriel taught it to the Prophet as a seal on the book; ʿAlī similarly calls it the seal of the Lord of the worlds. — BAYDAWI-FULL: Āmīn is not Qur'an, but ending the sura with it is recommended because Gabriel taught it to the Prophet as a seal on the book; ʿAlī similarly calls it the seal of the Lord of the worlds. [1 notes: BAYDAWI-FULL]
- 1:7/q30/p71 The Prophet said Gabriel taught him amin after he finished reciting the Fatiha and compared it to a seal on a letter; amin is not Qur’an because it does not appear in the codices. — NASAFI reporting النبي عليه السلام: The Prophet said Gabriel taught him amin after he finished reciting the Fatiha and compared it to a seal on a letter; amin is not Qur’an because it does not appear in the codices. [1 notes: NASAFI(النبي عليه السلام)]
- 1:7/q30/p72 The poet's evidence shows both long and short forms of Amin, and a Prophetic report says Gabriel taught Amin at the end of al-Fatiha, like a seal on a letter; it is not Qur'an because codices omit… — NASAFI-FULL: The poet's evidence shows both long and short forms of Amin, and a Prophetic report says Gabriel taught Amin at the end of al-Fatiha, like a seal on a letter; it is not Qur'an because codices omit it. [1 notes: NASAFI-FULL]
- 1:7/q30/p73 It is recommended to say amin after al-Fatiha, pronounced either with a long or short first vowel; it means “O God, answer.” A report from Waʾil says the Prophet lengthened it, and al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan. — IBNKATHIR: It is recommended to say amin after al-Fatiha, pronounced either with a long or short first vowel; it means “O God, answer.” A report from Waʾil says the Prophet lengthened it, and al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR]
- 1:7/q30/p74 Waʾil ibn Hujr reports hearing the Prophet say amin aloud after al-Fatiha; al-Tirmidhi grades the hadith hasan, and reports also come from ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud. — IBNKATHIR reporting وائل بن حجر: Waʾil ibn Hujr reports hearing the Prophet say amin aloud after al-Fatiha; al-Tirmidhi grades the hadith hasan, and reports also come from ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR(وائل بن حجر)]
- 1:7/q30/p75 Bilal asked the Prophet not to say amin before him. — IBNKATHIR reporting بلال: Bilal asked the Prophet not to say amin before him. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR(بلال)]
- 1:7/q30/p76 Saying amin is recommended outside prayer and especially within it, whether alone, imam, or follower; the sound reports promise forgiveness when one's amin coincides with the angels'. — IBNKATHIR: Saying amin is recommended outside prayer and especially within it, whether alone, imam, or follower; the sound reports promise forgiveness when one's amin coincides with the angels'. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR]
- 1:7/q30/p77 In the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections, the Prophet says that when the imam says amin, worshippers should say it; agreement with the angels' amin brings forgiveness of prior sins. — IBNKATHIR reporting أبو هريرة: In the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections, the Prophet says that when the imam says amin, worshippers should say it; agreement with the angels' amin brings forgiveness of prior sins. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR(أبو هريرة)]
- 1:7/q30/p78 The matching between a worshipper's amin and the angels' may mean matching in time, in the response received, or in sincerity. — IBNKATHIR: The matching between a worshipper's amin and the angels' may mean matching in time, in the response received, or in sincerity. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR]
- 1:7/q30/p79 A Prophetic report in Muslim says that when the imam recites “nor the astray,” worshippers should say amin and God will answer them. — IBNKATHIR reporting أبو موسى: A Prophetic report in Muslim says that when the imam recites “nor the astray,” worshippers should say amin and God will answer them. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR(أبو موسى)]
- 1:7/q30/p80 A report through Juwaybir and al-Dahhak explains amin as “Lord, do”; al-Jawhari says “so let it be,” al-Tirmidhi says it means do not disappoint our hope, and most interpreters say “O God, answer us.” — IBNKATHIR reporting ابن عباس: A report through Juwaybir and al-Dahhak explains amin as “Lord, do”; al-Jawhari says “so let it be,” al-Tirmidhi says it means do not disappoint our hope, and most interpreters say “O God, answer us.” [1 notes: IBNKATHIR(ابن عباس)]
- 1:7/q30/p81 Mujahid, Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, and Hilal ibn Kaysan are reported to call amin one of God's names, but Ibn al-ʿArabi says the Prophetic report from Ibn ʿAbbas for this is unsound. — IBNKATHIR reporting مجاهد: Mujahid, Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, and Hilal ibn Kaysan are reported to call amin one of God's names, but Ibn al-ʿArabi says the Prophetic report from Ibn ʿAbbas for this is unsound. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR(مجاهد)]
- 1:7/q30/p82 Malik's companions say the imam does not say amin but the follower does, citing Abu Hurayra's report that followers should say it when the imam reaches “nor the astray”; Ibn Kathir counters with reports that the Prophet… — IBNKATHIR reporting أصحاب مالك: Malik's companions say the imam does not say amin but the follower does, citing Abu Hurayra's report that followers should say it when the imam reaches “nor the astray”; Ibn Kathir counters with reports that the Prophet himself said amin. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR(أصحاب مالك)]
- 1:7/q30/p83 The new Shafiʿi position, also held by Abu Hanifa and one Maliki report, is that a follower does not say amin aloud when the imam does; it is a remembrance like other prayer remembrances. — IBNKATHIR reporting القول الجديد: The new Shafiʿi position, also held by Abu Hanifa and one Maliki report, is that a follower does not say amin aloud when the imam does; it is a remembrance like other prayer remembrances. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR(القول الجديد)]
- 1:7/q30/p84 The old Shafiʿi position, held by Ahmad and another Maliki report, is that the follower says amin aloud, based on the report that the mosque echoed with it. — IBNKATHIR reporting القول القديم: The old Shafiʿi position, held by Ahmad and another Maliki report, is that the follower says amin aloud, based on the report that the mosque echoed with it. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR(القول القديم)]
- 1:7/q30/p85 A third position has the follower say amin quietly in a small mosque, where the imam can be heard, and aloud in a large mosque so it reaches its far sides. — IBNKATHIR: A third position has the follower say amin quietly in a small mosque, where the imam can be heard, and aloud in a large mosque so it reaches its far sides. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR]
- 1:7/q30/p86 A report from ʿAisha says Jews envy Muslims for Friday, the qibla, and saying amin behind the imam; Ibn Majah's wording adds greeting and amin. — IBNKATHIR reporting عائشة: A report from ʿAisha says Jews envy Muslims for Friday, the qibla, and saying amin behind the imam; Ibn Majah's wording adds greeting and amin. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR(عائشة)]
- 1:7/q30/p87 Anas reports that the Prophet was given amin in prayer and supplication; only Moses had it earlier, with Harun saying amin to Moses' prayer, so supplications should end with amin for acceptance. — IBNKATHIR reporting أنس: Anas reports that the Prophet was given amin in prayer and supplication; only Moses had it earlier, with Harun saying amin to Moses' prayer, so supplications should end with amin for acceptance. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR(أنس)]
- 1:7/q30/p88 The account of Moses' prayer and the dual reply that “your two prayers” were answered implies that Harun said amin; this makes the person who says amin to a prayer like one who prayed it.; cited verses:… — IBNKATHIR: The account of Moses' prayer and the dual reply that “your two prayers” were answered implies that Harun said amin; this makes the person who says amin to a prayer like one who prayed it. | mentions 10:88, 10:89 [1 notes: IBNKATHIR]
- 1:7/q30/p89 Some use this reasoning to argue that the follower need not recite aloud behind the imam because amin after al-Fatiha counts as recitation; they cite “whoever has an imam, the imam's recitation is his recitation” and Bilal's… — IBNKATHIR: Some use this reasoning to argue that the follower need not recite aloud behind the imam because amin after al-Fatiha counts as recitation; they cite “whoever has an imam, the imam's recitation is his recitation” and Bilal's request not to be preceded in amin. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR]
- 1:7/q30/p90 A report through Kaʿb says that when the imam says amin and the amins of earth and heaven coincide, God forgives the worshipper; one who omits amin is compared to a warrior whose lot was not drawn. — IBNKATHIR reporting أبو هريرة: A report through Kaʿb says that when the imam says amin and the amins of earth and heaven coincide, God forgives the worshipper; one who omits amin is compared to a warrior whose lot was not drawn. [1 notes: IBNKATHIR(أبو هريرة)]
- 1:7/q30/p91 Stopping after these phrases is good because their sense is understood, but starting with attached phrases such as rabb al-ʿālamīn, ṣirāṭ alladhīna, or ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim is poor, except at verse ends per the Sunnah. — NASHR: Stopping after these phrases is good because their sense is understood, but starting with attached phrases such as rabb al-ʿālamīn, ṣirāṭ alladhīna, or ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim is poor, except at verse ends per the Sunnah. ## 1:7/q31 Is Āmīn said aloud or quietly?  [* · law]
turns on: The cited reports, transmitted wording, and differing grammatical or legal inferences.
- 1:7/q31/p1 Say Āmīn quietly — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting وائل بن حجر عن النبي: Wa'il reports that the Prophet said Amin quietly after al-Fatiha, placed his right hand over his left in prayer, and gave salutation to both sides. KASHSHAF reporting أبو حنيفة وأصحابه: The well-known position of Abu Hanifa and his followers is to say Amin silently. KASHSHAF-FULL reporting الحسن وأبو حنيفة: Hasan says the imam should not say Amin because he is the one supplicating; Abu Hanifa shares this view and is known to recite it quietly. IBNATIYYA reporting مالك: In the Mudawwana, Mālik says the imam does not say Āmīn, while followers say it quietly and a person praying alone says it. IBNATIYYA reporting مالك: Other reports from Mālik say that the imam says Āmīn either quietly or aloud, or does not say it during audible prayer. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting مالك: In the Mudawwana, the imam does not say amin; followers say it quietly, while a solitary worshipper does say it. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting مالك: A report from Malik allows the imam to say amin either silently or aloud. BAYDAWI reporting أبو حنيفة: A report from Abū Ḥanīfa says not to say āmīn; his better-known position is to say it quietly, as narrated from ʿAbd Allāh b. Mughaffal and Anas. IBNKATHIR: A third position has the follower say amin quietly in a small mosque, where the imam can be heard, and aloud in a large mosque so it reaches its far sides. ALUSI reporting الحسن: Al-Ḥasan says the imam should not say Āmīn because he is the supplicant; this is also found in a less famous report from Abū Ḥanīfa, whereas the famous view is that he says it silently. ALUSI-FULL reporting رسول الله: The Prophet instructed congregants to say amin after the imam recites the ending of al-Fatiha, saying God will love them; Hanafis say it quietly, while Shafiʿis say it aloud. ALUSI-FULL reporting علي وعبدالله بن مسعود: Quiet amin is attributed to ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud and is the Hanafi position; Shafiʿis vocalize it, Hasan says the imam should omit it, and one uncommon report from Abu Hanifa also favors concealment. ELMALILI: Amin is established by Sunna and should be said quietly by the imam, congregation, and a person praying alone. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: Because sound hadiths support saying amin aloud after audible Fatiha, most legal schools adopt that practice; Hanafis always say it silently in prayer. STUDYQURAN: Sunnis customarily say Āmīn after the Fātiḥah; it is recommended, not obligatory, and scholars differ whether it should be said aloud or quietly. [15 notes: MUSNAD-AHMAD(وائل بن حجر عن النبي); KASHSHAF(أبو حنيفة وأصحابه); KASHSHAF-FULL(الحسن وأبو حنيفة); IBNATIYYA(مالك); IBNATIYYA-FULL(مالك); BAYDAWI(أبو حنيفة); IBNKATHIR; ALUSI(الحسن); ALUSI-FULL(رسول الله,علي وعبدالله بن مسعود); ELMALILI; KURANYOLU-TEFSIR; STUDYQURAN]
- 1:7/q31/p2 Say Āmīn aloud — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting وائل بن حجر: Wa'il saw the Prophet place his right hand over his left and raise his hands to his ears at the prayer's opening; the Prophet said Amin aloud after al-Fatiha. SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Anger follows innovations, while error is abandoning guidance and Sunnah, including the Sunnah of saying Amin aloud after the chapter in prayer. KASHSHAF reporting الشافعي: Al-Shafii holds Amin is said aloud. KASHSHAF reporting وائل بن حجر والنبي: Waʾil ibn Hujr reports that the Prophet said Amin aloud after wa-la al-dallin. KASHSHAF-FULL reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: Wail ibn Hujr reports that the Prophet said Amin aloud after reciting wa-la al-dallin. IBNATIYYA: The author infers from these reports that supplicants should say Āmīn at the end of every supplication and after al-Fātiḥa outside prayer, without loud recitation. IBNATIYYA-FULL: Given these reports, anyone praying or reciting al-Fatiha outside prayer should end the supplication with amin, but outside prayer it is not said aloud in the manner of formal recitation. BAYDAWI: The imam says āmīn aloud in audible prayers, based on the report that the Prophet raised his voice after al-ḍāllīn. IBNKATHIR reporting وائل بن حجر: Waʾil ibn Hujr reports hearing the Prophet say amin aloud after al-Fatiha; al-Tirmidhi grades the hadith hasan, and reports also come from ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud. IBNKATHIR reporting أبو هريرة: Abu Hurayra reports that the Prophet said amin loudly enough for the first row to hear; Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah add that the mosque resounded, and al-Daraqutni calls the chain hasan. IBNKATHIR reporting القول الجديد: The new Shafiʿi position, also held by Abu Hanifa and one Maliki report, is that a follower does not say amin aloud when the imam does; it is a remembrance like other prayer remembrances. IBNKATHIR reporting القول القديم: The old Shafiʿi position, held by Ahmad and another Maliki report, is that the follower says amin aloud, based on the report that the mosque echoed with it. IBNKATHIR: Some use this reasoning to argue that the follower need not recite aloud behind the imam because amin after al-Fatiha counts as recitation; they cite “whoever has an imam, the imam's recitation is his recitation” and Bilal's request not to be preceded in amin. ALUSI reporting الحنفية: The Ḥanafīs conceal Āmīn, following ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd; the Shāfiʿīs say it aloud. The report of the majority’s loud recitation is interpreted as instruction or discussion. ABUDAWUD reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Abu Hurayra reports that when the Prophet recited al-Fatiha’s closing words, he said Amin loudly enough for the first row to hear. IBNMAJAH reporting أبو هريرة: Abu Hurayra says people had stopped saying amin; the Prophet said it aloud after the Fatiha's closing words, loud enough for the first row to hear and the mosque to reverberate. [16 notes: MUSNAD-AHMAD(وائل بن حجر); SULAMI(بعضهم); KASHSHAF(الشافعي,وائل بن حجر والنبي); KASHSHAF-FULL(رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم); IBNATIYYA; IBNATIYYA-FULL; BAYDAWI; IBNKATHIR(أبو هريرة,القول الجديد,القول القديم,وائل بن حجر); ALUSI(الحنفية); ABUDAWUD(أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم); IBNMAJAH(أبو هريرة)]
- 1:7/q31/p3 Wāʾil b. Ḥujr heard the Prophet say Āmīn after al-Fātiḥa’s ending, prolonging his voice. — DURR reporting وائل بن حجر: Wāʾil b. Ḥujr heard the Prophet say Āmīn after al-Fātiḥa’s ending, prolonging his voice. [1 notes: DURR(وائل بن حجر)]
- 1:7/q31/p4 Wail ibn Hujr heard the Prophet say amin after the final words of al-Fatiha, prolonging his voice. — DURR-FULL reporting وائل بن حجر: Wail ibn Hujr heard the Prophet say amin after the final words of al-Fatiha, prolonging his voice. [1 notes: DURR-FULL(وائل بن حجر)]
- 1:7/q31/p5 Wail ibn Hujr reports that the Prophet recited “Amen” after “those astray,” prolonging his voice. — ITQAN reporting وائل بن حجر: Wail ibn Hujr reports that the Prophet recited “Amen” after “those astray,” prolonging his voice. [1 notes: ITQAN(وائل بن حجر)]
- 1:7/q31/p6 Wāʾil b. Ḥujr reports that the Prophet recited the verse’s ending, said amin, and extended his voice on it. — TIRMIDHI reporting وائل بن حجر: Wāʾil b. Ḥujr reports that the Prophet recited the verse’s ending, said amin, and extended his voice on it. [1 notes: TIRMIDHI(وائل بن حجر)]
- 1:7/q31/p7 Tirmidhi says many Companions, Successors, and later scholars, including al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, and Isḥāq, hold that a man raises his voice when saying amin rather than hiding it. — TIRMIDHI: Tirmidhi says many Companions, Successors, and later scholars, including al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, and Isḥāq, hold that a man raises his voice when saying amin rather than hiding it. ## 1:7/q32 What does agreement with the angels' Āmīn mean?  [* · reports]

- 1:7/q32/p1 Agreement is in receiving the answer — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting النبي عن أبي هريرة: When the imam finishes al-Fatiha, worshippers should say Amin; if their response coincides with the angels' and imam's, their past sins are forgiven. [1 notes: MUSNAD-AHMAD(النبي عن أبي هريرة)]
- 1:7/q32/p2 The Prophet instructs the congregation to say Amin after the imam's recitation; agreement with the angels' Amin brings forgiveness for past sins. — MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting النبي عن أبي هريرة: The Prophet instructs the congregation to say Amin after the imam's recitation; agreement with the angels' Amin brings forgiveness for past sins. ## 1:7/q34 Where may reciters pause in or after this verse?  [* · readings]
- 1:7/q34/p1 Both are normally paused sounds rather than verb-derived forms; nūn is opened to resolve adjacent quiescent letters, since kasra is heavy after yāʾ, as in ayna and kayfa. — ZAJJAJ: Both are normally paused sounds rather than verb-derived forms; nūn is opened to resolve adjacent quiescent letters, since kasra is heavy after yāʾ, as in ayna and kayfa. [1 notes: ZAJJAJ]
- 1:7/q34/p2 Final alif is retained in pauses and rhyme while yāʾ may be deleted; exceptional deletion of alif is poetic necessity, so it does not refute the rule. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Final alif is retained in pauses and rhyme while yāʾ may be deleted; exceptional deletion of alif is poetic necessity, so it does not refute the rule. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q34/p3 The shared deletion in pause follows naturally because plural glide deletion already occurs in liaison, and pause permits still more changes. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The shared deletion in pause follows naturally because plural glide deletion already occurs in liaison, and pause permits still more changes. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q34/p4 Ṭayyiʾ uses yāʾ where other dialects use final alif in both pause and liaison, as in afʿay for afʿā; this supports treating yāʾ in ʿalayhim like alif. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Ṭayyiʾ uses yāʾ where other dialects use final alif in both pause and liaison, as in afʿay for afʿā; this supports treating yāʾ in ʿalayhim like alif. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q34/p5 Yāʾ and wāw do not assimilate into alif because alif is long and always still; sibilants likewise resist stops because their extra hiss is absent from stops. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Yāʾ and wāw do not assimilate into alif because alif is long and always still; sibilants likewise resist stops because their extra hiss is absent from stops. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q34/p6 Those favored with this path are saints and the elect, whom God has annihilated from themselves and established through Himself, without hidden divine stratagems stopping them. — QUSHAYRI: Those favored with this path are saints and the elect, whom God has annihilated from themselves and established through Himself, without hidden divine stratagems stopping them. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q34/p7 The reciter should say Amin after a separate pause; the word is normally light, though grammarians allow a long or short vowel, and means ‘God, hear and answer.’ — BAGHAWI-FULL: The reciter should say Amin after a separate pause; the word is normally light, though grammarians allow a long or short vowel, and means ‘God, hear and answer.’ [1 notes: BAGHAWI-FULL]
- 1:7/q34/p8 He treats lafẓ, literally throwing, as metaphorical for spoken sounds: breath is expelled, and the letters produced by that breath are as if thrown outward. — RAZI: He treats lafẓ, literally throwing, as metaphorical for spoken sounds: breath is expelled, and the letters produced by that breath are as if thrown outward. - 1:7/q34/p10 The Creator formed articulatory passages in the throat, tongue, teeth, and lips so breath produces distinct letters and limitless words containing wisdom beyond human grasp. — RAZI: The Creator formed articulatory passages in the throat, tongue, teeth, and lips so breath produces distinct letters and limitless words containing wisdom beyond human grasp. - 1:7/q34/p11 Those under wrath are like Jews who stop at outward forms and bodily pleasures, veiling themselves from spiritual truths and intellectual delight; wrath entails expulsion, distance, and darkness of appearances. — QASHANI: Those under wrath are like Jews who stop at outward forms and bodily pleasures, veiling themselves from spiritual truths and intellectual delight; wrath entails expulsion, distance, and darkness of appearances. - 1:7/q34/p12 The astray are like Christians who stop at inner lights and special mercy, overlooking God’s outward manifestation and losing vision of the beloved’s beauty throughout creation. — QASHANI: The astray are like Christians who stop at inner lights and special mercy, overlooking God’s outward manifestation and losing vision of the beloved’s beauty throughout creation. - 1:7/q34/p14 One classification calls a stop sufficient when the next verse has verbal attachment, good and sufficient when attachment is semantic, complete when neither holds, and bad when the sense conflicts; 1:6 continues verbally into 1:7. — BURHAN: One classification calls a stop sufficient when the next verse has verbal attachment, good and sufficient when attachment is semantic, complete when neither holds, and bad when the sense conflicts; 1:6 continues verbally into 1:7. - 1:7/q34/p18 An incomplete pause leaves the preceding part sufficient but the following part dependent; one may stop at “straight,” but cannot begin with “the path of those.”; cited verses: 1:7 — BURHAN: An incomplete pause leaves the preceding part sufficient but the following part dependent; one may stop at “straight,” but cannot begin with “the path of those.” | mentions 1:7 [1 notes: BURHAN]
- 1:7/q34/p19 Qur'anic verse endings use either identical letters or letters close in sound; examples include the matched moon and two nearly matched Fatiha endings. — BURHAN: Qur'anic verse endings use either identical letters or letters close in sound; examples include the matched moon and two nearly matched Fatiha endings. - 1:7/q34/p20 Stopping after these phrases is good because their sense is understood, but starting with attached phrases such as rabb al-ʿālamīn, ṣirāṭ alladhīna, or ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim is poor, except at verse ends per the Sunnah. — NASHR: Stopping after these phrases is good because their sense is understood, but starting with attached phrases such as rabb al-ʿālamīn, ṣirāṭ alladhīna, or ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim is poor, except at verse ends per the Sunnah. [1 notes: NASHR]
- 1:7/q34/p21 A pause on an incomplete fragment such as “bi-smi,” “al-ḥamdu,” or “rabbi” leaves the utterance unfinished and without an intelligible meaning. — NASHR: A pause on an incomplete fragment such as “bi-smi,” “al-ḥamdu,” or “rabbi” leaves the utterance unfinished and without an intelligible meaning. [1 notes: NASHR]
- 1:7/q34/p22 Sajawandi's mark lā means that one should not begin with the following words; it does not make stopping on the preceding phrase blameworthy, as some imitators assume. — NASHR: Sajawandi's mark lā means that one should not begin with the following words; it does not make stopping on the preceding phrase blameworthy, as some imitators assume. [1 notes: NASHR]
- 1:7/q34/p23 Stopping deliberately at ghayr or alladhīna is unanimously forbidden because the first is in construct and the second is connected; Sajawandi's lā forbids beginning there, not stopping before it. — NASHR: Stopping deliberately at ghayr or alladhīna is unanimously forbidden because the first is in construct and the second is connected; Sajawandi's lā forbids beginning there, not stopping before it. [1 notes: NASHR]
- 1:7/q34/p24 A stop before the phrase is complete is a bad, unintended stop because it gives no benefit or corrupts the sense; “path of those” is an example, and stopping at verse endings is generally permitted. — ITQAN: A stop before the phrase is complete is a bad, unintended stop because it gives no benefit or corrupts the sense; “path of those” is an example, and stopping at verse endings is generally permitted. [1 notes: ITQAN]
- 1:7/q34/p25 Starting is always elective and must begin at a self-contained, adequate meaning; it has the same four quality grades as stopping, with examples showing that a bad stop can force an even worse restart. — ITQAN: Starting is always elective and must begin at a self-contained, adequate meaning; it has the same four quality grades as stopping, with examples showing that a bad stop can force an even worse restart. - 1:7/q34/p26 Qur'anic verse endings fall into only two kinds, identical or near-sounding; their similarity supports counting al-Fatiha as seven verses with the basmala and treating the final phrase as one verse. — ITQAN reporting الإمام فخر الدين وغيره: Qur'anic verse endings fall into only two kinds, identical or near-sounding; their similarity supports counting al-Fatiha as seven verses with the basmala and treating the final phrase as one verse. ## 1:7/q35 How is this verse counted within al-Fātiḥa?  [* · sciences]
- 1:7/q35/p1 Count the basmala and combine the closing words as one verse — BAGHAWI-FULL: All agree the Fatiha has seven verses, but those counting the basmala begin the final verse at ‘those You favored’; others begin it at ‘not those under wrath.’ BAGHAWI-FULL: Those counting the basmala cite its Quranic-script placement and a report from Ibn Abbas through Saʿid b. Jubayr: it is the seventh of the seven oft-repeated verses. | mentions 15:87 IBNATIYYA: Consensus counts al-Fātiḥa as seven verses, ending them respectively at العالمين, الرحيم, الدين, نستعين, المستقيم, أنعمت عليهم, and ولا الضالين; he says the weak dispute over the basmala was discussed earlier. TABRISI reporting النبي: The Prophet says God bestowed the Opening of the Book from a treasure of Paradise, including the basmala and the verse about people turning away when God alone is mentioned. | mentions 17:46 RAZI-FULL reporting أم سلمة عن النبي: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited al-Fatiha while counting the basmala as its first verse, followed by the rest of its verses. RAZI-FULL: The seven-verse count supports al-Shafi'i's division, with the basmala as one verse and the final phrase as one; Abu Hanifa denies the basmala verse and splits that final phrase, a weak view for Razi. ABUHAYYAN: Abū Ḥayyān concludes that the sūra is seven verses by consensus apart from disregarded dissent; Meccan and Kufan counters differ over whether the basmala or صراط الذين is an āya, while ʿAmr b. ʿUbayd counts eight and Ḥusayn al-Juʿfī six. ABUHAYYAN: Reports about the sūra's letter count, supposed occasions of revelation, basmala's merit, and many titles are not necessarily causes of revelation or core tafsīr; only sound Prophetic clarification, occasions, and abrogation are indispensable to tafsīr. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting الجمهور المكيون والكوفيون: The Meccan and Kufan majority count the basmala as a verse and do not count “whom You favored” separately; other counters reverse those choices. BURHAN: Al-Shafiʿi counts the basmala and makes the rest of 1:7 one verse; Abu Hanifa omits the basmala and divides its two phrases. Both count seven verses, but al-Shafiʿi's division better preserves the endings because anʿamta ʿalayhim does not match prior endings. DURR-FULL reporting أم سلمة: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited the Fātiḥa including the basmala and called it seven verses. ITQAN reporting أبو ميسرة عمرو بن شرحبيل: A mursal report with trustworthy narrators recounts Muhammad telling Khadija he feared the voice he heard; Waraqa advised him to listen, then taught him the opening of al-Fatiha from the basmala through “those astray.” | mentions 1:1, 1:7 ITQAN reporting الإمام فخر الدين وغيره: Qur'anic verse endings fall into only two kinds, identical or near-sounding; their similarity supports counting al-Fatiha as seven verses with the basmala and treating the final phrase as one verse. IBNASHUR-FULL: The verse division differs by region: Medinans exclude the basmala and count “those You favored” as a verse; Meccans and Kufans include the basmala and combine that phrase with its verse; Hasan counts both separately. [14 notes: BAGHAWI-FULL; IBNATIYYA; TABRISI(النبي); RAZI-FULL(أم سلمة عن النبي); ABUHAYYAN; ABUHAYYAN-FULL(الجمهور المكيون والكوفيون); DURR-FULL(أم سلمة); ITQAN(أبو ميسرة عمرو بن شرحبيل,الإمام فخر الدين وغيره); IBNASHUR-FULL; BURHAN+; RAZI-FULL+]
- 1:7/q35/p2 Seven verses — TAB reporting أهل الإلحاد الطاعنون في القرآن: Critics ask why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses when, they argue, the meaning of its remaining verses is already contained in “Master of Judgment Day” and “You alone we worship and ask for help.” TAB-FULL: Answering why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses if two contain its meanings: earlier scriptures each included only some meanings, while the Qur'an gathers all of them for Muhammad's community and adds many more. IBNATIYYA-FULL: There is agreement that al-Fatiha has seven verses, counted as al-ʿalamin, al-Rahim, al-Din, nastaʿin, al-mustaqim, anʿamta ʿalayhim, and wa-la al-dallin; the earlier discussion noted anomalous contrary reports. RAZI-FULL: Al-Fatiha has seven verses to counter these seven vices; its opening three names answer the three basic vices, and the Qur'an and moral traits branch from these foundations. QUTB-ZILAL: Al-Fatiha is Meccan and has seven verses; Muslims recite it at least seventeen times daily, more with voluntary prayers, and may repeat it without limit. [5 notes: TAB(أهل الإلحاد الطاعنون في القرآن); TAB-FULL; IBNATIYYA-FULL; RAZI-FULL; QUTB-ZILAL]
- 1:7/q35/p3 Six verses — DURR reporting أبو هريرة: Abū Hurayra identifies the phrase as the sixth verse. DURR-FULL reporting أبو هريرة: Abu Hurayra counts “those You favored” as the sixth verse. [2 notes: DURR(أبو هريرة); DURR-FULL(أبو هريرة)]

## 1:7/q37 What does the divine report say about the servant's closing request?  [* · reports]
- 1:7/q37/p1 God answers the recitation and grants the servant's closing petition — MUQATIL reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: A report from Abū Hurayra says the Prophet related that God divided this sūra between Himself and the servant: praise is thanks, the two mercy names are praise, the King verse is glorification, and the rest belongs to the servant; seeking help is God's special acknowledgment of the servant's plea. TAB reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet said God answers the worshipper's recitation: He calls al-ḥamdu praise, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm commendation, Mālik Yawm al-Dīn glorification, and the rest of the surah the servant's share. BAGHAWI reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: In a qudsi report, God divides prayer between Himself and His servant and answers each part of al-Fatiha; Baghawi grades it sahih. | mentions 1:4 RAZI-FULL reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي: In the divided-prayer report, God calls the basmala glorification, al-Hamd praise, the two mercy names extolling, the Master of Judgment entrustment, and the remaining response a sharing and a request granted. RAZI-FULL: A divine report says God remembers a servant in a gathering better than the servant's; the angels then long to visit, and the worshipper greets them on both sides. NASAFI reporting أبو هريرة عن النبي: Abu Hurayra reports God’s dialogue dividing the Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise, glorification, and exaltation belong to God; the worshipper’s request for guidance and the response to it belong to the servant, while worship and aid are shared. IBNKATHIR reporting الله تعالى: In a divine report, God divides the prayer between Himself and His servant, responds to each recited section, calls 1:5 shared between them, and grants the servant's request. BIQAI-FULL reporting الحرالي: Al-Harali explains the sound report that God divided prayer between Himself and His servant: the first three verses are God's praise, which He accepts from the reciting servant as praise and glorification. BIQAI-FULL reporting أبو هريرة: In the authentic report in Muslim and the four Sunan, God says the Fatiha is divided between Himself and His servant: He answers praise, glorification and worship, and grants the servant's final requests. DURR-FULL reporting الله عز وجل: In Abū Hurayra's report, God says the prayer is divided between Him and His servant: the opening praise is His, the middle is shared, and the servant receives what he asks in the remainder. ITQAN reporting الطيبي: Al-Tibi divides the Fatiha’s religious knowledge into foundations (God and attributes, prophethood, resurrection), branches (worship), ethical perfection and seeking the path, and accounts of earlier peoples with promise and threat. | mentions 1:2, 1:4, 1:6, 1:7 QUTB-ZILAL reporting رسول الله: Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih Muslim that God calls al-Fatiha a prayer divided between Himself and His servant: praise, mercy, and glorification are the Lord's; worship and aid are shared; guidance and the servant's request belong to the servant, who receives what he asks. IBNASHUR-FULL reporting النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم: A hadith in both Sahihs from Abu Hurayra has God divide prayer between Himself and the servant, answering each portion of al-Fatiha and granting the servant's request. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7 TABATABAI reporting النبي: The Prophet transmits God's division of al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: each phrase receives divine acknowledgement and a tailored promise of blessing, mercy, ease of judgment, reward, help, and fulfillment of the servant's requests. ABUDAWUD reporting الله تعالى: In a hadith qudsi transmitted by Abu Hurayra, God divides al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise and glorification receive divine responses, worship is mutual, and the guidance petition belongs to the servant. MALIK reporting الله تبارك وتعالى: The qudsi report assigns the final plea for guidance to the servant and says the servant receives what he asks. MUSLIM reporting الله تعالى: When the servant asks for the guided path and names those favored rather than those under anger or astray, Allah says this request is for the servant and grants what was asked. NASAI reporting رسول الله: The same report assigns the servant’s request for the favored path, away from those under wrath and those astray, to the servant; God grants what the servant asks. TIRMIDHI reporting الله تعالى: In the divine report the Opening is divided into halves: praise belongs to God, the central pledge of worship and seeking help is shared, and its closing requests belong to the worshipper, who receives what he asks. [19 notes: MUQATIL(أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم); TAB(رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم); BAGHAWI(النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم); RAZI-FULL(أبو هريرة عن النبي); NASAFI(أبو هريرة عن النبي); IBNKATHIR(الله تعالى); BIQAI-FULL(أبو هريرة,الحرالي); DURR-FULL(الله عز وجل); ITQAN(الطيبي); QUTB-ZILAL(رسول الله); IBNASHUR-FULL(النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم); TABATABAI(النبي); ABUDAWUD(الله تعالى); MALIK(الله تبارك وتعالى); MUSLIM(الله تعالى); NASAI(رسول الله); TIRMIDHI(الله تعالى)]

## 1:7/q41 What inward path and states does the verse evoke?  [* · inward]
- 1:7/q41/p1 Alternatively, genitive ghayr qualifies alladhīna; although ghayr usually describes an indefinite noun, alladhīna here denotes a category rather than particular people. — ZAJJAJ: Alternatively, genitive ghayr qualifies alladhīna; although ghayr usually describes an indefinite noun, alladhīna here denotes a category rather than particular people. [1 notes: ZAJJAJ]
- 1:7/q41/p2 The blessed are knowers granted knowledge, saints granted sincerity, contentment, and certainty, the righteous granted patience and compassion, seekers granted obedience's sweetness, and believers granted steadfastness. — SULAMI reporting ابن عطاء: The blessed are knowers granted knowledge, saints granted sincerity, contentment, and certainty, the righteous granted patience and compassion, seekers granted obedience's sweetness, and believers granted steadfastness. [1 notes: SULAMI(ابن عطاء)]

- 1:7/q41/p4 They have cosmic darkness removed from their secrets and spirits purified by holy light, so their aspiration witnesses God alone. — SULAMI reporting بعضهم: They have cosmic darkness removed from their secrets and spirits purified by holy light, so their aspiration witnesses God alone. [1 notes: SULAMI(بعضهم)]
- 1:7/q41/p5 God's favor includes teaching them the path's dangers, Satan's tricks, and the ego's treachery. — SULAMI reporting أبو عثمان: God's favor includes teaching them the path's dangers, Satan's tricks, and the ego's treachery. [1 notes: SULAMI(أبو عثمان)]
- 1:7/q41/p6 The blessed were assigned happiness in pre-eternity. — SULAMI reporting بعضهم: The blessed were assigned happiness in pre-eternity. [1 notes: SULAMI(بعضهم)]
- 1:7/q41/p7 God's favor annihilates attention to blessings through the lasting joy of nearness and intimacy. — SULAMI reporting بعض البغداديين: God's favor annihilates attention to blessings through the lasting joy of nearness and intimacy. [1 notes: SULAMI(بعض البغداديين)]
- 1:7/q41/p8 The blessed see what was decreed for them eternally without that disclosure distracting them from God. — SULAMI reporting بعضهم: The blessed see what was decreed for them eternally without that disclosure distracting them from God. [1 notes: SULAMI(بعضهم)]
- 1:7/q41/p9 Those under anger are consumed in Satan's wastelands; the astray are expelled from obedience to the Merciful. — SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Those under anger are consumed in Satan's wastelands; the astray are expelled from obedience to the Merciful. [1 notes: SULAMI(بعضهم)]
- 1:7/q41/p10 God keeps the seekers from settling among likenesses through the gentle gift of union and disclosure of majesty and beauty. — QUSHAYRI: God keeps the seekers from settling among likenesses through the gentle gift of union and disclosure of majesty and beauty. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q41/p11 They have been freed from Satan's snares, the soul's errors, and imagined arrival before human traces have faded. — QUSHAYRI: They have been freed from Satan's snares, the soul's errors, and imagined arrival before human traces have faded. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q41/p12 They preserve the rules of sacred law even during overpowering disclosures of spiritual realities, never exceeding knowledge or neglecting a ruling. — QUSHAYRI: They preserve the rules of sacred law even during overpowering disclosures of spiritual realities, never exceeding knowledge or neglecting a ruling. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q41/p13 The favored remain servants even when the power of spiritual reality appears. — QUSHAYRI: The favored remain servants even when the power of spiritual reality appears. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q41/p14 They are also described as humiliated and ruined, occupied with pursuing gratification while imagining they possess something; their misery has a divine secret. — QUSHAYRI: They are also described as humiliated and ruined, occupied with pursuing gratification while imagining they possess something; their misery has a divine secret. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q41/p15 Guidance to truth prevents reliance on the means of spiritual practice and keeps conjecture from clouding the oneness of God. — QUSHAYRI: Guidance to truth prevents reliance on the means of spiritual practice and keeps conjecture from clouding the oneness of God. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q41/p16 Another group tasted nearness for a time, then was turned to distance and failed to reach the intimacy it desired; its effort and hope came to nothing. — QUSHAYRI: Another group tasted nearness for a time, then was turned to distance and failed to reach the intimacy it desired; its effort and hope came to nothing. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q41/p17 The straight path keeps Satan's impulses, the soul's notions, inherited imitation, routine instruction, habit, fatigue, weak resolve, and greed from delaying arrival or insight. — QUSHAYRI: The straight path keeps Satan's impulses, the soul's notions, inherited imitation, routine instruction, habit, fatigue, weak resolve, and greed from delaying arrival or insight. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q41/p18 Those favored with this path are saints and the elect, whom God has annihilated from themselves and established through Himself, without hidden divine stratagems stopping them. — QUSHAYRI: Those favored with this path are saints and the elect, whom God has annihilated from themselves and established through Himself, without hidden divine stratagems stopping them. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]

## 1:7/q42 What discussions of language and speech does this commentary derive from the sūra?  [* · meaning]
- 1:7/q42/p1 Kalima can denote one word or extended connected speech; the latter is metaphorical, by part-for-whole naming or because connected speech resembles a single unit. — RAZI: Kalima can denote one word or extended connected speech; the latter is metaphorical, by part-for-whole naming or because connected speech resembles a single unit. [1 notes: RAZI]
- 1:7/q42/p2 The Qurʾānic uses of kalima include Jesus, created by God's command or in a short time, and God's acts, called His words; both uses are explained by the preceding metaphorical grounds.; cited verses: 3:45, 18:109 — RAZI: The Qurʾānic uses of kalima include Jesus, created by God's command or in a short time, and God's acts, called His words; both uses are explained by the preceding metaphorical grounds. | mentions 3:45, 18:109 [1 notes: RAZI]
- 1:7/q42/p3 Razi reads the six permutations of ق و ل as expressing movement or lightness, explaining qawl as easy on the tongue and adducing examples such as the swift bird and animal.; cited verses: 24:15 — RAZI: Razi reads the six permutations of ق و ل as expressing movement or lightness, explaining qawl as easy on the tongue and adducing examples such as the swift bird and animal. | mentions 24:15 [1 notes: RAZI]
- 1:7/q42/p4 Ibn Jinnī derives lugha from laghawtu, meaning I spoke, and proposes an original form ending in wāw, supported by related forms such as kurra and qulla.; cited verses: 25:72 — RAZI reporting ابن جني: Ibn Jinnī derives lugha from laghawtu, meaning I spoke, and proposes an original form ending in wāw, supported by related forms such as kurra and qulla. | mentions 25:72 [1 notes: RAZI(ابن جني)]
- 1:7/q42/p5 He treats lafẓ, literally throwing, as metaphorical for spoken sounds: breath is expelled, and the letters produced by that breath are as if thrown outward. — RAZI: He treats lafẓ, literally throwing, as metaphorical for spoken sounds: breath is expelled, and the letters produced by that breath are as if thrown outward. [1 notes: RAZI]
- 1:7/q42/p6 The permutations of ʿ-b-r share crossing or transition: speech moves between letters and transfers meaning to a hearer, with related examples including tears, crossing, and interpretation. — RAZI: The permutations of ʿ-b-r share crossing or transition: speech moves between letters and transfers meaning to a hearer, with related examples including tears, crossing, and interpretation. [1 notes: RAZI]
- 1:7/q42/p7 Most grammarians define kalima as a single word and kalām as a meaningful sentence; Ibn Jinnī sides with them, though Razi finds his evidence weak. — RAZI reporting النحويون: Most grammarians define kalima as a single word and kalām as a meaningful sentence; Ibn Jinnī sides with them, though Razi finds his evidence weak. [1 notes: RAZI(النحويون)]
- 1:7/q42/p8 Most legal theorists see no difference between kalima and kalām: either term may cover a single utterance or a compound expression. — RAZI reporting الأصوليون: Most legal theorists see no difference between kalima and kalām: either term may cover a single utterance or a compound expression. [1 notes: RAZI(الأصوليون)]
- 1:7/q42/p9 Legal theorists argue that a single word counts as speech because it opposes silence, affects a listener through meaning, and can naturally be described as something a person said. — RAZI reporting الأصوليون: Legal theorists argue that a single word counts as speech because it opposes silence, affects a listener through meaning, and can naturally be described as something a person said. [1 notes: RAZI(الأصوليون)]
- 1:7/q42/p10 In an unconsummated marriage, Zufar says that repeating the conditional phrase إن كلمتك completes the condition before the divorce clause, so the ensuing divorce does not take effect. — RAZI reporting زفر: In an unconsummated marriage, Zufar says that repeating the conditional phrase إن كلمتك completes the condition before the divorce clause, so the ensuing divorce does not take effect. [1 notes: RAZI(زفر)]
- 1:7/q42/p11 Abū Ḥanīfa and his two companions treat the condition as incomplete until the whole sentence is finished, so one divorce takes effect when the sentence is complete. — RAZI reporting أبو حنيفة: Abū Ḥanīfa and his two companions treat the condition as incomplete until the whole sentence is finished, so one divorce takes effect when the sentence is complete. [1 notes: RAZI(أبو حنيفة)]
- 1:7/q42/p12 Scholars disagree whether kalima and kalām include meaningless speech: some say yes because it can be called unused or unintelligible speech, while others require meaningful expression. — RAZI: Scholars disagree whether kalima and kalām include meaningless speech: some say yes because it can be called unused or unintelligible speech, while others require meaningful expression. [1 notes: RAZI]
- 1:7/q42/p13 Scholars also dispute whether naturally meaningful sounds, such as pain cries, coughs, or bird calls, count as words; the issue affects whether hearing one triggers an oath. — RAZI: Scholars also dispute whether naturally meaningful sounds, such as pain cries, coughs, or bird calls, count as words; the issue affects whether hearing one triggers an oath. [1 notes: RAZI]
- 1:7/q42/p14 Ibn Jinnī says qawl literally applies to a sentence or a single word, kalām only to a complete sentence, and kalima only to an isolated word; a poem treating qāf as a qawl supports the first distinction. — RAZI reporting ابن جني: Ibn Jinnī says qawl literally applies to a sentence or a single word, kalām only to a complete sentence, and kalima only to an isolated word; a poem treating qāf as a qawl supports the first distinction. - 1:7/q42/p15 Ibn Jinnī says qawl can metaphorically mean a belief or opinion, as in attributing a doctrine to Abū Ḥanīfa or Mālik, because belief is apprehended through its expression. — RAZI reporting ابن جني: Ibn Jinnī says qawl can metaphorically mean a belief or opinion, as in attributing a doctrine to Abū Ḥanīfa or Mālik, because belief is apprehended through its expression. [1 notes: RAZI(ابن جني)]
- 1:7/q42/p16 Qāla can be used for nonverbal events, as when birds, eyes, or a full basin are said to speak; Razi also cites two Qurʾānic examples of such speech.; cited verses: 16:40, 41:11 — RAZI: Qāla can be used for nonverbal events, as when birds, eyes, or a full basin are said to speak; Razi also cites two Qurʾānic examples of such speech. | mentions 16:40, 41:11 [1 notes: RAZI]
- 1:7/q42/p17 Those who affirm inner speech say the inward meaning is itself called kalām and qawl; they cite the hypocrites' false claim to be witnesses and Umar's recollection of an inwardly prepared speech.; cited verses: 63:1 — RAZI reporting مثبتو كلام النفس: Those who affirm inner speech say the inward meaning is itself called kalām and qawl; they cite the hypocrites' false claim to be witnesses and Umar's recollection of an inwardly prepared speech. | mentions 63:1 [1 notes: RAZI(مثبتو كلام النفس)]
- 1:7/q42/p18 Razi illustrates how analyzing Aʿūdhu billāh requires definitions and subdivisions of nouns, verbs, particles, and the possible derivations of the name Allah. — RAZI: Razi illustrates how analyzing Aʿūdhu billāh requires definitions and subdivisions of nouns, verbs, particles, and the possible derivations of the name Allah. - 1:7/q42/p19 A report from ʿUmar says that at the Saqīfa he had composed words within himself, but Abū Bakr spoke first; Razi gives no grading. — RAZI reporting عمر: A report from ʿUmar says that at the Saqīfa he had composed words within himself, but Abū Bakr spoke first; Razi gives no grading. - 1:7/q42/p20 The poet al-Akhṭal is cited for the claim that speech resides in the heart and the tongue serves as its guide; Razi gives no grading. — RAZI reporting الأخطل: The poet al-Akhṭal is cited for the claim that speech resides in the heart and the tongue serves as its guide; Razi gives no grading. - 1:7/q42/p21 Those denying inner speech argue that someone who neither speaks nor pronounces letters is described as not having spoken, and that oaths attach to uttered words. — RAZI reporting من أنكر كلام النفس: Those denying inner speech argue that someone who neither speaks nor pronounces letters is described as not having spoken, and that oaths attach to uttered words. - 1:7/q42/p23 Utterances are called aḥādīth because their successive letters occur one after another, or because hearing them brings knowledge and meanings into hearts.; cited verses: 52:34 — RAZI: Utterances are called aḥādīth because their successive letters occur one after another, or because hearing them brings knowledge and meanings into hearts. | mentions 52:34 [1 notes: RAZI]
- 1:7/q42/p24 Razi lists kalima, kalām, qawl, lafẓ, ʿibāra, ḥadīth, and nuṭq as terms needing comparison, leaving the derivation and precise relation of nuṭq for inquiry. — RAZI: Razi lists kalima, kalām, qawl, lafẓ, ʿibāra, ḥadīth, and nuṭq as terms needing comparison, leaving the derivation and precise relation of nuṭq for inquiry. - 1:7/q42/p25 Meaningful sound has four form-meaning combinations: both simple, both compound, simple form with compound meaning, or compound form with compound meaning; compound form with simple meaning is impossible. — RAZI: Meaningful sound has four form-meaning combinations: both simple, both compound, simple form with compound meaning, or compound form with compound meaning; compound form with simple meaning is impossible. - 1:7/q42/p27 The inquiry can descend from words into speech and phonetics, respiratory and vocal anatomy, sensory qualities, philosophical categories, substances, accidents, existence, and knowledge. — RAZI: The inquiry can descend from words into speech and phonetics, respiratory and vocal anatomy, sensory qualities, philosophical categories, substances, accidents, existence, and knowledge. ## 1:7/q43 How does reciting al-Fātiḥa shape prayer?  [* · law]

- 1:7/q44/p79 Al-Kisāʾī keeps hāʾ kasra unless the mim meets a following sukūn, then restores both hāʾ and mim to damma to avoid switching from kasra to damma. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting الكسائي: Al-Kisāʾī keeps hāʾ kasra unless the mim meets a following sukūn, then restores both hāʾ and mim to damma to avoid switching from kasra to damma.
