- 1:7/q44/p80 The author prefers kasra on hāʾ because it is easier to pronounce and is the majority reading. — FARISI-HUJJA: The author prefers kasra on hāʾ because it is easier to pronounce and is the majority reading. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA+]
- 1:7/q44/p81 Sibawayh explains kasra hāʾ after yāʾ or kasra by its hidden quality and closeness to yāʾ and alif; adjacent kasra also changes wāw to yāʾ. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting سيبويه: Sibawayh explains kasra hāʾ after yāʾ or kasra by its hidden quality and closeness to yāʾ and alif; adjacent kasra also changes wāw to yāʾ. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(سيبويه)]
- 1:7/q44/p82 Abū ʿAlī argues that hāʾ resembles alif in articulation and hiddenness, so a preceding kasra or yāʾ draws its damma toward kasra as imāla draws alif toward yāʾ. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Abū ʿAlī argues that hāʾ resembles alif in articulation and hiddenness, so a preceding kasra or yāʾ draws its damma toward kasra as imāla draws alif toward yāʾ. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p83 The pronunciation ḍarabtu ḍarbih shows hāʾ can trigger imāla even without a preceding kasra or yāʾ, like imāla in some proper names. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The pronunciation ḍarabtu ḍarbih shows hāʾ can trigger imāla even without a preceding kasra or yāʾ, like imāla in some proper names. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p84 Hāʾ and alif both clarify a preceding vowel in pause; al-Khalīl permits either hāʾ or alif after a consonant, supporting their parallel treatment in ʿalayhim. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Hāʾ and alif both clarify a preceding vowel in pause; al-Khalīl permits either hāʾ or alif after a consonant, supporting their parallel treatment in ʿalayhim. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p85 The optional hāʾ or alif suffix is allowed because each resembles and can stand for the other; alif also occurs in the same pause pattern after bāʾ, tāʾ, and thāʾ. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The optional hāʾ or alif suffix is allowed because each resembles and can stand for the other; alif also occurs in the same pause pattern after bāʾ, tāʾ, and thāʾ. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p86 Although hāʾ lacks the sustained sound of alif, their shared hiddenness, weakness, and articulation allow one to be brought near the other. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Although hāʾ lacks the sustained sound of alif, their shared hiddenness, weakness, and articulation allow one to be brought near the other. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p87 Hāʾ can replace other letters in pause just as alif can, another sign of their similarity. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Hāʾ can replace other letters in pause just as alif can, another sign of their similarity. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p88 The reported phrase lam aḍribihimā is treated as liaison pronounced like pause, not as a general rule for inflectional sukūn; inflectional endings do not assimilate freely. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The reported phrase lam aḍribihimā is treated as liaison pronounced like pause, not as a general rule for inflectional sukūn; inflectional endings do not assimilate freely. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p89 A jussive consonant may move to avoid a following sukūn, as in the cited yattaqihi form, unlike a freely altered inflectional ending. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: A jussive consonant may move to avoid a following sukūn, as in the cited yattaqihi form, unlike a freely altered inflectional ending. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p90 Hāʾ behaves like weak letters: it can be deleted word-finally, as in shāh, shafah, and sanah, and shared rules strengthen the analogy. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Hāʾ behaves like weak letters: it can be deleted word-finally, as in shāh, shafah, and sanah, and shared rules strengthen the analogy. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p91 Hāʾ substitutes for yāʾ in ذه/هذه; Ḥijāzī and Tamīmī dialects differ in whether it drops or becomes yāʾ in pause and liaison. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Hāʾ substitutes for yāʾ in ذه/هذه; Ḥijāzī and Tamīmī dialects differ in whether it drops or becomes yāʾ in pause and liaison. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p92 Hāʾ also alternates with yāʾ under doubling, as in dahdayt for dahdaht and related forms. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Hāʾ also alternates with yāʾ under doubling, as in dahdayt for dahdaht and related forms. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p93 Abū Zayd records the forms māhat and tamūhu/tamīhu, and a poetic line using māh as a word for a heart softened by tears. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو زيد: Abū Zayd records the forms māhat and tamūhu/tamīhu, and a poetic line using māh as a word for a heart softened by tears. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو زيد)]
- 1:7/q44/p94 Some speakers kasra hāʾ despite an intervening consonant, as in minhum; this weaker analogy still supports kasra when yāʾ is adjacent. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Some speakers kasra hāʾ despite an intervening consonant, as in minhum; this weaker analogy still supports kasra when yāʾ is adjacent. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p95 Abū Zayd reports a Bakrī speaker saying minhu, minhuma, and minhumī, breaking the pronoun in both connected and paused speech. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو زيد: Abū Zayd reports a Bakrī speaker saying minhu, minhuma, and minhumī, breaking the pronoun in both connected and paused speech. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو زيد)]
- 1:7/q44/p96 Other Bakrī speakers say bikum and faḍlu aḥlāmikum with kasra on kāf, since kāf shares hāʾ’s whispering and pronoun function. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Other Bakrī speakers say bikum and faḍlu aḥlāmikum with kasra on kāf, since kāf shares hāʾ’s whispering and pronoun function. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p97 The author replies that proximity can override a default vowel; Arabic regularly abandons original sounds for harmony or ease, including ṣād in ṣirāṭ and several broken forms. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The author replies that proximity can override a default vowel; Arabic regularly abandons original sounds for harmony or ease, including ṣād in ṣirāṭ and several broken forms. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p98 Numerous forms depart from their expected morphology: ʿīd has plural aʿyād, dunya’s pattern is otherwise abandoned, and Adam/Akhir form plurals with wāw despite an expected hamza. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Numerous forms depart from their expected morphology: ʿīd has plural aʿyād, dunya’s pattern is otherwise abandoned, and Adam/Akhir form plurals with wāw despite an expected hamza. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p99 The expected form of qasī is abandoned in three respects, illustrating that a linguistic default need not prevail when analogy or ease favors another form. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The expected form of qasī is abandoned in three respects, illustrating that a linguistic default need not prevail when analogy or ease favors another form. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p100 Hamza’s reading in buyūt shows that kasra can replace a default damma because of nearby yāʾ; Sibawayh’s diminutive bayyit supports the same allowance. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Hamza’s reading in buyūt shows that kasra can replace a default damma because of nearby yāʾ; Sibawayh’s diminutive bayyit supports the same allowance. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p101 The hāʾ in bihi and ʿalayhi can therefore follow kasra or yāʾ just as alif does, despite being pronounced with a movement. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The hāʾ in bihi and ʿalayhi can therefore follow kasra or yāʾ just as alif does, despite being pronounced with a movement. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p102 A moving hāʾ is often ignored as a separator: imāla occurs before it in yadribahā, yanziʿahā, and baynī wa-baynahā, as before alif. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: A moving hāʾ is often ignored as a separator: imāla occurs before it in yadribahā, yanziʿahā, and baynī wa-baynahā, as before alif. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p103 The shared opening of the doubled dāl in raddahā and raddā likewise shows that hāʾ does not block the alif-like pattern. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The shared opening of the doubled dāl in raddahā and raddā likewise shows that hāʾ does not block the alif-like pattern. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p104 When moving hāʾ is not counted, retaining its following yāʾ or wāw would leave two adjacent sukūns; deletion is therefore favored in fīhi hudan and khudhūhu. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: When moving hāʾ is not counted, retaining its following yāʾ or wāw would leave two adjacent sukūns; deletion is therefore favored in fīhi hudan and khudhūhu. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p105 Weak letters are deleted in many settings where other letters remain, including suffixes, possessive forms, pauses, and rhyme, so deleting the glide after mim is ordinary. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Weak letters are deleted in many settings where other letters remain, including suffixes, possessive forms, pauses, and rhyme, so deleting the glide after mim is ordinary. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p106 Poetic examples demonstrate deletion of weak endings in verse and rhyme; the text also reports a variant wording for the line with sawāfa. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Poetic examples demonstrate deletion of weak endings in verse and rhyme; the text also reports a variant wording for the line with sawāfa. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p107 Repeated deletion of weak endings makes it legitimate to apply the same deletion to nouns as well as other forms. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Repeated deletion of weak endings makes it legitimate to apply the same deletion to nouns as well as other forms. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p108 Both lexical and grammatical weak endings are deleted elsewhere, even without a surviving marker; that makes deletion from ʿalayhim especially fitting. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Both lexical and grammatical weak endings are deleted elsewhere, even without a surviving marker; that makes deletion from ʿalayhim especially fitting. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p109 Retaining the mim vowel could restore the missing glide through vowel lengthening, so a still mim best realizes the intended lightening. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Retaining the mim vowel could restore the missing glide through vowel lengthening, so a still mim best realizes the intended lightening. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p110 A kasra or damma may be lengthened into the very yāʾ or wāw that was deleted; still mim prevents that reversal and preserves the lighter form. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: A kasra or damma may be lengthened into the very yāʾ or wāw that was deleted; still mim prevents that reversal and preserves the lighter form. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p111 A vowelled mim would create four or five consecutive moving syllables, a sequence avoided in Arabic word patterns and poetic meters; deleting its vowel prevents that sequence. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: A vowelled mim would create four or five consecutive moving syllables, a sequence avoided in Arabic word patterns and poetic meters; deleting its vowel prevents that sequence. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p112 Arabic meter alternates deletions in mustafʿilun to avoid five consecutive movements, an analogy for removing mim’s vowel. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Arabic meter alternates deletions in mustafʿilun to avoid five consecutive movements, an analogy for removing mim’s vowel. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p113 Arabic alternations such as ḥāḥayt, ṭāʾī, and ḥārī support the close relation of yāʾ and alif; alif from wāw is comparatively rare. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Arabic alternations such as ḥāḥayt, ṭāʾī, and ḥārī support the close relation of yāʾ and alif; alif from wāw is comparatively rare. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p114 Against the claim that dāwiya has an alif derived from wāw, Abū ʿAlī suggests it may derive from daw with a nisba ending, supported by a cited poetic use. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Against the claim that dāwiya has an alif derived from wāw, Abū ʿAlī suggests it may derive from daw with a nisba ending, supported by a cited poetic use. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p115 The common analogy should prevail over a rare alternative unless evidence forces the exception; poetic shortening of nisba yāʾ does not do so. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The common analogy should prevail over a rare alternative unless evidence forces the exception; poetic shortening of nisba yāʾ does not do so. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p116 Abū Zayd reports an eloquent Arab saying ḍarabat yadāh and waḍaʿtuhu ʿalāh; al-Khalīl used such speech to explain forms with alif-like treatment. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو زيد: Abū Zayd reports an eloquent Arab saying ḍarabat yadāh and waḍaʿtuhu ʿalāh; al-Khalīl used such speech to explain forms with alif-like treatment. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو زيد)]
- 1:7/q44/p117 Ḥijāz and Qays use final hāʾ in both pause and liaison, paralleling Ṭayyiʾ’s yāʾ substitution and strengthening the analogy. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Ḥijāz and Qays use final hāʾ in both pause and liaison, paralleling Ṭayyiʾ’s yāʾ substitution and strengthening the analogy. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p118 The attested dialect and the analogous Ḥijāzī/Tamīmī alternations establish the language and make its use for Ḥamza’s reading legitimate. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: The attested dialect and the analogous Ḥijāzī/Tamīmī alternations establish the language and make its use for Ḥamza’s reading legitimate. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p119 Poetic meter balances duration, so the longer alif cannot share the rhyme position of yāʾ and wāw. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Poetic meter balances duration, so the longer alif cannot share the rhyme position of yāʾ and wāw. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p120 Unlike long alif, short fatha can precede a rhyme with damma or kasra; examples from Abū al-Ḥasan show the distinction. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Unlike long alif, short fatha can precede a rhyme with damma or kasra; examples from Abū al-Ḥasan show the distinction. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p121 Alif’s greater duration appears in how hamza is softened after alif but not after yāʾ or wāw, strengthening its distinct treatment. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Alif’s greater duration appears in how hamza is softened after alif but not after yāʾ or wāw, strengthening its distinct treatment. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p122 Examples such as ruwiya, ruwiyya, and nuwwi show that a replacement wāw can inherit the behavior of its source; bīs similarly keeps its original kasra after hamza is dropped. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Examples such as ruwiya, ruwiyya, and nuwwi show that a replacement wāw can inherit the behavior of its source; bīs similarly keeps its original kasra after hamza is dropped. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p123 Yāʾ can also be fixed across case positions like alif, preserving one surface form; he cites ayādī sabā, bādī badā, qālī qalā, and maʿdīkarib. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: Yāʾ can also be fixed across case positions like alif, preserving one surface form; he cites ayādī sabā, bādī badā, qālī qalā, and maʿdīkarib. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p124 These fixed-yāʾ forms occur in accusative position, whether analyzed as one of the cited nominal patterns or as an attached ending. — FARISI-HUJJA reporting أبو علي: These fixed-yāʾ forms occur in accusative position, whether analyzed as one of the cited nominal patterns or as an attached ending. [1 notes: FARISI-HUJJA(أبو علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p125 Abū Bakr counts seven transmitted vocalizations of the pronoun in عليهم; al-Akhfash adds three, yielding ten forms, five with hāʾ ḍamma and five with kasra. — IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB reporting أبو بكر أحمد بن موسى: Abū Bakr counts seven transmitted vocalizations of the pronoun in عليهم; al-Akhfash adds three, yielding ten forms, five with hāʾ ḍamma and five with kasra. - 1:7/q44/p127 Ibn Jinnī regards the plural wāw as original: mīm marks more than one, including the dual, while wāw specifically marks the plural. — IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB: Ibn Jinnī regards the plural wāw as original: mīm marks more than one, including the dual, while wāw specifically marks the plural. - 1:7/q44/p128 He derives عليهمي from kasra spreading from the preceding yāʾ to the weak, nearby hāʾ, then to mīm; the wāw becomes yāʾ after a kasra. — IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB: He derives عليهمي from kasra spreading from the preceding yāʾ to the weak, nearby hāʾ, then to mīm; the wāw becomes yāʾ after a kasra. - 1:7/q44/p129 The blessed relinquish personal interests and stand with God in good etiquette. — SULAMI reporting بعض البغداديين: The blessed relinquish personal interests and stand with God in good etiquette. [1 notes: SULAMI(بعض البغداديين)]
- 1:7/q44/p130 The blessed witness the Benefactor rather than the gift itself. — SULAMI reporting بعضهم: The blessed witness the Benefactor rather than the gift itself. [1 notes: SULAMI(بعضهم)]
- 1:7/q44/p131 God's favor restrains their limbs through awe while they serve Him. — SULAMI reporting محمد بن علي: God's favor restrains their limbs through awe while they serve Him. [1 notes: SULAMI(محمد بن علي)]
- 1:7/q44/p132 The blessed path is acceptance of the obligations God imposed. — SULAMI reporting محمد بن الفضل: The blessed path is acceptance of the obligations God imposed. [1 notes: SULAMI(محمد بن الفضل)]
- 1:7/q44/p133 Divine care keeps the blessed steadfast on the path of intimate conversation with God. — SULAMI reporting أبو الحسن الوراق: Divine care keeps the blessed steadfast on the path of intimate conversation with God. [1 notes: SULAMI(أبو الحسن الوراق)]
- 1:7/q44/p134 The blessed path means following the Prophet. — SULAMI reporting مالك بن أنس: The blessed path means following the Prophet. [1 notes: SULAMI(مالك بن أنس)]

- 1:7/q44/p136 The blessed path means following the Sunnah. — SULAMI reporting سهل بن عبد الله: The blessed path means following the Sunnah. [1 notes: SULAMI(سهل بن عبد الله)]
- 1:7/q44/p137 The supplicant asks God to act accordingly and not leave him to himself for even an instant. — SULAMI reporting ابن عطاء: The supplicant asks God to act accordingly and not leave him to himself for even an instant. [1 notes: SULAMI(ابن عطاء)]
- 1:7/q44/p138 The condemned follow the path of the doomed, while the astray follow desire away from guidance. — SULAMI reporting بعضهم: The condemned follow the path of the doomed, while the astray follow desire away from guidance. [1 notes: SULAMI(بعضهم)]
- 1:7/q44/p139 Anger is associated with seeing one's own acts or seeking compensation for deeds; error is failing to see favors or thank God for enabled service. — SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Anger is associated with seeing one's own acts or seeking compensation for deeds; error is failing to see favors or thank God for enabled service. - 1:7/q44/p140 Anger follows bad etiquette in service; the contrasting phrase refers to turning back in repentance, though its wording is broken in this segment. — SULAMI reporting بعضهم: Anger follows bad etiquette in service; the contrasting phrase refers to turning back in repentance, though its wording is broken in this segment. - 1:7/q44/p142 ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read with ḍamma on both hāʾ and mīm and an added wāw. — THALABI reporting عيسى بن عمر: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read with ḍamma on both hāʾ and mīm and an added wāw. [1 notes: THALABI(عيسى بن عمر)]
- 1:7/q44/p143 Ibn Kathīr and al-Aʿraj read with kasra on hāʾ, ḍamma on mīm, and an appended wāw. — THALABI reporting ابن كثير: Ibn Kathīr and al-Aʿraj read with kasra on hāʾ, ḍamma on mīm, and an appended wāw. [1 notes: THALABI(ابن كثير)]
- 1:7/q44/p144 Al-Ḥasan reads with kasra on both hāʾ and mīm and an appended yāʾ. — THALABI reporting الحسن: Al-Ḥasan reads with kasra on both hāʾ and mīm and an appended yāʾ. [1 notes: THALABI(الحسن)]

- 1:7/q44/p146 Shahr ibn Ḥawshab identifies them as the Prophet's companions and his household. — THALABI reporting شهر بن حوشب: Shahr ibn Ḥawshab identifies them as the Prophet's companions and his household. [1 notes: THALABI(شهر بن حوشب)]
- 1:7/q44/p147 ʿIkrima says they were granted steadfastness in faith and uprightness. — THALABI reporting عكرمة: ʿIkrima says they were granted steadfastness in faith and uprightness. [1 notes: THALABI(عكرمة)]
- 1:7/q44/p148 ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Dāwūd says they give thanks in ease and patience in hardship. — THALABI reporting علي بن الحسين بن داود: ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn ibn Dāwūd says they give thanks in ease and patience in hardship. [1 notes: THALABI(علي بن الحسين بن داود)]

- 1:7/q44/p152 Misguidance is the opposite of guidance. — MAWARDI: Misguidance is the opposite of guidance. [1 notes: MAWARDI]
- 1:7/q44/p153 Another view identifies them as believers in earlier scriptures. — MAWARDI reporting unattributed: Another view identifies them as believers in earlier scriptures. [1 notes: MAWARDI(unattributed)]
- 1:7/q44/p154 Waki‘ identifies them as Muslims. — MAWARDI reporting وكيع: Waki‘ identifies them as Muslims. [1 notes: MAWARDI(وكيع)]
- 1:7/q44/p155 Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd identifies them as the Prophet and his Companions. — MAWARDI reporting عبد الرحمن بن زيد: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd identifies them as the Prophet and his Companions. [1 notes: MAWARDI(عبد الرحمن بن زيد)]
- 1:7/q44/p156 One interpretation takes God’s wrath in its familiar sense as anger among people. — MAWARDI reporting unattributed: One interpretation takes God’s wrath in its familiar sense as anger among people. [1 notes: MAWARDI(unattributed)]
- 1:7/q44/p157 One account understands divine anger as the anger known among human beings. — MAWARDI-FULL: One account understands divine anger as the anger known among human beings. [1 notes: MAWARDI-FULL]
- 1:7/q44/p158 Another description of the favored is that they fulfill God's rights without turning aside to secure their own interests. — QUSHAYRI: Another description of the favored is that they fulfill God's rights without turning aside to secure their own interests. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q44/p159 They are also described as purified of their own traces so that they reach God through God. — QUSHAYRI: They are also described as purified of their own traces so that they reach God through God. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q44/p160 The favored preserve proper etiquette in service and remain aware of reverent awe. — QUSHAYRI: The favored preserve proper etiquette in service and remain aware of reverent awe. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q44/p161 The suns of their knowledge do not extinguish the lights of their scrupulousness, and they never neglect a rule of the Law. — QUSHAYRI: The suns of their knowledge do not extinguish the lights of their scrupulousness, and they never neglect a rule of the Law. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q44/p162 Those under wrath forgot divine enabling and closed their eyes to the sight of divine support. — QUSHAYRI: Those under wrath forgot divine enabling and closed their eyes to the sight of divine support. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q44/p163 Those under wrath also neglect the etiquette of service and fall short in fulfilling the conditions of obedience. — QUSHAYRI: Those under wrath also neglect the etiquette of service and fall short in fulfilling the conditions of obedience. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q44/p164 They can also be people cut off in the deserts of absence, scattered by worries through valleys of conjecture. — QUSHAYRI: They can also be people cut off in the deserts of absence, scattered by worries through valleys of conjecture. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q44/p165 The strongest means for the needy is continual seeking of God's aid, expressed through sincere supplication and disavowal of one's own power and ability. — QUSHAYRI: The strongest means for the needy is continual seeking of God's aid, expressed through sincere supplication and disavowal of one's own power and ability. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q44/p166 “Guide us” asks God to remove the darkness of one's states and the shadow of one's striving so that His holiness and generosity become lights by which one finds Him. — QUSHAYRI: “Guide us” asks God to remove the darkness of one's states and the shadow of one's striving so that His holiness and generosity become lights by which one finds Him. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q44/p167 The straight path is proved by Scripture and Sunna; innovation has no authority or route upon it. — QUSHAYRI: The straight path is proved by Scripture and Sunna; innovation has no authority or route upon it. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q44/p168 It is also the path validated by signs of monotheism, witnesses of realization, the early Muslim community, and lessons drawn from evidence. — QUSHAYRI: It is also the path validated by signs of monotheism, witnesses of realization, the early Muslim community, and lessons drawn from evidence. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q44/p169 The path separates its travelers from self-interest and its seekers from claims to personal entitlement. — QUSHAYRI: The path separates its travelers from self-interest and its seekers from claims to personal entitlement. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q44/p170 The path leads to monotheism and lets its traveler witness divine care and generosity, so effort is not mistaken for a claim that reward is owed. — QUSHAYRI: The path leads to monotheism and lets its traveler witness divine care and generosity, so effort is not mistaken for a claim that reward is owed. [1 notes: QUSHAYRI]
- 1:7/q44/p171 A singular indeclinable relative gains case marking in the dual because particles are not dualized, but the plural is again a single form like hāʾulāʾ and remains indeclinable. — WAHIDI-BASIT: A singular indeclinable relative gains case marking in the dual because particles are not dualized, but the plural is again a single form like hāʾulāʾ and remains indeclinable. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT]
- 1:7/q44/p172 God's inʿām is His favor and gift; niʿma is a verbal noun used in place of the infinitive inʿām, as nafaqa stands for infāq. — WAHIDI-BASIT: God's inʿām is His favor and gift; niʿma is a verbal noun used in place of the infinitive inʿām, as nafaqa stands for infāq. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT]
- 1:7/q44/p173 Sībawayh says wāw was added after masculine hāʾ just as alif was added after feminine hāʾ, balancing their added endings. — WAHIDI-BASIT reporting سيبويه: Sībawayh says wāw was added after masculine hāʾ just as alif was added after feminine hāʾ, balancing their added endings. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT(سيبويه)]
- 1:7/q44/p174 Al-Zajjāj says wāw was added to make the faint throat-produced hāʾ clearer with a labial long vowel; the connecting wāw drops in pause and changes to yāʾ after kasra. — WAHIDI-BASIT reporting الزجاج: Al-Zajjāj says wāw was added to make the faint throat-produced hāʾ clearer with a labial long vowel; the connecting wāw drops in pause and changes to yāʾ after kasra. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT(الزجاج)]
- 1:7/q44/p175 Warsh lengthens before an open hamza rather than transferring its fatḥa to mīm, which could make the plural resemble the dual; he follows the same pattern before other hamza vowels. — WAHIDI-BASIT: Warsh lengthens before an open hamza rather than transferring its fatḥa to mīm, which could make the plural resemble the dual; he follows the same pattern before other hamza vowels. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT]
- 1:7/q44/p176 Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī pronounce hāʾ and mīm with ḍamma at a following hamzat al-waṣl: mīm returns to its original vowel to break two sukūns, then hāʾ follows it. — WAHIDI-BASIT reporting حمزة والكسائي: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī pronounce hāʾ and mīm with ḍamma at a following hamzat al-waṣl: mīm returns to its original vowel to break two sukūns, then hāʾ follows it. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT(حمزة والكسائي)]
- 1:7/q44/p177 Abū ʿAmr uses kasra for mīm as the usual vowel when breaking two sukūns and also gives hāʾ kasra to avoid a heavy kasra-to-ḍamma transition. — WAHIDI-BASIT reporting أبو عمرو: Abū ʿAmr uses kasra for mīm as the usual vowel when breaking two sukūns and also gives hāʾ kasra to avoid a heavy kasra-to-ḍamma transition. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT(أبو عمرو)]
- 1:7/q44/p178 Readers who keep hāʾ kasra but give mīm ḍamma restore mīm to its original vowel without restoring hāʾ, which was not forced by the context. — WAHIDI-BASIT: Readers who keep hāʾ kasra but give mīm ḍamma restore mīm to its original vowel without restoring hāʾ, which was not forced by the context. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT]
- 1:7/q44/p179 ʿIkrima says God favored them by keeping them firm in faith and steadfast. — WAHIDI-BASIT reporting عكرمة: ʿIkrima says God favored them by keeping them firm in faith and steadfast. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT(عكرمة)]
- 1:7/q44/p180 Ibn al-Sarrāj additionally allows accusative as an implied aʿnī, I mean; al-Khalīl reportedly allowed it as a detached form of praise. — WAHIDI-BASIT reporting ابن السراج: Ibn al-Sarrāj additionally allows accusative as an implied aʿnī, I mean; al-Khalīl reportedly allowed it as a detached form of praise. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT(ابن السراج)]
- 1:7/q44/p181 Apposition differs from an adjective because an indefinite can replace a definite and an expressed noun can replace a pronoun, neither of which is allowed for modifiers. — WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب الحجة: Apposition differs from an adjective because an indefinite can replace a definite and an expressed noun can replace a pronoun, neither of which is allowed for modifiers. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT(صاحب الحجة)]
- 1:7/q44/p182 Apposition also repeats the understood governing case factor, while both apposition and adjective clarify the first noun. — WAHIDI-BASIT reporting صاحب الحجة: Apposition also repeats the understood governing case factor, while both apposition and adjective clarify the first noun. [1 notes: WAHIDI-BASIT(صاحب الحجة)]

- 1:7/q44/p224 Ḥamza reads the pronoun with ḍamma on hāʾ and a quiescent mīm; the other readers use kasra on hāʾ and differ over mīm. — IBNATIYYA reporting حمزة: Ḥamza reads the pronoun with ḍamma on hāʾ and a quiescent mīm; the other readers use kasra on hāʾ and differ over mīm. - 1:7/q44/p226 Reports give Nāfiʿ a choice between mīm with ḍamma and sukūn; since he did not object to ḍamma, the author infers his own reading used sukūn. — IBNATIYYA reporting نافع: Reports give Nāfiʿ a choice between mīm with ḍamma and sukūn; since he did not object to ḍamma, the author infers his own reading used sukūn. - 1:7/q44/p233 He says hāʾ varies between kasra and ḍamma only when preceded by kasra or a quiescent yāʾ; otherwise hāʾ is ḍamma. — IBNATIYYA reporting أبو بكر أحمد بن موسى: He says hāʾ varies between kasra and ḍamma only when preceded by kasra or a quiescent yāʾ; otherwise hāʾ is ḍamma.
